Once, for example, I came home with a book I had been looking for for ages. I had taken a picture of it in the shop, then decided not to send it. I knew what the reply would be: great, you finally found it. Then the conversation would return to someone at her office who had spoken to her in an unpleasant tone.

She knew I liked to read. She had even bought me books. But when I wanted to tell her about something I had found in one, I felt as though I was prolonging a visit after the host had started washing the dishes.

There was also a night when I told her that something she had said had hurt me. Twenty minutes later, I was comforting her because she felt she was a terrible partner. I still remember that shift, though I could not tell you which sentence had moved us from one position to the other.
The next morning, I bought her breakfast.
Sinta once asked what I had hoped for when I did that.
“For her to have a better day.”
“And your day?”
At the time, I answered by explaining the breakfast place: close to her house, good porridge, hardly any wait. Sinta let me finish. Only afterwards did I hear her question.

My job had taught me to believe that things could be fixed if we could find the part that wasn't working. At the shipyard, I put together procedures for requesting materials and brought together people who each thought their part of a job was finished. Sometimes a signature sat waiting for four days because everyone was waiting for everyone else. Sometimes a perfectly good procedure was useless because the forms were in a locked cupboard and the person with the key was on leave.
There was a small satisfaction in getting things like that moving again.

I brought the habit home. If someone was angry, I looked for a reason. If she was disappointed, I examined what I could have done better. I did not always succeed, but I rarely stopped trying. That quality used to make me feel safe. As long as there was still something I could fix, I had a reason to believe it wasn't over.
“I used to think that if I did my best, people would stay,” I told Sinta.
She did not rush to answer. Earlier, in the car park, someone had moved a plant pot to let a car through. I remembered the movement without knowing why.
“You've been thinking about that again?”
“Yes. But this time was different.”

I looked at my hands. There was a thin scratch across a knuckle from the edge of a cardboard box. That morning, I had cleared out a cupboard, something I had been planning to do for three weeks. I found receipts, cables that no longer fitted anything, and a button I left at the bottom of a drawer, though I could no longer remember which shirt it came from.
“What was different?”
“I don't feel like I was lied to.”
The words made the room feel larger, and somehow harder to sit in.

Outside, it began to rain. At first I could hear it only on the metal surface below the window; then the sound spread. I have always liked the first few minutes of rain when I am indoors. Something shifts in the air, as though the whole city has just been given a reason to lower its voice.
“What's been hardest today?” Sinta asked.
I had prepared an answer about sleep, work, and the habit of checking my phone. Instead, I remembered a glass mug.

At home, I have a mug with a handle too small for two fingers. You once said its designer had clearly never used it. Ever since, whenever I pick it up, I think of a mug designer who drinks only from bowls.
That morning, the thought had made me laugh to myself.
Then I sat on the kitchen floor for quite a while.
“There are still things I want to tell her,” I said.
“Things you want to share with her?”
I nodded.
“Nothing big. A cat got into the meeting room this morning. Everyone went quiet, waiting for it to decide which way to leave. In the end, the director opened the door.”
Sinta smiled. I smiled too, and somewhere in the middle of that smile, something caught behind my nose.
“I know it sounds small.”
“You wanted to tell her before the meeting was even over?”
I nodded again.

The rain made the window behind Sinta look as though someone had stopped halfway through washing it. Below it, beside the shelves, stood a plant with one yellowing leaf. I could not remember whether it had been at the old office too. I wanted to ask, then decided I didn't need to.
“I still like those things too,” I said. “The idea of meeting someone by chance. Before you know it, you've been talking for hours. Before you know it, the journey home feels too short.”
“Do you feel you should have stopped liking them?”
I looked at the dented tissue box.
“People say not to expect too much.”
“And what do you think?”

I had no answer that would sound reassuring. I still wanted the same things, only now I knew what it felt like when there was nowhere left to put them. Knowing that did not make the wanting go away. Sometimes it only made it more specific.

I did not picture a long journey somewhere. I pictured a day with nothing to celebrate. Someone cutting fruit in the kitchen. Me bringing unfinished work to the dining table. Neither of us making the day special for the other, but when one of us looked up, the other would still be there.
I told Sinta some of this. Not all of it. Some sentences sound too much like a plea when spoken in a brightly lit room.
“I still want that,” I said.
Sinta nodded, without smiling as though I had just found the right answer.

Near the end of the session, she asked whether I would like to come back the following week. I opened my calendar and looked at the days filled with little boxes. Meetings, a service appointment, a friend's birthday I had almost forgotten. Thursday had an empty space in the afternoon.
I chose Wednesday.
Outside her office was a long bench. A woman was straightening the lid of her child's water bottle. The child was looking at my wet shoes.
“Is it raining hard?” the child asked.
“Fairly hard.”
The child pulled both feet onto the bench, preparing for something that had not yet arrived.

I waited near the building's entrance. The smell of earth rose from the courtyard with the cool air. My phone was in my pocket. For a while I could feel its shape very clearly, a small rectangle I did not have to do anything with.
Then I took it out, opened my notes, and wrote about the cat in the meeting room.
I did not send it anywhere.

chapters.title: Nara — The Same Page
body: On the form she had to fill in before seeing Sinta, Nara spent a long time on the emergency contact field. She had her mother, her older sibling, and two friends who would pick up the phone. She just did not know whom she wanted to be the first to hear that something was wrong.
In the end, she put down her sibling's name.

In the waiting room, one leg of the table was shorter than the others. Folded cardboard from a medicine box had been tucked beneath it. The walls were pale blue. Nara liked the colour, but the overhead light made it look a little unwell.

She had arrived twelve minutes early because she was afraid of being late. Now she was afraid of how long those twelve minutes might feel. From the pharmacy downstairs came the voice of someone asking for children's cough medicine. Nara opened the book she had brought and read the same paragraph three times.
When her name was called, she almost apologised for not having finished.

Sinta did not ask Nara to tell her whole life story. Nara had imagined having to do just that, from her childhood to the last message that went unanswered. Instead, they began with sleep and work. Nara helped archive images at a small studio, restoring scans of old photographs and illustrations. She took on other jobs at night: pictures for packaging, invitations, sometimes a family portrait assembled from separate photographs of every family member.
“Do you often work late?” Sinta asked.
“Sometimes. But if I say I'm tired, please don't tell me to quit.”
Sinta looked at her, then smiled a little.
“Do people often say that to you?”
Nara laughed. She had not meant to open with something that sounded confrontational. She was simply too familiar with having to defend something she loved the moment she complained about it.
“I like my work,” she said. “My eyes just don't always agree.”

They talked about working hours, messages she still answered in bed, and her habit of assuming she could borrow tomorrow's energy to finish today's work. The conversation settled her a little. She let her bag slide from her lap to the floor.
“Is there anything else you'd like to talk about?”
Nara looked at the book spines on the shelf.
“I'm afraid I'll start liking someone again.”
Once she had said it, she felt she ought to laugh. Sinta did not laugh with her, but neither did she make it sound like a statement that called for a solemn face.
“Which part frightens you?”
“I get happy too soon.”
“Too soon?”
“Before I know very much. I like the way someone talks, and by the next day I'm already imagining little things.”
“What sort of things?”
Nara rubbed her thumb along a seam in her bag.
“Places he might like to eat. Films I'd want to watch with him. And then, somehow, I suddenly have opinions about how we'd shop for vegetables.”
This time Sinta smiled. Nara felt a little relieved.
“I know. It's a bit far ahead.”
“Do you feel you have to follow through on everything you've imagined?”

Nara thought about it. In her last relationship, there had been a lot she accepted because she still remembered how it had felt at the beginning. She did not know whether the imagined vegetable shopping had anything to do with that. Perhaps it did. Perhaps she had simply spent too long hoping the next explanation would make things add up.
Once she had asked a simple question: were their plans still going ahead?

The answer arrived in three versions over two days. For a while, she thought she must have remembered wrong, until she opened their messages again. Afterwards, it was not only the cancelled plans that upset her. She felt she had been moved from one reality to another without being told.
Nara did not give Sinta every detail. She offered the pieces she could bear to give that day.
“I can take it better when someone says they've changed their mind,” she said. “It hurts. But at least I know where I stand.”
Sinta asked what Nara usually did when she didn't know.
“Guess.”
“And then?”
“Feel embarrassed for being so suspicious. Then apologise.”

Outside the door, footsteps stopped, then moved away again. Nara followed the sound until it faded. Only then did she realise how often her mind did something similar: following what she could not see, hoping to work out where it was going before it was too late.

Sinta did not tell Nara she had to learn to trust again. They talked about questions she could ask, the time it took to see a pattern, and the fact that accepting someone's answer did not have to mean making a decision for the rest of her life.
As the session was drawing to a close, Nara remembered something.
“I still like romantic scenes in films.”
“Yes?”
“I'm afraid all of this is going to mean I have to become more sensible.”
Sinta put down her pen.
“Which parts would you like to keep?”

Nara thought of someone remembering a thing she had said in passing. Someone asking another question after hearing her first answer. She thought of the foolish happiness of a particular name appearing on a screen. Things she could not achieve on her own by improving her sleep schedule.
“A lot of them,” she said.

Afterwards, she stood in the pharmacy and bought ginger sweets she did not need. Outside, it had not yet begun to rain. She had time before the next bus, but did not want to go straight home. There was a pile of work there, and a message from her mother asking whether she had eaten. She had. She simply did not want to explain why her voice would sound a little different if she called.

The café across the road was called Halaman Belakang—the Backyard—though its door faced the street and it had no yard. Nara had noticed the discrepancy from the bus before. That day, she crossed the road.

Near the till stood a shelf of second-hand books. Some were for sale; others had been left there for people to borrow. The rules were written in marker: leave your name and phone number, return when finished. Beneath them, in different handwriting, someone had added that being finished with a book did not necessarily mean reaching the end.
Nara liked the addition. She took a picture, then deleted it because her own reflection showed in the glass.
A server asked where she would like to sit.
“Could I sit by the window?”
“Of course. A bit of rain gets in if it starts coming down. Just let us know.”

Nara ordered hot tea and fried bananas. The bananas arrived first. She ate them while messaging her sibling: i went today. A thumbs-up came back, followed by an offer to pick her up. Nara said not yet.
She opened her book. This time the paragraph moved. A child was looking for someone in an unfamiliar city, and Nara followed the child until the tea in front of her had stopped steaming.
It began to rain as she was about to mark her place.

The server moved a pot from the windowsill. Two people carried their chairs further inside. Outside, motorcyclists pulled over beneath an awning that was too short. Nara moved her bag, but a few drops still reached the edge of her book.

Beside the shelves stood a table with two chairs. A man occupied one of them, looking at a laptop. The chair opposite was empty. There was a socket on the wall, an unopened bottle of water, and a plate of chips that appeared to have been abandoned by the person who had ordered them.
Nara carried her cup over.
“Sorry. Is anyone sitting here?”
The man looked up. It took him a moment to come back from whatever he was doing.
“No. Go ahead.”
“The rain's getting in over there.”
“Oh.” He looked at the window, as though the rain had only begun when she mentioned it. “Yes, of course.”
He lifted his bag off the chair and tucked it under the table instead of putting it on another seat. Nara sat down. She thanked him, and he nodded.
They returned to their own things.

Outside, a drain overflowed. A sandal floated several metres down the road, chased by its owner, who was laughing while shouting at someone behind him. Nara turned. The man opposite turned too. They watched the sandal get caught near a pole.
“Lucky,” the man said.
“Yes. Hard to get home with just one.”
He nodded with a seriousness that almost made her laugh.

Then they were quiet again. No questions about names, what had brought them there, or their plans for later. Nara could hear the pages of her book between the sounds of rain. For a while, she did not think about whether her face looked friendly.

chapters.title: Sinta — The Door That Never Quite Closed
body: Tegar had already started packing his books when I came home. He was crouched in the living room on knees he would complain about later, though not yet. On the floor lay dictionaries, family albums, and a book about birds I had spent years imagining he had once read.
“Is this coming?” he asked, holding it up.
“That's up to you.”
“I'm asking because you usually have a reason not to throw something away.”

I put down my bag. There was rice in the cooker and fish on the table, covered with a plate. Tegar had eaten. I saw a trace of sambal on a small dish in the sink and felt grateful and guilty in a very ordinary way.
“You don't have to throw it away. We could give it to someone.”
“That's a reason too.”

He smiled. I did not smile back immediately because I was struggling with a knot in my shoelaces. Once I had freed it, I sat at the dining table and suddenly felt as though every sentence from the day was still inside my body.

We were getting ready to move house. The landlord of my office had also decided not to renew the lease, so within the same few months I had to decide what to bring from two different places. Tegar saw this as a chance to get rid of things. I saw it as extra work with the word chance attached to the front.

The blue chair at the office needed repairing. One of its springs made a noise whenever someone shifted. I once asked a client whether it bothered them. They said no, then spent the rest of the session sitting very straight. After that, I stopped making other people bear the responsibility for the chair.
I saved a furniture repairer's number on my phone. I had not called it yet.
“Eat first,” Tegar said.
“In a minute.”
“I've been hearing your stomach for a while now.”
“That might be yours.”

He patted his own stomach to test it, then went back to packing. I laughed. In thirty years together, we had left many arguments improperly resolved and repeated many jokes that had not improved with age. That night, I was glad to hear one of them.
I ate while looking at the inventory. Tegar had labelled every box. One read THINGS SINTA WILL LOOK FOR AFTER WE MOVE. Underneath, he had added DO NOT PUT AT THE BOTTOM.
“What's in it?”
“If I tell you now, you'll unpack it.”
“Not my workbooks.”
“No.”
“Not the files, is it?”
He looked at me, no longer smiling.
“I know.”

I nodded. I never kept client files among our household things. There was a separate cabinet and a separate job involved in moving them. I still felt the need to ask him things he already knew, especially when I was tired. Tegar had a similar habit, just with different things: the stove, the back door, whether the tax bill had been paid.

After eating, I helped dust the books. From the backyard, I heard a neighbour drawing water. Several houses in our lane had low water pressure whenever everyone used the taps at once. For years, that sound had told me what time of night it was better than the clock on the wall.
“Are you sad about moving?” Tegar asked.
“A little.”
“Me too.”
“But you seem excited.”
“I can be both.”
I held the book I had just wiped for longer than necessary.

At work, I often listened to people waiting until their feelings could fit into a single sentence. They wanted to know whether a relationship was good or bad, whether they were ready or not, whether they wanted to stay or leave. Sometimes those questions really did require a decision. Sometimes a person simply needed a few minutes in which nobody demanded consistency.
Remembering this did not always make me easier to live with.

Once, when Tegar was worried about the cost of moving, I explained all the reasons we could afford it. I showed him our records, added up the money, listed the jobs we could put off. He listened until I finished, then said he had actually wanted me to sit with him in his worry for a while.
I was annoyed because I should have understood without being told.
Tegar was more annoyed because I was busy being annoyed with myself when he was trying to talk to me.
It took us two days and a trip to buy drinking water to return to that conversation.

That night, he handed me the bird book. Inside it was a dried leaf neither of us remembered putting there. Its shape was still intact, but the green had long since gone. Tegar picked it up with two fingers.
“If this comes with us, don't take that to mean we're collecting rubbish again.”
“We could keep it in the book.”
“There you go.”
He looked at me as though he had just proved a theory he had held for years. I gave in and smiled.

After he went to bed, I sat at my desk for a while. There were calls to return and appointments to rearrange. Some people would struggle to reach the new address. I would have to discuss it with each of them, give them time, avoid treating the extra distance as a small matter just because the new place suited me better.
I also opened the household notebook where we kept track of expenses. On a blank page, I wrote a question for Tegar: what would you most like to see first when we get there?

I almost crossed it out. It sounded like something designed to be touching. But I did want to know. Tegar had things I had moved from place to place for years without ever asking why he wanted to keep them.
He called from the bedroom.
“Don't turn off the porch light yet.”
“Why?”
“The neighbour's cat is asleep on the mat. So people can see it if they come to the door.”
I went to look. The cat was curled up with its front paws over its nose. There was a muddy mark on the edge of the mat, a little earth it had brought from somewhere.
I stood behind the glass door. Night air came through the gap we could never quite close. Tomorrow I might complain again about the dust that came through it. That night, I let it be.

chapters.title: Nara — The Chair Opposite
body: The man typed three lines, read them, and deleted two. Nara was not watching him. His screen simply reflected in the glass of the bookcase, and the act of erasing something was familiar to her. At the studio, she could spend an hour restoring the corner of a photograph, then decide the original had been better.
The rain had not eased. Water dripped into a bucket near the kitchen. The server came past with a cloth to wipe the floor and asked them to be careful if they went to the toilet.
“You can see my screen, can't you?” the man asked.
Nara startled.
“A little. In the glass. Sorry.”
“It's all right. I'm just checking that this makes no sense from any distance.”
He angled the laptop slightly, not to hide it, but so she would not have to keep looking away. Nara laughed. She pointed to the book in front of her.
“I've been on the same page for a while too.”
“Difficult book?”
“No. My head's still somewhere else.”
The man nodded. He did not ask where. Nara liked that, although she had no reason yet to like anything about him.

They introduced themselves when the server brought an extra order and put it in the wrong place. His name was Arka. He had ordered warm water, but iced tea had arrived. Nara noticed that he said thank you before explaining the mistake.
“I'm not saying you have to do that too,” he said when he saw her smile.
“I haven't said anything.”
“Your face was about to.”
“It was. But I'm polite.”

Arka gave a small laugh, then closed his laptop. He did not make a ceremony of it, as though announcing that Nara now had his undivided attention. His battery was at four per cent. He had left his charger behind.
“I chose a seat by a socket for a reason that turns out not to exist,” he said.
Nara showed him her phone charger. The connector did not fit.
“We tried.”
“We did.”

Outside, spaces were beginning to open between the raindrops. A little afternoon light returned, showing the film of water on the road. Nara could go home. She checked the bus times, then put her phone face down.
Arka asked whether she drew. There was a graphite smudge along the side of her hand and a pencil tucked into her book.
“I mostly remove damage for a living,” Nara said. “Old photographs, scans. Sometimes people want their face from thirty years ago to be clearer than it possibly could have been.”
“Can you do that?”
“You can make it look that way. But there are parts you have to guess.”
Arka considered this. Usually people asked whether she could fix a family photograph, then sent it without telling her how big it was. Instead, Arka asked how she decided when to stop.

Nara explained dust spots, scratches on negatives, wrinkles that were already there when the photograph was taken. Sometimes she had to keep something she could technically remove. A person's face was not a worksheet that needed every mark cleaned off.
She stopped, worried she had gone on too long.
“What if they ask you to take out all the wrinkles?” Arka asked.
Nara laughed and went on.

They only realised how long they had been talking when the server took away the bucket near the kitchen. Outside, the sky had a brief, exhausted brightness, like someone trying to get back to work after crying. Nara opened a ride-hailing app and saw that the fare was still high.
Arka did not offer her a lift. He said his car was at the garage, and he was waiting for prices to come down too. They compared the figures on their screens. They were going in opposite directions.
“Even if we split it, we'd still be going the wrong way,” Nara said.
“True. But we'd get an experience out of it.”
“I've had enough of those.”
Arka nodded solemnly, and then they both laughed.

Before they left, Nara wrote the name of a book on the back of Arka's receipt. A slim book about photographs and memory, with a cover whose colour she could never remember. Arka asked whether he could message her if he couldn't find it.
Nara reached for her phone. The movement was quicker than she had intended. She did not try to slow it down.

On the ride home, she noticed how people had got wet in different places. One man had a soaked left sleeve but a dry head. A small child held a raincoat as though carrying the skin of a creature that had just shed it. Nara wanted to tell someone. She had not messaged Arka yet. It felt too soon to send him a report on a stranger's arm.
Arka sent a photograph of the receipt first.
He had just noticed that the title looked like the name of a skin condition, he wrote. He wanted to make sure he wouldn't say something wrong to a bookseller.
Nara laughed in the back seat. The driver glanced at her in the mirror.

That evening, she finished two jobs. On the third, a patch of a woman's hair could not be made clearer without changing its shape. Nara stopped. She saved the file, turned off the screen, and read the message that had arrived a few minutes earlier.
Arka had found the book online. He had not bought it straight away. He asked whether she thought it was a good book to read in the gaps of an already crowded day.
Nara said there were parts you needed to read slowly.
His reply: that's all right. i'm taking things slowly too.
She did not know whether he meant the book or his life. She did not ask. There was plenty of time before she needed to understand everything he said.

The following week, when Sinta asked how her days had been, Nara told her about work, a small argument with her mother, and the encounter. She mentioned it in an overly casual voice, then laughed when she heard herself trying.
“I don't know what he's like yet,” she said.
“What do you know so far?”
Nara thought about his further questions about her work. The way he had asked for his warm water. The absence of any attempt to get something out of the time they had happened to spend together.
“He can just sit,” she said.
Sinta waited.
“I mean, I can read. He can be quiet. And if there's something to say, we say it.”
“How does that feel for you?”
Nara looked at the small window behind Sinta's chair. All she could see through it was the wall of the next building. There was a water stain on it, a shape that might change before her next visit.
“I'm not in a hurry to go home.”

On the stairs after the session, she opened a message from Arka. He was asking whether she was free the next afternoon. There was a small photography exhibition at the city library. He had checked: free admission, no registration, a car park that wasn't too depressing.
Nara said she would like to go.
Then she added that she might not be very talkative. Work was piling up at the studio.
Arka's reply arrived while she was still standing on the bottom step.
that's fine. the photographs do most of the work at an exhibition anyway.
Nara put her phone away. Outside the pharmacy, the sky was clear. She found herself slightly disappointed that she had no reason to linger across the road.

chapters.title: Arka — What the Photograph Leaves Out
body: There are two sugar jars on my kitchen shelf. One is empty. I bought a new one because the old lid had cracked, then kept the old jar because it could still be used for something. It had been waiting four months to become something.
That morning, I moved it to the cupboard below. Some things only make a house feel cluttered when someone no longer comes over to laugh at them.

You once said my house was full of objects on probation. A stationery box, cables with ends I did not recognise, a T-shirt with a small hole that I only wore to bed. I said they might come in useful. You asked when I was going to start charging them rent.
I never quite knew which part of me would make you laugh. That was one of the things I liked.

The first time we went to an exhibition, I spent too long in front of a photograph of a ship. Not because it was the best photograph. I was looking at the repairs to its hull. You stood beside me, your head slightly tilted.
“Are you working here too?”
“No.”
“Your face says otherwise.”
I tried to explain why the lines along the bottom of the ship looked different. Halfway through, I stopped. You raised an eyebrow.
“What?”
“Too technical.”
“I did ask.”

I went on. You did not pretend to understand every term. When I said something that wasn't clear, you stopped me. At one point, I used a bottle cap to demonstrate a cross-section, and an attendant told us off for sitting too close to the entrance.

Afterwards, you took me over to a family portrait. A child was turning away from the camera and a mother looked as though she had just told the child to keep still. You liked it because nobody had managed to become the person they wanted to show.
“Maybe this is what they actually remember,” you said.
I thought about my own photographs. In so many of them, everything looked fine. I had not told you everything yet. At the time, I did not know how.

We ate at a small place near the library. The plastic table wobbled. You tucked two pieces of paper under one leg, then lifted your plate and announced that we could begin. I asked whether you always fixed things before complaining about them.
“No. Sometimes I complain while I'm fixing them.”

I remember your face as you said it: tired, a little shiny from the heat, quite different from your profile picture, taken on a day with better lighting. I wanted to see that face again. The wish felt simple until I got home and began wondering how to say it without making you feel you had to answer something immediately.
You sent a picture of another table first. The desk in your room, one corner covered in paper.
can't prop this one up. it's my life that's off balance.
I laughed for longer than the joke itself deserved.

At work, I began saving small things for you. A worker who named the photocopier because it would only work if you coaxed it. A meeting about speeding things up that started an hour late. A bird that flew into the workshop and left before anyone managed to photograph it.

You sent things that did not need long replies too. The colour of the sky behind the laundry. An old photograph with a dog at the edge that you had only noticed after working on it for two hours. A packed lunch with no spoon. I liked being the person who knew these things.
One night, you told a friend about my job and sent me your explanation: he makes sure people know whose turn it is to do something.
“That's a pretty good way of putting it,” I said on the phone.
“I left out the people who still won't do it.”
“That's the advanced part.”

You laughed. I was sitting on the floor with my back against the bed. A motorbike went past outside, its exhaust so loud that we stopped talking. When the sound faded, you did not immediately pick up your story. Neither did I.
I remember the sound of your fan. Every so often, something was set down on a table. You were cleaning your brushes. I was folding a T-shirt that had been in my lap for half an hour.
“Still there?” you asked.
“Yes.”
“Just checking. Carry on.”
I folded the T-shirt. Several minutes passed without producing a conversation, but I did not feel as though I was waiting for the call to end.
When I told Sinta, I almost made it sound like a great discovery. Then I saw her reaching for her cup and realised how ordinary it must have looked from the outside.
“I could fold my clothes,” I said at last.
“While you were on the phone?”
“Yes.”
She waited. I laughed because I could find no better way of getting to what I meant.
“I didn't feel I had to think of something to say.”
“Would you like more time like that?”
I nodded.

In the new office, afternoon light fell across the legs of the chair. I sometimes forgot that the window was in a different place. There were moments when I turned the wrong way to look at the weather. Sinta once said she still did that too.

That day, we talked about my habit of putting off meals until I had finished work. She asked whether I ever thought of rest as something I had to earn. I answered with a story about deadlines, then stopped because I realised I was doing something I had done before: giving a good explanation in answer to a different question.
“I find it hard to stop when people are still waiting,” I said.
“What if it's your own body that's waiting?”
I looked at the clock. There were six minutes left in the session. I had been hungry for some time and felt ashamed to admit it, as though hunger proved I was not taking my life seriously enough.
Sinta asked whether we needed to pause. I said no, then corrected myself.
“Maybe we do.”

She nodded. I took some biscuits from my bag. The packet was too loud in the quiet room. I laughed, and Sinta smiled too, and for a little while the most important thing in my life was eating two biscuits without dropping crumbs on the chair.
After the session, I walked to the place where we had eaten. It had been repainted. The wobbly table was gone. The owner did not recognise me, or perhaps saw no reason to show it.

I ordered the same food, then changed my mind because I realised I didn't want it. The server rewrote the order without objection. I sat near the door and listened to someone on the phone ordering food for an entire household.
A small child came in carrying a plastic bag and asked if Mum could pay tomorrow. The owner nodded and added two extra pieces of tempeh, all the while scolding an employee about the unswept floor.
I wanted to tell you that too.
After eating, I opened my notebook. There were expenses, shopping lists, and a few sentences I had not moved anywhere else. I wrote the date at the top of a page, then stopped.
Through the doorway came the smell of drains, cooking oil, and wet earth. Life kept offering me things to like. I stayed longer than I needed to pay the bill.

chapters.title: Nara — Ninety and Ten
body: Arka arrived with two drinks, one of them wrong. He was already at the studio door when Nara read the label. There was another woman's name on the cup. They looked at each other, and Nara said he seemed to be having a rather busy afternoon.
“I can explain.”
“Of course. I'm listening.”

Arka showed her the order number. The café staff had mixed them up, and he had only checked after crossing the road. Nara tasted the drink. Too sweet, but drinkable. Arka offered to take it back. Nara looked at his work shirt, already damp with sweat.
“Sit down first. Where have you been?”
“The office.”
“I mean after that.”
He named two places. Nara pushed a chair out with her foot.
“Have you eaten?”
Arka looked at her for a moment. Then he said he hadn't.

Nara opened her lunch box. There was rice, an egg, and stir-fried green beans that had gone cold. She divided the food onto the lid, asked a colleague for another spoon, and told Arka to choose the side without a crack.
“I came to bring you a drink,” Arka said.
“Yes. And now you're eating.”

They sat at the back of the studio, near a door opening onto the lane. The smell of frying onions drifted from the kitchen next door. A child was reciting something loudly, corrected by a mother in another room.

Arka told her about a meeting that had gone on longer than it should have. Nara did not understand all the terminology, but she could follow that someone wanted changes without changing how they requested the work. She asked who ended up sorting out the consequences.
“Us, of course.”
“You too?”
“Yes.”

She asked a little more. At first, Arka answered as though giving a work report, then slowly began to complain. Nara listened while picking the chillies out of her green beans. At one point, he stopped and asked whether he was talking too much.
“Not yet,” Nara said. “But if we get as far as the organisational chart, I might need a break.”
Arka laughed. He went on more easily.

They had met several times by then. An exhibition, a stationery shop, a dinner that started late because Nara had not finished work. One afternoon, they actually read. After forty minutes, Arka looked up and said he had only managed seven pages because he kept thinking about something. Nara did not ask what it was until he brought it up himself.

Another night, they tried a question game on Arka's phone. Some questions were funny; others were too large to answer at a café table while the fried chicken went cold. Nara refused to explain the entire meaning of life before eating.
When a question about equality came up, Arka said he preferred to imagine two people giving the best they could.
“Sometimes I've got ninety to give and you've got ten. Tomorrow it might be the other way round.”
Nara nodded, but did not move to the next question.
“I agree. We don't always have the same amount of energy.”
“But?”
“The one giving ninety is still allowed to say they're tired, right?”
Arka looked at her.
“Of course.”
“Sometimes people say that. Then they're surprised when you actually say it.”
She put down her fork. They were not arguing. That was precisely why she wanted to keep going until her words reached the right place.
“I don't want to keep count of who gives more every day,” she said. “I just want either of us to be able to say something hurts without being overruled by whoever has sacrificed more.”
Arka looked at his glass. He moved the straw, already bent.
“Has that happened to you?”
Nara nodded.

She did not tell him the whole story. Some things still felt like opening the door to an old house when someone else was already living in it. She only said she had once been grateful for one thing and hurt by another, and had struggled to explain that neither feeling cancelled the other out.
“I might do that sometimes,” Arka said quietly.
“What do you mean?”
“Feel like I've tried hard, then not understand why the other person still isn't all right.”
Nara looked at him. He did not say it as though offering a reason to be forgiven. He seemed to be looking at something properly for the first time.
“I can do it too,” Nara said. “Sometimes, because I've been honest, I think the other person should be ready to hear it.”
Arka nodded.
Their chicken had gone cold. Nara took a piece, tasted it, and said the problem could have been avoided if the question game had a reminder to eat. Arka made a note on his phone.
“Are you actually writing that down?”
“User feedback.”
Nara laughed until the people at the next table turned to look.

Afterwards, they walked to the car park without hurrying. There were puddles to get around. When a motorbike passed, Arka did not pull her out of the way. He stopped, let her know, and waited for her to choose which side of the road to take. It was too small a gesture to be a reason for liking someone, yet she remembered it in bed that night.
A few days later, Arka messaged to say he was upset and did not yet have the energy to explain it properly.
Nara read it while standing at the till in a convenience store. She paid, carried her shopping outside, and sat on the bench out front before replying.
She asked whether he would like a call or some time alone.
His answer: a call would be good. but i might be quiet.
Nara called from the bench. Nearby, a delivery rider was eating bread while checking an address. She told Arka where she was, then let the sounds of the street into their conversation.
After a few minutes, Arka thanked her.
“I haven't done anything yet.”
“I know.”

Nara did not look for a prettier answer. She watched water fall one drop at a time from the edge of the awning near her shoes. The shopping bag in her lap was growing cold from the milk she had bought.
Then Arka told her about his day. He stopped several times. Nara sometimes asked a question, sometimes simply said she was still listening.

When she got home, she was late to help her mother prepare dinner. Her mother asked where she had been. Nara held up the shopping and said the convenience store, feeling that the answer was true, but incomplete.

That night, Arka asked whether they could meet on Saturday. He wanted to tell her something in person. Nara looked at the message long enough for her mother to ask whether she had another job coming in.
“No,” she said.

In her room, she took out two tops and hung them on her wardrobe door. Both looked as though she had tried too hard. She left them there until morning, because perhaps by then she would feel differently about colour.
Before bed, she wrote in her notebook: i still want to find out.
She read the sentence again. The word forever was nowhere in it. Strangely, that was what gave her the courage to close the book and turn out the light.

chapters.title: Arka — The Way Home
body: I once drove you to a copy shop to print your application. The first machine jammed. The second put a black line across the photograph of your face. The owner said that, for documents like these, we should not expect too much from a machine that had been working since morning.
You looked at the photograph and asked whether the selection committee might take it for an artistic choice.
“They might,” I said. “You look like you have a past.”
“I do have a past.”
“Now it's in your paperwork.”

We laughed among the smell of toner and the piles of paper. You carried a yellow folder with corners softened by rain. I held the umbrella. When the machine was done, you checked every page beneath a flickering light. There was a seriousness in your face that made me want to leave you undisturbed, although I also wanted to know everything.

The programme lasted eighteen months. Image restoration and visual archives, some of it in classrooms, some working directly with institutional collections in another city. You had applied before and not got in. This time, you had told very few people you were trying again.
“It's not that I'd be embarrassed if I didn't get in,” you said. “I'm tired of giving progress reports.”
I understood that better than I expected. Some things are easier to do when every step does not have to become news.
On the way home, you asked whether I thought you could do it. I began listing work you had already completed. You listened until I stopped at a red light.
“I know you're trying to encourage me,” you said. “But right now I just want to be scared for a while.”
I looked at the light. Someone was selling tissues between the cars. A baby slept against the seller's shoulder, its face turned towards the cloth.
“Which part scares you?” I asked.
You leaned your head back. For the first time that afternoon, you were not holding the folder as though it might break if you stopped watching it.

You told me about unfamiliar rooms, about people who seemed to know what they were doing, about the possibility that the work you had always loved would become the place where you felt least capable. I listened. Now and then I had to ask you to repeat something because the traffic swallowed your words.
Outside your house, you did not open the car door straight away. We sat with the air conditioner already switched off. The heat slowly returned.
“Thank you for not saying it'll definitely be easy,” you said.
“I nearly did.”
“I know. I saw you catch yourself.”
You laughed. I wanted something better than my own memory to keep that sound in.

At other times, I did keep too much. Photographs of food, receipts, useless parking tickets, your remarks about little things. Some days, I was afraid my memory would alter something I loved. I collected evidence that it had all existed, exactly as it was.
Sinta once asked what would happen if I did not record it.
“I might forget.”
“And if you forgot?”
I did not answer straight away. From the outside, it sounded like an ordinary question. In my head, it opened a cupboard whose contents fell out one by one.

I had once believed my old relationship would be easier to understand if I could remember every conversation. I saved messages, checked dates, compared what had been said with what happened afterwards. Sometimes it helped me know my memory was not wrong. Sometimes I was simply getting hurt again at a different time of day.
With you, I did not want to be someone who was always collecting things to examine later. But my hand reached for the camera faster than I could decide not to.

One afternoon, you fell asleep in the car. We were coming back from helping move things at the studio. There was dust on the hem of your trousers and a trace of paint near your ear that you had not managed to wash off. I raised my phone, then put it down again.
You woke before we reached your house.
“Was I snoring?”
“A little.”
“Don't save that.”
“There's no recording.”

You looked at me suspiciously, then nodded as though deciding to put your trust in a small government. I laughed. Even now, I remember the dust on your trousers, though there is no photograph I can open to check its colour.

At the next session, Sinta asked what I had been thinking about before coming in. I said I had been calculating distance. Not the distance to her new office. Another distance, one that could be converted into ticket prices and hours of travel but still felt different when spoken aloud.
“What did you work out?”
“It's possible,” I said.
Sinta did not write anything down.
“It can be done,” I repeated. “That doesn't mean it'll be easy.”
“Are you describing the plan, or remembering it?”
I rubbed the scratch on my knuckle. The skin had closed over; only the colour was still different.
“Both.”

A ship was being repaired at work while you waited for the selection results. It had arrived with a reasonable list of defects, but once it was opened up, other problems were found underneath. We had to revise the plan. People complained about the change in schedule. A department head said it was better to find the problems now than to pretend a plate that looked sound on the outside meant everything was fine.
I kept those words. Unfortunately, understanding something at work did not always mean I could use it at home.
The night your acceptance came, I had just got out of the shower. My phone vibrated on top of the cupboard. You had sent a screenshot with one line highlighted. I read it twice, then called.

You were crying and laughing. I laughed too. We spoke over each other, asking again and again whether it was real. You read the letter out. In the background, your mother asked what had happened, and I heard her voice change when you explained.
“I got in,” you said again, more quietly this time.
“You did.”
I sat on the edge of the bed. Water still dripped from my hair onto the collar of my T-shirt. I was so happy that for a while I did not think about you leaving.
Only after the call did I look at the calendar.
The happiness did not go away. Something else came and sat beside it.
I did not tell you straight away.

The next day, I bought a small cake with crooked writing on it. The person behind the counter offered to fix it, but I was afraid of being late to your house. You photographed it close up, trying to find an angle that made it worse.
“So you can see the effort,” you said.

We ate with your mother. She mentioned the money you would need, accommodation, warm clothes. You answered each point, then asked us to stop talking about suitcases until we had finished the cake. Everyone laughed. I can still remember where the spoons lay on the table and how you set aside a piece of cake for your sibling, who was not home yet.
When I was leaving, you walked me to the gate.
“Are you really happy?”
“Very happy.”
“I know. I mean, is there something else too?”
You gave me an opening. I saw it. I even knew how to use it.
“Of course I'll miss you,” I said.
You nodded, waited a moment, then hugged me. I hugged you back. Over your shoulder, I could see a plant pot with fresh soil in it. The damp smell was very close.
I wanted to say I was afraid. But that night, the word afraid felt like something heavy I would be putting into your suitcase. I chose to be someone who did not add to the weight.

Now, in the room with green walls, I can tell all of it in order. Sinta listens. She does not say I should have spoken, as though words that never came out could be called back to serve the life we used to have.
“What did you want to say then?” she asks.
I look at my hands. For a long time, I do not move.
“I'm happy for you,” I say at last. “And I don't know how to do this yet.”
Sinta nods. There is nothing I need to prove at the end of that sentence. I sit and listen to the water the rain has left in the gutter.

chapters.title: Nara — Things to Take Along
body: On the Saturday when Arka wanted to tell her something, Nara arrived with puffy eyes. Not from crying. She had slept too long that afternoon, with a pillow pressed against one side of her face. She messaged him so he would not think something bad had happened.
Arka replied that he had just shaved and now looked like a man regretting a decision.
They met at the same café. Three students dividing up an assignment occupied the table by the shelves. Nara and Arka sat outside, under a light surrounded by small insects.
Arka did not say anything straight away. He asked about her day, listened to her answer, then appeared to forget how to move on to another subject. Nara waited while cutting her cake.
“You said you wanted to talk about something.”
“Yes.”
“If this is an insurance pitch, I have to go.”
Arka laughed with too much relief. Then he put both hands on the table, moved them again, and finally let one hold his glass.
“I like you,” he said.
Nara watched a drop of water run down the glass. She wanted to remember the sentence without making his face any more tense.
“I like you too.”
Arka nodded. A few seconds later, he laughed at himself.
“I had more prepared.”
“You can carry on. I'm not going anywhere.”

He continued more slowly. He wanted to get to know her properly. He did not know everything that would happen, but wanted them to tell each other if something changed. He also said that sometimes he would seem calmer than he really felt.
Nara nodded at the last part.
“Sometimes I ask more than once,” she said. “It's not always because I don't believe you. Sometimes the first answer hasn't quite reached me.”
“That's all right.”
“If you get tired of the questions, tell me.”
“I will.”

They made no other rules that night. Nara had once imagined a more beautiful confession, somewhere quieter, with words uninterrupted by a blender. But when Arka moved the tissues closer to her plate because there were crumbs on her chin, she felt no wish to exchange that evening for a tidier scene.

They began to have routines. Arka messaged when he got to the office, sometimes forgetting and only sending a photograph of lunch. Nara called on her way home from the studio, except when she wanted to listen to music. She told him that, and he learned not to regard music as competition.

Some days, Arka talked for too long about something that excited him. Nara followed as far as she could, then said her head was getting full. The first time it happened, Arka fell silent with an expression that made her regret saying it.
“I still want to hear,” she said. “Just later, all right?”
Arka nodded. That night, he asked whether he often wore her out.
Nara thought before answering. She did not want to reassure him with an answer she would be unable to rely on later.
“Sometimes I'm tired because of my own day. If I say that's enough for now, I want you to believe that's all I'm saying.”

They talked about it again a few days later. No agreement made everything easy at once. But the next time Nara said she could not manage a long explanation that evening, Arka did not ask for more reassurance. He sent a photograph of a page in his book and said he would save it for tomorrow.
The next day, Nara asked him about the page.

One Sunday afternoon, Arka came to her house with another book and a very tired face. He had just helped a friend move. Nara had spread newspaper over the table on the veranda; she was working on an old frame with peeling paint. Arka sat down, offered to help, and yawned halfway through the sentence.
“You can hold this if you like,” Nara said, handing him one side of the frame. “But you don't have to if you're tired.”
Arka held it for a few minutes. Nara sanded the rough patches. Fine dust gathered on the newspaper, and an ant kept returning to a tea stain.
“I'm actually sleepy,” Arka said at last.
Nara looked up.
“Have a nap.”
“Then you'll be on your own.”
“I've been doing all the sanding anyway.”
Arka smiled, but still looked uncertain. Nara pointed to the bench near the door. Her mother often napped there. On it lay a small cushion that was no longer symmetrical.

Arka put down his book, took off his watch, and lay down with his legs slightly bent so his feet would not hang over the end. Nara returned to the frame. Several times, she stopped to blow away the dust, then remembered and blew it in the other direction.
Arka slept for almost half an hour. When he woke, the fabric had left lines on his cheek. He looked at his watch and immediately sat up.
“Sorry.”
“What for?”
“That was quite a while.”
Nara handed him the small mirror she was going to put in the frame. Arka looked at his cheek and laughed. Nara said he had an extra pattern now, to match the tablecloth.

Her mother came out with fruit. She handed Arka a plate without commenting on the fact that he had just slept at their house. The three of them ate and talked about the vegetable seller, who had started coming earlier. Arka answered a few questions, then listened.

When he was about to leave, he picked up the book he had not read. Nara was still wiping the frame. No important conversation had been concluded that afternoon. Arka asked whether he could see it once the mirror was in.
“Of course,” Nara said. “Just don't fall asleep when I show you.”
He laughed, raised a hand to say goodbye, and walked to the gate. Nara watched the pillow marks on his cheek, which had not quite faded.

There was also their first argument. Arka cancelled a date because he had to work, but only told Nara after she had finished getting ready. Nara was angry. Arka apologised, then began explaining everything that was happening at the office. The more detailed the explanation became, the more she felt she was being asked to conclude that she had no right to be disappointed.
“I understand that you have to work,” she said. “I just needed to know sooner.”
Arka stopped. He looked at the clothes she had put on and the bag waiting by the door.
“You're right. I should have told you when it started looking like I wouldn't finish in time.”
Nara was still upset. They did not immediately hug. Arka left; Nara took off her shoes, then sat with her hair carefully done for something that was no longer going to happen.
She felt guilty for being angry, then angry for feeling guilty. Towards evening, she messaged to say she was still upset, but wanted to know whether he had eaten.
Arka said he had. Then he asked whether he could come over the next day, after she finished work. Not to replace that evening as though it had never been cancelled. He simply wanted to see her.
Nara said he could.
She told Sinta about the argument. When she asked whether she was being too demanding, Sinta asked her to repeat what she had actually requested. Nara heard her own words and fell quiet.
“I'm afraid that if I get angry, people won't want to tell me things,” she said.
“How did Arka respond afterwards?”
“He came over. He was still a bit awkward. So was I.”
“And then?”
“We bought food. Afterwards, he asked what time I'd actually been ready.”

Sinta nodded. She did not give their relationship a score. Nara went home feeling she could pay attention to what happened after a difficult conversation without having to decide immediately that everything was safe or about to fall apart.

In the months that followed, Arka's name became part of life at home. Her mother set aside food when she knew he was coming. Her sibling borrowed tools from him and was slow to return them. Nara began to recognise the sound of his car before the message saying he had arrived.

Sometimes they sat on the veranda with their own work. Nara drew; Arka read. There were mosquitoes, the neighbour's television, her mother calling for help bringing in the laundry. Nara liked the incompleteness of it. They did not have to shut out the whole world to feel close.
One night, Arka asked whether she believed in serendipity.
“I believe people can meet by chance,” Nara said.
“I mean the kind in films.”

Arka described bookshops, hands reaching for the same book, the feeling that something had been waiting there for them. Nara looked at the shoe rack by the door and tried to imagine him doing that without first apologising for being in somebody's way.
She laughed. Arka covered his face for a moment.
“I know.”
“I'm not saying it's bad. I just think you'd say, go on, you take it.”
“Maybe.”
“And then go home.”
“Maybe there wouldn't be a story.”
Nara rested her head on his shoulder. She said she still liked the idea of a love that felt like coming home. She knew the phrase had been used too often. She still wanted to know what it felt like.
Arka did not say he would be that home. He asked which part she imagined most.
“Being allowed to be a bit ugly,” she said.
“Ugly how?”
“Tired. Irritable. Uninteresting. And still being allowed to sit in the same place the next day.”
Arka was quiet for a long time. Nara lifted her head to look at him.
“I like that,” he said.

When the acceptance letter arrived, all those routines were still new, yet already hard to imagine living without. Nara read the letter again and again. She wanted very much to go. The wish had existed before she knew Arka, through days when nobody asked how her application was going.
That same night, she wanted to see him too. The two wishes refused to take turns.

A few weeks before leaving, she brought her suitcase into the living room. Her mother packed a towel that was too thick. Her sibling contributed an extension cable. Arka arrived with a luggage scale, then helped weigh the case until they had to remove two books and some of the snacks.
Nara kept one book she had been reading since the day they met.
“How far have you got?” Arka asked.
She opened it at the bookmark. He laughed.
“You haven't got very far.”
“I've been busy.”
“I feel accused.”
Nara threw a T-shirt at him. It fell short, making them laugh harder.

But after the house grew quiet and everyone went to bed, Nara sat in front of her suitcase. There were clothes for weather she had never experienced, documents, medicine, and small objects that looked strange once she had to choose them from everything in her room.
She picked up her phone and typed: i'm so happy. i'm scared too.
Arka replied: i'm here.
Nara looked at the answer. She wanted his voice, but it was past midnight. She almost wrote never mind, tomorrow's fine. Then she deleted it and asked whether she could call for ten minutes.
Arka called first.

They did not spend the whole time talking about the future. Arka complained about a gecko that kept hiding behind the wall clock. Nara told him about her new socks, all too small in the same place. They talked about trivial things until she could touch the suitcase without feeling something press against her chest.
“Are you sleepy?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“Get some sleep.”
“You too.”
They said goodnight, then did not hang up straight away. Nara heard him shift something on the bed. She waited for one more breath, then ended the call.
In the quiet room, she returned to her packing. She slipped the book between her clothes, where she thought it would be safest from knocks. The bookmark stuck out a little.

chapters.title: Sinta — Two Years at One Table
body: In September, when we had been in the new house for almost a year, Tegar found the leaf from the bird book in a folder of bills. I did not know how it had got there. Tegar accused me of rescuing it twice. I pointed out that he had not thrown it away when he found it either.
“I'm giving you a chance to decide,” he said.
“That's a lot of time to decide.”
He set the leaf on the windowsill. A few days later, it was gone. Perhaps the wind had taken it; perhaps we had swept it away while cleaning. Neither of us looked for it.

The blue chair from the old office did not come with us. The furniture repairer said fixing it would cost almost as much as buying a new one. I gave it to the manager of a tutoring centre near the pharmacy, who said a relative could replace the spring. People in my office now sat in grey chairs. Sometimes I still thought of the person who had sat so straight to keep the old chair from making a sound.

On Wednesday afternoon, Arka came for his third session since getting back in touch. His first appointment with me was on record from the year before last, when the pharmacy building still had a red sign and his story came in fragments. Back then, we talked about his old relationship, things he no longer wanted to accept, and the difficulty of knowing when enough was enough.
After a few months, he stopped coming. We discussed the decision, including how he could contact me again if he needed to. He did not promise he would always be all right. I did not ask him to.
Now he was back. His weight had changed a little, and he carried a black notebook. He did not bring it to every appointment. That day it rested in his lap, held in both hands.
He talked about someone he had not seen in several months.
“I've been writing as though she's still sitting in front of me,” he said.
I asked whether he would like to read something aloud. He shook his head, then opened the notebook for himself. From my chair, I could not see the writing. I did not try to.
“I read some parts and I seem like such a good person.”
“How do you feel when you read them?”
“Suspicious.”
He smiled faintly. I waited.
“I don't mean I'm making things up. But I get to choose which parts I write down.”

We talked about a trip he had made when he was very tired. He said he had wanted to surprise her. In the end, he arrived with a body that could barely manage to be there. He slept through most of the day, woke with a headache, and felt offended because he thought she did not understand what it had taken to come.
“Even though she'd told me not to come yet if I still had work to finish,” he said.
“What did you need when you decided to go?”
Arka looked at the notebook in his lap.
“To see her. For her to know I still wanted to.”
“Did you tell her the second part?”
He shook his head.
“I thought coming would make it obvious.”
Outside, a cleaner moved a bucket. Water ran through a pipe close to the window. Arka followed the sound for a moment, then said the woman's name.
Nara.

I had heard that name in another room, on Thursdays that still carried the smell of medicine from downstairs. A woman who held her bag in her lap, then slowly lowered it. She worked with old images. In one session, she told me about a man who did not make her feel in a hurry to go home. A few months later, she brought news of her acceptance into a programme in another city.

There were enough similarities to make me careful, no reason to add knowledge that had not been given to me. I did not ask for a surname, an address, or whether the man Nara meant was someone who had once come to see me. I did not need that certainty to listen to her.

Nara ended our sessions before she left. We talked about support she might need in the new place and the options she could look for there. On the last day, she said she was afraid people would think she loved something less because she still wanted to leave.
That was at the end of last year.
This afternoon, Arka was telling me what happened after the suitcase reached another city.
I looked at him. He did not know that I had also seen part of the beginning from another direction. I had no right to make that part of this conversation.
“I used to think that if I found a better relationship, I'd be easier to live with,” he said.
“What did you find?”
He breathed out and looked at the window.
“Still me.”
He laughed briefly. I let the laugh finish.
“Some things were easier,” he went on. “I could speak up. A lot of the time, I was heard. But sometimes, because she was kind, I wanted even less to make things difficult for her.”
I asked what he imagined would happen if he told her he was struggling. He said he did not know. Perhaps Nara would worry, feel guilty, change something that mattered to her.
“You were trying to protect her choices.”
“Yes.”
“And what did she know when she made those choices?”
Arka closed the notebook. His hand stayed on the cover, pressing just enough to bend its edge.
“What I'd told her I could manage.”
He said it without using the sentence to beat himself with. At least that day, he could do that. I waited when he needed time before going on.

Before the session ended, Arka took a slip of paper from between the pages. A ticket or receipt; I could not see clearly. He said there was a date he kept reading, as though finding the right sequence would tell him the day things had begun to get difficult.
“Have you found it?” I asked.
“It's different every time.”
I nodded. He put the paper back.

After he left, I made the notes I needed for our next meeting. I closed his file before opening the schedule. There were two more people that day, each arriving with a life I must not treat as a continuation of the one before.

That evening, Tegar waited in the kitchen with two plates. He had warmed the food. There was a possibility of his teaching a few hours at his old workplace, adding to a schedule that was now less full. He wanted to try, but worried I would feel that all the housework was falling to me again.
I almost said it was fine. The words had reached my mouth. Then I put down my bag, pulled out a chair, and asked what time he would get home.
We went through the days. Two would be awkward. We named them one by one, moved what could be moved, and left one problem unresolved because the rice was getting cold.
“I'm glad you still want to do it,” I said.
Tegar looked at me.
“I'm afraid of getting tired too,” I added.
He nodded. Neither sentence seemed to wound anyone, though neither was easy to say.

After dinner, he washed the dishes and I dried them. In the new house, the kitchen window faced a wall. I still missed the sound of the neighbour drawing water. Tegar said we could put a small radio there. I said I did not miss sound in general. I missed a particular sound.
He stopped rinsing a plate.
“Yes,” he said. “Me too.”

A few weeks later, Nara contacted the practice through the administrative number. She would be home for a short visit and wanted an appointment. I read her request among the other things I needed to answer. She asked for Thursday, if it was still available.
I checked the calendar. There was room in the afternoon.

On the screen, her name stood beside a complete date: day, month, year. I remembered the blue chair, the book she had brought the first time, and what she had said about liking someone again. But when she came, I would need to ask where she wanted to begin.
There was a great deal she had never told me.

chapters.title: Arka — What We Didn't Say at the Airport
body: We managed to argue about breakfast on the morning you left. You weren't hungry. I worried about the long journey, your empty stomach, not knowing when you would eat. You said you could buy something after security. I still brought the bread from the car.
“I know you're worried,” you said outside departures. “But please don't make me eat right now.”
I stopped. The bread was in my hand, a little warm from being held too long.
“Okay.”
You looked at my face, then touched my arm.
“Can I take it with me?”
“Of course.”

I put it in the front pocket of your bag. We did not immediately become cheerful. Your mother was still holding a tissue, your sibling kept checking the departure board, and the announcements made every conversation feel as though it had to be finished at once.
You hugged me. I could feel the strap of your bag pressing between us. I wanted to say many things, but what came out was a request to let me know when you arrived.
“I will,” you said.

You walked through the doors, looked back, and raised a hand. I raised mine. It was a gesture I made to other people all the time. That day, I did not understand how something so ordinary could feel so inadequate.

On the way home, I stopped to buy myself breakfast. The place was crowded. A man complained that he had been given the wrong order. I stood with a queue number and my phone in my hands, feeling it had been too long since I heard from you when your plane had not even taken off.
That afternoon, you sent a photograph of the bread, its wrapping open. You were eating it in a seat near the next departure gate.
turns out it's quite nice when nobody makes you eat it.
I laughed. Until that evening, the sentence was enough to make me feel we would be able to learn it all.

At first, the distance made us diligent. You sent photographs of your room, the route to your classes, a market where the price of fruit made you suspicious. I sent news from work, stories about my mother, a dog asleep outside a shop that made people open the door slowly. There was a new curiosity, because your days now took place somewhere I had never seen.

We watched a film at almost the same time. The sound was a few seconds out of sync, and you asked me not to laugh before you did. Other evenings, we left the call open while you worked on assignments and I read. Sometimes the connection dropped. We called back without taking it as a sign.

Then the work grew. You had to spend longer in the lab. I was given responsibilities I had wanted for a long time and discovered they came with meetings I had never imagined. We still liked each other. We also began to find each other at hours when neither body had much left to offer in conversation.

The first time I visited, it all felt manageable. We ate near your place, walked until my feet blistered, and fell asleep too early after planning to talk about so many things. The next morning, you brought me water before I asked. I still remember the happiness of seeing my toothbrush beside yours, two objects finally no longer in different cities.

The second visit was harder. You had an assignment you could not leave. I said it was fine, then waited in a guesthouse room with an air conditioner that blew too hard. I opened my laptop and tried to work, but kept checking the time.
When you arrived, you brought food and a tired face. I tried to hide my disappointment. You recognised it, asked, and I said I was just tired from the journey.

That night, we ate on the bed because there was no table big enough. Sauce spilled onto the sheet. We laughed while trying to clean it with tissues that immediately fell apart. Then you fell asleep with your head on my shoulder. There was one very good hour in the middle of a weekend that had not gone as I planned.

I did not know how to judge something so mixed. I wanted to say I had enjoyed the visit. I also wanted to say I had been lonely in the room before you came. I felt the second sentence would take something away from the first.

The third visit came after a bad week at the office. You told me to put it off because I had barely slept. I said I had already bought the ticket. In fact, I could still change it for an extra fee. I chose not to mention that.
I arrived with a headache and barely spoke on the drive from the airport. You asked whether I was angry. I said no. By the third time you asked, I really was annoyed, and you went quiet.

In the room, I slept. When I woke, you had set out food and were working at the small desk by the window. A pencil was tucked into your hair. For a few seconds, before I remembered that I wanted to be understood, I was very happy to see you.
We only talked after eating. You said you were worried. I said I had made the effort to come. We spoke as though the two statements contradicted each other.
“I didn't ask you to push yourself this hard,” you said.
“I know.”
“But you look as though I'm the one making you do it.”
I was about to deny it. Then I looked at my bag, still unpacked. Part of me wanted my coming to answer every question about love, including those you had not asked.
“I just wanted to see you,” I said.
“So did I.”
You sat on the edge of the bed. We were less than a metre apart after travelling so far. I did not know how to move closer without first feeling I had to repair what I had said.

The next morning, we had breakfast somewhere that served watery porridge. You passed me the soy sauce. I asked about your assignment. We could still do kind things for each other. Sometimes I think that was precisely why it took me so long to admit the difficult parts.

After I got home, I sent a breakdown of expenses I did not really need to send. I was not asking to be paid back. I wanted us to talk honestly about the cost of visiting. But I was late. The figures showed you a burden I had not told you about, including the times you offered to contribute and I said I had it all covered.
You called that night.
“I didn't know,” you said.
“I'm the one who said it was fine.”
“Yes. So what am I supposed to believe next time?”
I sat in a kitchen chair. A spoon fell in the house next door.
“I don't understand my limits yet,” I said.
“I want to help you understand them too. But I need to know before you've already gone past them.”

We made a new plan. Fewer visits. Costs divided according to what we could afford, without the person giving less having to make up for it by always being available. Two nights for calls, which could be changed as long as we let each other know. We wrote it down and laughed at how administrative it looked.
For a few weeks, the plan worked.

Then your mother needed you home for a family matter, the studio held up payment for some of your earlier work, and your programme's schedule changed. At my office, an inspection needed more preparation than expected. None of these events was extraordinary. They were all ordinary enough that none could be blamed as the single cause.
On the night we finally chose to talk, I had just got home and you were still in your work clothes. We had both eaten, having deliberately made sure our bodies would not have to bear one more thing.
You said you still loved me.
I said the same.
Then there was a silence different from the nights when we folded clothes. I listened to your breathing, unsure whether to fill the space or let you go on.
“I don't know how to keep doing this and still be myself,” you said at last.

I wanted to say we could try again. We had already tried several things. Some worked; some showed us how much would have to change. I still wanted to. But when I asked myself what we were trying to hold on to that day, I could find no answer that did not ask something you could not yet promise.
You also asked whether I truly still wanted this kind of relationship, or whether I was afraid to stop trying.
For a moment, I was angry. The question seemed to diminish everything I had done. Then you said you were not deciding the answer for me.
“I just don't want us to stay because we'd be ashamed to let all that effort go.”
I turned off my camera for a few minutes. First, I told you I needed time, that I was not leaving the conversation. You said you were still there.

I stood in the kitchen, drank some water, washed a glass that was already clean. When I came back, your face was still on the screen. I cried, unable to explain whether I was losing you or finally giving up the effort of holding something together alone inside my head.

We did not decide on that first call. There were three more conversations over two weeks, one very short because you could not manage it that day. We talked about whether taking a break meant the same thing to both of us. We talked about hopes that could become duties if we were not careful.
In the end, we stopped being a couple. Neither of us asked the other to wait. The sentence is easy to write now. On the night I said it, I had to stop several times to get through the syllables.

After the final call, I sat in the same chair until my back hurt. There was cut fruit on the table. I ate it because it would spoil otherwise. As I chewed, I hated the fact that my body still needed simple things.

A few weeks later, I almost contacted you on your sibling's birthday, simply because I remembered. I closed the conversation without typing. I was learning that remembering something did not always mean someone needed to know.

Sinta did not tell me I had to forget you. We talked about the days I still had to live, friends I could call, work I could put off. In one session, I said I was afraid this story proved there was no point in trying to become better.
Sinta asked what was different about the way I was going through this separation.

I thought about turning off the camera after telling you. About crying without having to turn it into an apology. The three conversations after that night. I thought about how you had heard my anger and still come back to answer my questions, even when the answers were not always what I wanted.
“I got to have a say,” I said.
My voice stopped there. I needed to take a tissue and wait before going on. There was something very tender in realising that I had lost someone without losing my right to be part of the story.

At home, I opened the black notebook. On the first page was a list of places I wanted to go with you. Some were crossed out. I had added others after we stopped speaking, not because I was planning anything, but because my mind still moved towards you before I could redirect it.
Above the list, in handwriting more eager than any of the entries that followed, was a title I had written when we first grew close: things that haven't happened yet.
I did not tear out the page.

I turned to a new one and wrote down what I had eaten that day. There was also a story about a friend learning to swim at thirty-two. He had invited me along. I had not answered yet, but I had already looked for my swimming shorts in the cupboard below.

chapters.title: Nara — News from Far Away
body: By the ninth month, Nara could walk from the bus stop to her place without checking a map. She knew the cracked stretch of pavement, the shop with cheaper eggs, and the hours when the shared washing machine was usually free. The city no longer made her feel she was visiting, but it had not quite let her feel at home.

She liked her work. There was one image she spent eleven days restoring, a portrait of a woman with a child whose face had been damaged by water. They could not bring all of it back. Her supervisor asked her to preserve the missing parts rather than draw them in from guesswork. At a small exhibition of their work, Nara stood near the image and heard someone whisper that the damage felt important.
She wanted to say the damage had not asked to be important. It was simply there. But the person had already moved on to another picture.

That night, she ate with two friends from the programme. One was celebrating good news; the other was considering going home early. They sat in a narrow café with mismatched plates. Nara laughed until her cheeks hurt. On the way home, she picked up her phone to tell Arka something, then remembered.
It still happened, that movement. She no longer treated it as an instruction.
