Some days, she was relieved not to have to fit her time around anyone else. On others, she would have traded a whole evening of freedom just to hear someone opening a cupboard at the other end of a call. She did not know how to tell her friends both things without making one sound untrue.
Her sibling once asked whether she regretted it.
Nara said she didn't know yet.
“Do you miss him?”
“Yes.”
“All right. That can be your answer for now.”

Nara cried after the call. Not the kind of crying that leaves you breathless. Tears fell while she was washing her lunch box, mixing with the tap water, and she only noticed when her nose grew blocked. She left the box to soak and sat on the small stool she usually used to reach the cupboards.

Near the window stood a plant a friend had given her. Two leaves were wilting. Nara had moved it three times, looking for the right light. She almost laughed: in the middle of everything she could not put right, she still felt responsible for making the plant comfortable.
She gave it a little water, then stopped so she would not overdo it.

In the weeks after the separation, she had been angry with Arka. She felt she was being asked to read a burden he had deliberately hidden. She was angry with herself too, because on several occasions she had seen the signs and chosen to accept the easiest answer.
In one difficult conversation, Arka said he felt he always had to understand Nara's future, while his own seemed to have been taken for granted as something available to her.

Nara had been about to list all the questions she had asked. She had asked them. But she also remembered a night when Arka began telling her about an opportunity at work that would take up more of his time, and she immediately explained how it would make their schedule harder. She had not yet asked what made him want it.

She called back the next day to tell him that. They still did not find a way through. An apology did not move cities, add money or hours of sleep. Yet Arka sounded different after hearing it, and Nara was glad she had called even though she could not use that conversation to keep everything together.

She kept a few things from the relationship. A pencil, a receipt for a book, a photograph printed on paper that was too glossy. She did not make a special box. They stayed among her other belongings, sometimes turning up when she was looking for something unrelated.

Her favourite photograph had been taken by her mother. Nara and Arka were moving a table. Neither looked at the camera. Arka's cheeks were puffed out as he held his breath; Nara looked angry because her toe was trapped. Behind them, her mother appeared in the mirror, smiling, her phone slightly tilted.

Nara had once wanted to delete it because it was not a good photograph. Arka asked for a copy. Later, she understood what he liked about it: the whole life of the house was there, nobody waiting to be ready.

When her mother said the back roof was leaking again, Nara opened her leave calendar. She had been planning to go home anyway. There were documents to sort out, a meeting with her old studio, and a wish to eat at home without opening a video call. She bought a ticket for ten days.
Then she contacted Sinta's practice.

The address they sent was different. Nara looked at the map, checked the transport, and saved the number. Before bed, she opened her conversation with Arka. Their last messages were not an argument. There was news that some belongings had arrived, a short reply, and a wish to take care.
She did not write that night.

On the flight home, she brought the same book. The bookmark was much further back now, though not yet at the end. Beside her, a child kept asking whether clouds could be eaten. The mother said no the first three times, then, on the fourth, said perhaps if you had a very long spoon.
Nara smiled. She wanted to tell Arka. She let the wish sit beside her until the plane landed.

The house felt smaller than she remembered. Her mother hugged her for too long, then said she was thin, though her weight was almost the same. Her sibling told her to carry her own bag so she would not get too used to being waited on after coming all that way. They laughed. There was food on the table, sandals still in their old place, and a fan that now made a noise on every third turn.
That night, rain woke Nara. Water was falling somewhere it should not. She came out of her room and found her mother moving a bucket under the leak. They did not turn on all the lights.
“Leave it until tomorrow,” her mother said when Nara went to get a cloth.
“The floor's wet.”
“It happens all the time.”

Nara wiped it anyway. Her mother held the bucket. In the kitchen light, the woman's hands looked older than they did on video calls. Nara felt something rise in her throat, something without a single name that she could not put off by calling it jet lag.
Afterwards, they sat at the dining table. Her mother took biscuits from a tin and broke them because they were too hard.
“Are you happy there?”
Nara thought about the restored image, the cracked pavement, her friends, the night on the little stool.
“Often.”
Her mother nodded.
“Good.”
“Sometimes I'm not.”
“It's like that here too.”
Nara laughed, then cried a little. Her mother reached for a tissue without asking questions too quickly. The rain kept falling. They ate biscuits with tea made weak enough to drink without waiting.

On Thursday, Nara went to Sinta's new address. The walls were green. The waiting room was brighter, and there was no longer the sound of people buying medicine downstairs. She sat on the long bench and messaged her mother to say she would be home a little late.
Inside, Sinta asked about her journey. Nara answered, then said she did not know where to begin. Sinta gave her time.
“We broke up,” Nara said at last.
The sentence sounded different spoken in a city that still held their places.

She talked about living away, her relationship with Arka, the things they had tried, the anger she had felt. Sinta listened without making her feel she was being asked to justify a decision already made. When Nara said she feared she had left a good person simply because she could not yet accept the life available to them, Sinta asked how she understood what she had been able to manage at the time.
“I was tired,” Nara said. “But I know tired isn't the answer to everything.”
“What hadn't there been room for?”

Nara looked at the window. She wanted to enjoy her achievements without feeling someone was paying a price she had not been told about. She also wanted a partner who could bring her his difficulties before they became conclusions about their relationship. And she wanted to learn to listen without immediately looking for something she needed to defend.
She said some of this, then stopped. Sinta did not fill in the rest.
“I still like him,” Nara said.
“What would you like to do with that feeling?”
Nara thought. She did not want to use longing as a reason to offer something she could not yet give. Nor did she want to use uncertainty as a reason to keep waiting until there was no risk.
“I want to ask him to meet.”
“What would you hope for from that meeting?”
“Before, I probably would have said I wanted to find out whether we still had a chance.”
“And now?”
She looked at her hands. A small stain of marker ink remained from the studio.
“I want to hear about his life. I want him to be able to say no if he isn't ready.”

On the way home, Nara walked past a bakery. She bought two pieces of bread, one for her mother. At the bus stop, she took out her phone and opened her conversation with Arka. She typed an invitation with a clear day and place. She reread it to make sure she had not slipped in a promise just to make it easier for him to say yes.
She sent the message.
Nara put her phone in her bag. She took it out again less than a minute later, felt foolish, then decided she did not have to be a very calm person to mean what she was doing.
She waited for the bus while eating her bread. Crumbs fell onto the hem of her top. Across the road, someone was sweeping water from a shopfront, pushing the puddle back onto the still-wet street.

chapters.title: Halaman Belakang
body: ### Arka

Your message arrived while I was at the swimming pool. My phone was in a locker, its key tied to my wrist. I did not read it straight away. For forty minutes, my biggest problem was working out how other people managed to breathe without swallowing water.
My friend said I was thinking too much about every movement. I said I had heard that advice in other circumstances. He laughed, then told me to try again.
After showering, I sat on a bench near the drinks stall and opened my phone. There were work messages, pictures from the family group, and then your name. I read the short sentences twice.
You were home. You wanted to know whether I would like to meet the following week. Thursday afternoon, at Halaman Belakang, if I had time and wanted to.
I put the phone on the bench. My friend arrived with two bottles of water. He saw my face and asked whether I had just received a bill.
“I don't know yet,” I said.
He did not push. We drank and watched a group of children fighting over sandals near the changing-room door. Afterwards, he asked whether I needed a lift. I said I wanted to sit a little longer.
At home, I unpacked my swimming bag, hung up the towel, and heated some food. I did it all with a mind that occasionally left my body to open the conversation again.
I wanted to go. The wish did not answer every question, but at least it was clear.
I wrote that I would like to. Then I added that there might be things we would need to talk about if the meeting went beyond catching up.
You replied: yes. i've been thinking about that too.

I put the phone on the table. My food was not cold yet. I ate with the window open and listened to a neighbour teaching a child to spell the same word over and over. At some point, the child got it right. I smiled too, though I did not know the child's name.
On Wednesday, I told Sinta about the invitation.
She asked how I felt. I named happiness, fear, and something that embarrassed me because it felt like being back at the beginning, waiting for a message from someone I had just met.
“Which part embarrasses you?”
“That I'm still hoping, it turns out.”

Sinta looked at me with the same expression she had worn when I said I still wanted ordinary days with someone. She did not tell me to hope less or be braver. We talked about what I could face, what I needed to ask, and whether I could accept a meeting that did not end in a decision.
I was not sure about the last part.
“I might go home sad,” I said.
“You might.”
The answer made me laugh a little. I was glad she did not tidy up every possibility so I could leave without being afraid.

Before going, I noticed that the yellowing leaf on the plant by the shelves had been cut away. A small shoot grew beneath it. I almost made something of the sight. Then I simply asked whether the back car park was open yet.
Sinta said it was, but the road still had potholes.

On Thursday afternoon, I arrived first. The rain had just stopped. The café had a new, smaller sign, but the shelves were in the same place. The table by the window was empty. I chose the one by the shelves, then asked myself whether I was trying to bring back too many things at once.
I stayed there because it was comfortable and out of the rain.

The server asked for my order. I requested warm water to begin with. This time, it was written down correctly. Near the till stood a menu with stickers covering some of the prices. A song played too softly for me to recognise.

I opened my notebook, not to prepare what to say. It held a swimming schedule, a repairman's number, and a note about someone I had met while helping a friend move. I added an item to the shopping list: sugar jar. Then crossed it out because I already had a new one.
When the door opened, I looked up.
### Sinta

On Thursday, Tegar picked me up earlier than usual. My last appointment had been moved at the client's request. I had an unexpectedly empty hour and almost filled it with things that could have waited until tomorrow.
Tegar called from downstairs.
“Want to see the old house?” he asked.
“Why?”
“I went past earlier. They've painted the gate.”

I shut down the computer. The files were put away; tomorrow's schedule had been checked. We drove through streets still full of puddles. Outside a shop, two people were lifting things out of reach of the water.

Our old house looked brighter with its newly painted gate. There was a small bicycle on the veranda. The pot I had left behind had been moved to the other side and filled with a plant I did not recognise. We stopped across the road for long enough to look like people searching for an address.
“Looks nice,” Tegar said.
I nodded. I was glad someone was there. I also wanted to ask for one minute in the living room, just to hear the house without having to do anything.
We did not get out. Tegar asked whether I wanted to eat somewhere. I said yes, then mentioned that I did not have it in me to choose a place.
“Shall I choose?”
“Yes.”
He started the engine. Drops remained on the side window, not all of them moving when the car began to roll. I watched one slide slowly down and stop at the rubber seal.
People were making choices that afternoon. I did not know all of them. I did not have to be everywhere for something good to happen.
At a red light, Tegar placed his hand beside mine, palm up. I took it. His hand was cold from the air conditioning. With my other hand, I turned the fan down a little.
### Nara

From across the road, Nara saw Arka sitting by the shelves. He wore a shirt she had never seen. His hair was a little shorter. There was warm water on the table and the notebook she knew, but he was not bent over preparing something. He looked outside, then down briefly to check the time.

Nara stood beneath the awning of a closed shop. The rain had left the smell of asphalt, soil from plant pots, and cooking oil from the cart at the end of the street. A motorbike went through a puddle too fast. She stepped back a little too late; water speckled the bottoms of her trousers.

She wanted to call her sibling and say she had arrived but had not gone in. She wanted to be told she could go home if she was not ready. She knew she could. She simply had to make a decision with a body less calm than her thoughts.
When the road grew quieter, she crossed.

Arka stood when he saw her. They smiled with a caution that made Nara want to laugh and cry at the same time. She almost hugged him. He seemed about to do the same, then they both stopped at an awkward distance.
“Hi,” Nara said.
“Hi.”
“I'm a bit wet.”
“Yes. Sit down.”
Arka moved the chair for her. Nara thanked him. She put her bag in her lap, then moved it to the next chair. The gesture reminded her of a blue room, but she did not follow the memory further.

They talked about her journey home. Arka asked about her mother. Nara asked about the work he had told her about before they stopped speaking. Some of it had changed. He had new responsibilities. He was also learning to swim, which he mentioned with the expression of a man not ready for too many questions.
“Can you swim yet?”
“I can get into the pool on my own.”

Nara laughed. Arka laughed too, then seemed a little surprised by how easily the sound had come. Nara felt it as well. Something was still there, but they did not immediately use it to draw a larger conclusion.

The server came over. They ordered tea and snacks. Arka asked whether she still liked the fried bananas. Nara said yes, then added that lately she preferred them less ripe. Arka nodded and asked the server whether they could choose some that way.
There were old things they could still use. Small things needed asking again.

Nara told him about the image she had restored and the friend who had decided to leave the programme. Arka listened and asked about the parts he did not understand. When he talked about the office, Nara found she still had to ask him to explain certain terms. She was glad she did not feel the need to pretend she could follow.
Then the conversation stopped.
Outside, an employee lifted a doormat and wrung it out near the drain. The falling water made a clear sound. Nara could feel the damp hems of her trousers against her ankles.
“I still have nine months there,” she said.
Arka nodded.
“I remember.”
“And I don't know what comes after that either. There might be work. It's not certain yet.”
She said it without making the news smaller. Arka held his cup in both hands, then set it down again.
“I still can't travel often either,” he said. “My work needs me here now. And I want to give it a proper chance.”
Nara nodded. She wanted to hear more about the last part, but something else needed a little time first.
“I didn't come to ask you to decide anything straight away,” she said.
“I know.”
Arka looked at his notebook. He did not open it.
“I'm glad you came,” he said. “I'm still afraid we'll do the same things again too.”
“So am I.”
Nara waited for the urge to reassure one of them with a promise. The urge came. She let it pass without becoming a sentence.
“I've missed you,” she said at last.
Arka nodded. His jaw moved slightly, as though he was deciding how to breathe.
“I've missed you too.”

Nara saw his eyes grow wet and felt her own doing the same. No new bad news had been delivered. Nobody was leaving the table. She reached for a tissue and laughed a little at how hard it was to separate one sheet from the packet.
Arka helped by holding the box.

They sat like that for a while. Nara did not feel she had to explain her tears so he would know what to do. Nor did she treat his silence as something she needed to examine immediately. If anything was unclear later, she could ask. For now, Arka was still holding the tissue box, one corner slightly raised.
“This is so stupid,” Nara said softly, smiling.
“The tissues?”
She laughed. Arka smiled and finally set the box down.
On the shelf, Nara saw the book they had talked about long ago. Its spine was faded. She pointed to it. Arka turned, then said he still had not finished it.
“Neither have I,” Nara said.
“Did you bring it?”

She took her copy from her bag. It had creases and a small stain at one corner. Arka pulled his own copy from beneath his notebook. They compared their places, then laughed because they had stopped in different chapters, not very far apart.

Nara put her book on the table. Between them were still nine months, two cities, work, money, and conversations that could not be finished simply because they both missed the same thing. She could see all of it without having to get up at once.
The fried bananas arrived. The plate was too full to fit between two books, two cups, and the tissue box. Arka picked up his notebook. Nara moved her bag, then slid her book beside his.
The server asked whether they wanted anything else.

Nara looked at Arka. They had only planned to have a drink. Outside, it was getting dark. She could still go home after this, or stay a little longer without having to know yet what this afternoon would one day mean to them.
“Have you eaten?” she asked.
Arka shook his head.
“Have you?”
“Not yet.”
She reached for the menu tucked beside the shelves. The edges of a few pages were damp. She opened it and laid it in the middle of the table, close enough for them both to read.
