The girl's steps faltered. Her shoes scraped softly against the frozen ground. Her stomach churned, reawakening the memory of the heavy, hot breath and the gaze from the man of fat the other day. Fear crept slowly up the back of her neck.
The woman stopped too, though her back remained turned to the girl. The wind instantly died, leaving a chest-crushing silence.

"His gaze was dirty and hungry, wasn't it?" the voice flowed softly again inside the girl's skull, smooth yet feeling as if it were flaying her. "Looking at you as if you were a piece of helpless fresh meat... or perhaps, an empty vessel he was free to fill with his rot. Whether he was merely a wretched man controlled by his feral lust, or something far more ancient and hungrier than that... his intentions were always equally vile."

The girl gripped her bag straps tightly until her knuckles turned white. The cold air she usually befriended now made her shiver. She began to realize that all this time, she hadn't just been poor; she was also being stalked, studied like lost prey.

"But it's only natural that many prey on you, dear," the echoing voice continued, its tone now softening, resembling the fake sympathy of someone admiring fragile porcelain. "You radiate a despair that is so pure. A young girl with hands that are always freezing, insisting on protecting memories that are slowly cracking. Something very appetizing to snatch away."
The girl swallowed the sharp lump in her throat. Her instinct screamed to drop her bag and run back to the village, but her feet felt as if they had taken root in the warm soil beneath her soles.

"But he was too noisy. Too vulgar," a small laugh followed, echoing inside the girl's head without vibrating the hat-wearing woman's shoulders at all. "I know you are not naive. You have a boundary regarding which despair you are willing to accept. That is why I didn't bother chasing that fatty creature away that day. Because from the start... I firmly believed, in the end, you would still come with me."

The woman finally turned around slowly. The shadow from the brim of her hat covered half her face, leaving a curved smile that now looked strained and far too wide—waiting for the girl to step forward and break the terrifying silence.

Without saying anything else, the woman raised one hand clad in a knitted glove, pointing forward. The girl swallowed the sharp lump in her throat, then gathered the courage to follow the direction of that index finger.
Her eyes slowly widened; her breath seemed forcefully pulled from her lungs.

The thick fog that had been obscuring their vision slowly parted, as if terrified by the existence of the woman's finger. Before them, the earth no longer lay flat. The map of the world the girl had known ended at this road. The ground ahead split to form a giant, perfectly circular ravine or pit—as if the world had a hole because something massive had just been plucked from there.

And at the bottom of that incredibly deep ravine, there was no snow. No frozen ice. There was only a majestic, looming structure made of pitch-black wood, distorted like a stilt house built upside down. The house stood silently in the middle of a sea of warm, slowly pulsating fog, waiting for its new occupant.

"Do you remember I promised a room at the bottom of my house?" the woman whispered. This time, the voice actually came from her own lips, breaking the absolute silence at the edge of that ravine. "Let us go down and meet your flame."

So the girl followed her down the stairs to the bottom of the house, so long and seemingly endless. The girl stumbled more and more, growing exhausted as she had to descend the stairs carrying a heavy bag. The woman glanced slightly to the right and muttered in a language the girl still couldn't understand. In an instant, her luggage felt light, as if she wasn't carrying anything. The girl still couldn't believe it and checked the contents of her bag. Which turned out to be completely intact, not missing a single thing; strangely, she was no longer surprised by the bizarre things before her. Deep in her heart, she believed that the one with her was not human.
The stone stairs stretched far too long. Far longer than a depth human logic could grasp, plunging through the fog until she began to doubt whether this ravine truly had a bottom.
"When will these stairs end?" the girl asked with an innocent, panting tone.
"Until you are ready, dear... oh, until you are ready," the woman replied, laughing slightly.
Time melted and rotted on those steps. The girl didn't know if they had been descending for hours, days, or just the span of one long breath.

At first, the girl's old habits took over. In silence, she began counting the steps in her head. A hundred and one, a hundred and two, fifteen hundred, who knows how many thousands. Rooted in her instinct, which was always faced with debts and measurable days. Every time she added a new number, the warm fog below them felt thicker, and the bottom of the ravine seemed to keep moving further away, mocking her efforts.

Ahead of her, the woman in the hat kept walking soundlessly, occasionally humming a tune that now sounded like the smoothed howling of the wind. Every beat of that hum seemed to strip a number from the girl's head. The more the girl tried to remember the amount of her mother's debt, the healers' bills, or the remaining coins in her hand—everything slowly blurred. Turning to ash.
Then, a realization struck the girl's chest, as cold as ice yet as clear as crystal.
*"Until you are ready..."*

Those words echoed again. As long as she kept counting steps, as long as she used numbers as the anchor of her rationality, these stairs would never touch the bottom. This world was not a world that could be measured. This was a world where memories and emotions were the sole currency.

So, taking a long, trembling breath, the girl stopped counting. She forced her head to discard the remaining coins, drown the rows of her mother's debts, and hold on to only one thing: the memory of her mother's warm breath on her hands every morning. She no longer cared which step she was on. She just walked, drowning in pure memory.
Right when the last number faded from her mind, the tip of her shoe hit something solid with a dull thud. No longer wooden planks, but black stone tiles gleaming with dew.
The girl opened her eyes wide. The stairs had ended.

They stood at the bottom of the ravine. The inverted stilt house structure now loomed right in front of her, pressing against the ceiling of fog with its dense and absolute aura. The tip of its roof was driven into the earth, while its foundation—which should have been on the ground—instead gripped the emptiness above. At the very bottom of that strange house was a carved oak door that looked centuries old.

The woman in the hat stepped to the side, no longer blocking the path. The girl turned and noticed a horrifying change. The forced smile that had stretched across the woman's face was now completely gone. Her face was blank, expressionless, lifeless. Her sorrowful gaze was now just two dark holes staring straight through the girl's soul, as if the essence that had been pretending to be human had now reverted to its apathetic, true form.

The oak door opened slowly without a sound, exhaling air that smelled like old books, frankincense, and something sweet yet charred. In the pitch-black darkness of the room, a few dozen paces inside, there was a beam of golden light pulsating weakly. Bright and dim. Bright and dim. Breathing.

"Go in," the woman's voice now sounded like thousands of dry leaves rustling against each other, no longer echoing in the girl's head, but whispering right in her ear. "Your flame is waiting for you. Keep it company. And remember..."
The woman leaned in slightly, her flat face now just a handspan away from the girl's.
"...do not let it sleep."
And with trembling steps, the girl entered the room. Behind the door of the windowless, soundless room, there was nothing but a small flame on a tiny pedestal in the center of the room.
"Why is it so quiet?" the girl asked, because in that room she could hear her own blood traveling, a soft rush like someone humming in the distance.

"So the flame is not disturbed," said the woman in the hat. "And so you never feel alone. Listen—the house is whispering to you, so you have a friend." She pointed to the flame. "As long as you love it, it will burn. Every time you love it, a little of your warmth transfers to it. That is love, dear. Love is always like that."

Then the woman stepped out. The wooden door closed without a sound. The girl now sat alone beside her small flame, staring at the dimly pulsating glow. And for the first time since her mother didn't wake up—deep within the crisscrossing paths of her confusion and fear—the girl felt useful.
The first winter arrived gently.

The girl didn't see it coming—there were no windows—but she felt it from the flame, which dimmed a little, just a fingernail's worth, as if sleepy. *Sleep, little flame,* the girl almost said, then remembered that was exactly what must not happen. So she inverted her mother's words. "Don't sleep, little flame," she whispered. "Let me keep watch." And she leaned in, loving that flame as hard as she could, and the flame grew bright again.

That morning—the girl called it morning, though there was no morning at the bottom of the house—she just felt that right after she woke up from sleep, it was morning. Her hands were colder than usual. But she didn't mind. She was used to befriending the cold. And didn't the woman in the hat say she would never be cold again? Surely she meant *later*. Surely the warmth would come later, after she proved herself, just as all good things always come later.

Strangely, her body seemed to understand that she was now in a world that no longer needed ordinary things. Days or perhaps weeks passed—she didn't know for sure—her stomach never whined to be filled. Her throat no longer demanded water. Even the urge to relieve herself simply evaporated. In that windowless room, she no longer felt entirely human; it was as if she were slowly turning into a lump of feeling whose only task was to sit, breathe, and guard.

The only human thing that occasionally came to greet her was an incredibly heavy drowsiness. At first, the girl was terrified. She squeezed her fingers tightly, bit her lip, and kept glaring at the flame. *Let me keep watch,* she whispered to herself, afraid that if she dozed off even for a second, the flame would die too. However, the silence of the room was too thick, stroking her head like an irresistible lullaby. In the end, she always surrendered. Her body slumped to the cold floor, and she fell into a dreamless sleep.

Then, every time she woke up from her long slumber, something had always changed in the corner of the room. Objects appeared silently, as if the room birthed them when she closed her eyes. Sometimes a cup of water or a piece of hard biscuit that strangely made her stomach feel full for days. But what appeared most often were stacks of old books with dull covers.

The girl had nothing else to do, so she read. The books contained strange tales from places she didn't know, yet their loneliness felt so close. She read about a little girl who kept swinging alone in a dead playground, waiting for a figure she thought was a friend when it was actually a monster. On another page, she found a story about a gloomy flower shop where someone arranged grief on paper. And there was also a story that made her ponder for a long time; about a desperate man digging empty graves near a cluster of blue flowers, searching for his lost wife.

Even on one slightly torn page, she found a description of a flabby, fat creature that wandered preying on human despair—making the girl shudder softly, remembering the heavy breath behind her door back then.

Besides that, sometimes those books contained stories or perhaps histories from a world she had never known. There were writings about eyeless creatures that ate the echoes of voices, about a civilization built upon the eyelids of a sleeping giant, and about ancient rituals where a human's shadow could be flayed. Reading those strange books became her new routine, distracting her mind from the absolute silence pressing against the stone walls. The dark stories inside those dusty pages somehow felt like they validated her sorrow, as if whispering to her that the world up there was indeed too broken to live in.

And every time she finished reading, she would return to her routine. Leaning in, loving the flame in front of her until it grew bright again, then pressing her hands together and starting to count to ensure she still existed.

She counted, to keep herself company. She counted not the hours, because there were no hours, but how many things she still remembered from up there. Her mother's face. The smell of rain on soil. The taste of salt. The name of the river near her house. She kept them like one keeps stars, and said to herself: *as long as I can still count them, I am still me.*
The third winter arrived without warning.

This time the flame did not dim a fingernail's worth, but almost half, and the girl had to lean in closer, had to love harder, had to give more. She gave the flame the name of the river near her house, because she thought maybe the flame would like having a name. When the flame grew bright again, the girl realized she could no longer remember the name of that river. She had given it. That was what giving meant.
*It's okay,* she told herself. *I still remember Mother's face. I still remember the smell of rain. I still have my stars. I still remember many things.*

But deep in the chambers of her heart, there was an aching longing for the outside world. And she didn't know how long she had to keep loving something whose true form she didn't even know. Something bizarre, something horrifying.
*But strangely, I love it more and more,* the girl thought, staring at the golden glow with eyes that were slowly dimming. *And I am not willing to leave it.*
Suddenly, after who knows how long. The door opened once, in that third winter. It wasn't the woman in the hat, just her voice, coming down from the top of the long stairs.
"You are guarding it well, dear," the voice said.
"How much longer?" the girl asked. Her voice sounded foreign, too loud in a room that ate sound.

A brief silence. A silence too long for such a simple question. "Until someone replaces you," the voice said, very softly, as soft as a blanket. "That is how it works. Your mother guarded a flame once too, did you know? Every guardian may go up, may go home, may rest—but only after she finds someone whose hands are cold enough, and whose heart is loving enough, to come down and replace her."

The girl fell silent. Her mother who warmed her hands with her breath every morning. Her mother whose hands, if the girl were honest with herself, were always colder than anyone's hands she had ever touched.
"How," the girl asked quietly, "do you find that person?"

"You tell them a fairy tale," the voice said. "A beautiful fairy tale, about a small flame that must be guarded, and the warmth that awaits, and a mother who never leaves. Tell it softly. They always believe it, as long as you tell it softly."

Then the door closed, and the girl was alone again with her flame, and for the first time she noticed something she should have noticed a long time ago: that the small flame, if she brought her face close enough, was not like fire.
It was beating.
The winter that never ends.

The girl—though it is hard to call her a girl now, because time at the bottom of the house does not age the body but erodes something much deeper—she had given the flame the smell of rain, the taste of salt, and everything she remembered. Until finally, in a winter whose length she could no longer calculate, her mother's face. She gave it because the flame was almost out and there was nothing left to give, and when the flame grew bright again she tried to remember who she had just sacrificed, and couldn't.
She brought her face to the flame, as close as she could. And inside that small, beating flame, she saw a face.

Her own face. Young, with hands that could still feel the cold, on the day when a woman in a hat knocked on her door and said, *I hear you are good at keeping the cold company.* The flame was not something she guarded. The flame was her—the final ember of a girl who was extinguishing, very slowly, slower than any nature intended, because there was a consciousness clinging to her refusing, out of love, because it is always out of love, to let her go.

There was no other flame. There was no other flame she had ever guarded but her own soul, which she kept burning not for the sake of living but for the sake of guarding—a task that consumed the exact thing she used to guard it. Every time she loved it, a little of her warmth transferred. That is love. Love is always like that.

And her mother—whose hands were always cold, who gave her breath every morning, who one morning did not wake up—her mother never left. Her mother simply succeeded. Her mother simply found someone whose hands were cold enough and whose heart was loving enough, and told her a fairy tale softly, and went up the long stairs, and rested finally, finally, after who knows how many countless winters.
*Sleep, little flame, let Mother keep watch.*
There is no Mother. "Mother" is the name given to whoever is guarding the flame. One day that name would be her name. And she sank.

She no longer remembered who she was, whose face was behind that glowing light, or what task exactly bound her there. She had completely surrendered everything just so the flame would keep breathing. Now, she simply sat like a statue. Her eyes stared blankly, not blinking a single time, not recognizing anything. The mountain of books piling up into the thousands or millions in the corner of the room was now just a mute landscape to her. Let alone remembering their contents; even just to spell and read... she no longer knew how.

Suddenly, the oak door creaked, breaking the silence that had pooled for who knows how many eons. The woman in the hat returned. Her forced smile was gone, leaving a pair of eyes that were sorrowful and full of grief.
"Finally you have nothing left, dear... forgive me," she whispered hoarsely. "But that is your task."

The woman crouched down, reached out her hand, and gently stroked the hair of the silently sitting girl. The girl had forgotten the woman before her. She had forgotten everything. However, right beneath the stroke of that hand, a flash of ancient longing and a foreign warmth suddenly crept into her chest.
And without knowing what sorrow was, without remembering how to grieve, a single tear fell down her freezing cheek.

"I will return you upstairs. I give you a final task: live your life well from now on. Rest, and I will tell you a final fairy tale so you will always remember," the woman said once again, and thus the girl fell asleep to the final fairy tale of the woman in the hat.
So it goes like this, my child. This is how the fairy tale ends, and listen carefully, because this is the important part.

Once upon a time lived a girl whose hands were always cold, and she was given a beautiful task: to guard a small flame so that spring would remain in the house. And she guarded it faithfully, with all her love, for years longer than you could count—until one day the door at the top of the stairs opened, and down came a child with cold hands, and a loving heart, and debts she desperately wanted to erase.
Look at your hands, dear. So cold. Come here, sit beside me, close to this small flame.
Listen to how it beats.
Let me tell you how warm it will be later.

title: Di Waktu yang Tepat
excerpt: Selama tiga puluh dua tahun aku menginterogasi manusia, dan tidak ada satu pun yang berhasil membuatku mengatakan sesuatu yang tidak ingin kukatakan. Anak buah memanggilku Tembok. Bukan…
body: Selama tiga puluh dua tahun aku menginterogasi manusia, dan tidak ada satu pun yang berhasil membuatku mengatakan sesuatu yang tidak ingin kukatakan. Anak buah memanggilku Tembok. Bukan julukan yang kupilih — aku tidak akan pernah memilih julukan yang begitu kurang ajar tidak puitisnya — tapi ia menempel, sebab memang begitulah aku. Kau bisa berteriak, menangis, menggebrak meja, berbohong dengan kelihaian iblis, dan aku hanya akan duduk diam menatapmu sampai kau lelah, sampai kau retak, sampai kebenaran keluar darimu sendiri seperti air merembes dari tembok yang akhirnya menyerah pada hujan.
Aku tidak pernah retak. Itu seluruh pekerjaanku. Orang lain dibayar untuk membangun sesuatu; aku dibayar untuk tidak runtuh.

Maka aku tidak akan menjelaskan kepadamu — sebab aku tidak punya penjelasan — mengapa pada suatu Selasa siang di ruang interogasi nomor tiga, di hadapan seorang maling motor kelas teri bernama Sukrim yang menangis memanggil-manggil ibunya, aku ikut menangis.

Bukan menetes. Menangis. Tersedu, dengan ingus, dengan bahu berguncang, dengan segala kehinaan yang menyertainya. Di depan Sukrim. Yang akhirnya berhenti menangisi dirinya sendiri dan, dengan bingung dan agak ngeri, menggeser sebungkus tisu ke seberang meja dan berkata, "Sa-sabar ya, Pak." Lalu, karena ia maling dan otak maling tidak pernah betul-betul libur: "Kalau Bapak lagi banyak masalah, motor yang kemarin itu sebenarnya bukan saya yang—"
"Diam, Sukrim."
"Siap, Pak."

Begitulah aku berakhir di ruangan ini, di hadapan perempuan ini, yang menjadi musuh terberatku dalam tiga puluh dua tahun karier — lebih berat dari bandar, lebih berat dari pembunuh, lebih berat dari semua orang yang pernah kupandang sampai mengaku.

Namanya Bu Laras. Psikolog. Mereka mewajibkanku menemuinya delapan kali sebelum boleh kembali bertugas, sebab seorang interogator yang menangis lebih kencang daripada tersangkanya adalah, kata atasanku dengan diplomatis luar biasa, "aset yang perlu dikalibrasi ulang." Aku lima puluh delapan tahun. Aku sudah dikalibrasi. Yang mereka maksud, kalau mereka jujur, adalah: Tembok-nya retak, suruh tukang lihat.
Aku masuk dengan satu strategi. Ini interogasi. Dan aku tidak akan menjadi yang diinterogasi.
Maka aku duduk di kursinya. Kursi psikolog, yang menghadap kursi pasien. Aku bersandar, dan ketika ia masuk, aku menunjuk kursi seberang dengan dagu. "Silakan duduk."
Bu Laras memandangi situasi itu sebentar — aku di kursinya, kursinya kosong di seberang — lalu, tanpa ekspresi sedikit pun, ia duduk di kursi pasien. Menyilangkan kaki. Melipat tangan. Menunggu.
Bagus, pikirku. Dia mengikuti permainanku.
"Jadi," kataku, dengan suara yang pernah membuat seorang begundal dua meter mengompol di kursi besi, "ceritakan tentang dirimu."
"Aku lebih dulu," katanya. "Kau menangis di depan Sukrim waktu dia memanggil ibunya. Ibumu kenapa?"
Hening tiga detik.

Tiga detik yang, dalam seluruh sejarah interogasiku, adalah tiga detik pertama ketika akulah yang merasa lantai bergeser. Aku baru saja merebut kursi interogator, menguasai ruangan dengan sempurna — dan perempuan ini, dari kursi pasien, dari posisi kalah, baru saja menusukku tepat di bawah rusuk sambil membiarkanku merasa menang.
Aku berdeham. "Ibuku sehat. Masih masak rendang."

"Bagus." Ia mengangguk. "Berarti kita masih punya tujuh setengah sesi buat cari tahu kenapa kau ganti topik secepat itu, dan kenapa orang yang ibunya masih masak rendang menangis waktu maling memanggil ibunya."

Saat itulah aku tahu ini akan jadi perang. Dan saat itu pula, walau aku tak akan mengakuinya bahkan di bawah todongan, aku merasakan sesuatu yang sudah lama tidak kurasakan di ruangan mana pun: tertarik.
Sesi kedua, aku membawa senjata terbaikku. Diam.

Diam adalah seni. Orang awam mengira interogasi soal pertanyaan; bukan. Interogasi adalah soal keheningan yang kau tata sedemikian rupa hingga lawan tak tahan dan mengisinya sendiri. Aku pernah memenangkan keheningan sembilan jam. Aku pernah membuat orang mengaku membunuh hanya untuk mengakhiri sunyi yang kuciptakan.

Maka aku masuk, duduk — di kursi pasien kali ini; aku tidak keberatan menyerahkan teritori kecil demi memenangkan perang — dan aku diam. Aku menatap satu titik di kening Bu Laras. Tidak bergerak. Tidak berkedip lebih dari yang perlu. Aku menjadi Tembok.

Bu Laras menatapku balik sekitar sepuluh detik. Lalu ia mengangguk, seolah aku baru saja mengatakan sesuatu yang masuk akal, membuka laci meja, mengeluarkan rajutan setengah jadi — sebuah syal, warnanya jelek minta ampun, hijau lumut, warna yang membuatmu memikirkan kolam mati — dan mulai merajut.
Klik. Klik. Klik.

Satu jam. Ia merajut satu jam penuh sementara aku duduk dalam keheningan tempurku yang agung, keheningan yang telah meruntuhkan penjahat-penjahat besar, dan perempuan ini memperlakukannya seperti acara santai sore. Sesekali ia bersenandung. Di menit keempat puluh ia menawariku teh. Aku tidak menjawab; menjawab adalah kalah. Ia menuangkannya tetap, menaruhnya di hadapanku, dan aku menatap teh itu mengepul lalu dingin lalu membentuk lapisan tipis di permukaan, dan aku tidak menyentuhnya, dan itu — kuyakinkan diriku — adalah kemenangan.

Di menit kelima puluh lima ia berkata, tanpa mendongak dari rajutannya: "Kau jago diam, Pak. Sungguh. Tapi aku dibayar per jam, bukan per kata. Jadi kau sedang menyiksa dompetmu sendiri, bukan aku." Klik. "Dan tehnya gratis. Sayang lho."
Aku pulang hari itu dengan perasaan yang belum pernah kurasakan sejak Akademi: kalah telak oleh seorang sipil bersenjata dua jarum rajut dan satu teko.
Sesi ketiga aku ganti taktik. Kalau dia mau cerita, akan kuberi dia cerita.

Aku mengarang trauma. Aku interogator terbaik di provinsi ini; aku tahu persis bentuk luka yang dicari psikolog, sebab sudah ribuan kali kupancing keluar dari orang lain. Maka kususun sebuah mahakarya: masa kecil keras, ayah pemabuk bertangan besi, seekor anjing kesayangan yang mati ditabrak truk di depan mataku — lengkap dengan jeda di tempat yang tepat, suara yang kucekik sedikit di klimaks, satu tetes air mata yang kuizinkan jatuh dan langsung kuseka seolah malu. Aku bahkan menambahkan detail kecil yang selalu meyakinkan: aku berhenti di tengah, minta maaf, bilang "maaf, saya tidak biasa cerita begini." Sentuhan profesional. Kalau ia menelannya, ia akan menulis di laporan bahwa aku sudah "memproses," dan aku bebas.
Bu Laras mendengarkan seluruhnya. Mengangguk-angguk. Mencatat. Ketika aku selesai, ia menatap catatannya, menatapku, dan bertanya dengan nada paling ramah sedunia:
"Anjingnya namanya siapa?"
"...Boni."
"Tadi kau bilang Doni."
Hening. Hening yang berbeda dari hening-ku. Ini hening seseorang yang ketahuan, dan aku tahu persis rasanya dari sisi seberang meja, ribuan kali, tapi tak pernah dari sisi ini.

"Pak." Ia meletakkan pulpennya. Dan untuk pertama kalinya ada sesuatu yang nyaris seperti kelembutan di suaranya, yang justru membuatnya lebih tak tertahankan. "Aku sudah dua puluh tahun mendengarkan orang berbohong tentang perasaannya. Kau jago. Sungguh. Lima besar yang pernah kutemui. Tapi orang yang benar-benar tidak punya luka tidak akan repot-repot mengarang luka sebagus itu cuma untuk kabur dari ruangan ini. Yang kosong, ngeloyor pergi. Yang menyusun anjing mati selengkap itu, dengan dua nama karena terlalu sibuk mengarang sampai lupa—" ia tersenyum tipis "—itu orang yang menyimpan sesuatu yang asli, dijaga begitu rapat sampai ia lebih rela menciptakan luka palsu daripada membuka yang betulan. Kau tidak mengarang untuk membohongiku, Pak. Kau mengarang supaya tidak perlu menyentuh yang asli. Bahkan bohongmu pun tameng."
Aku tidak menjawab. Tapi di bawah meja, tanganku mengepal sampai buku-buku jariku memutih.
Sebab perempuan ini, dengan rajutan jelek dan teh gratis dan deadpan-nya, baru saja melakukan hal yang tak pernah berhasil dilakukan siapa pun terhadap Tembok dalam tiga puluh dua tahun.

Ia menemukan retakannya. Dan ia tidak menekannya. Itu yang menakutkan. Penekan retakan bisa kulawan. Yang ini hanya menunjukkannya kepadaku, lalu menunggu, seolah retakan itu milikku dan terserah aku mau kuapakan.
Aku melawan. Tentu saja. Aku tidak menyerah semudah itu; aku Tembok.

Aku melakukan yang dilakukan polisi ketika terpojok. Aku menyelidikinya. Latar belakang Bu Laras kuperiksa lewat saluran yang sebaiknya tidak kujelaskan dan yang, secara hukum, sebaiknya juga tidak kulakukan. Aku mencari titik lemah, sebab begitulah perang dimenangkan: temukan retakan lawan, tekan.
Aku menemukannya, dan untuk sesaat aku merasa kembali memegang kendali, dan beberapa detik kemudian aku merasa seperti bajingan.

Kliniknya nyaris bangkrut. Tutup bulan depan. Dan dari beberapa hal yang kubaca dan beberapa kolega yang kutanyai dengan hati-hati, gambarnya cukup jelas: ini sesi-sesi terakhirnya. Bukan cuma kliniknya yang tutup. Dia yang berhenti. Keluar dari profesi yang ia jalani dua puluh tahun. Aku — pasien wajib yang menyebalkan, si Tembok yang menyusun anjing mati bernama Boni-slash-Doni — adalah salah satu kasus terakhir dalam karier seorang perempuan yang sudah memutuskan untuk berhenti percaya pada pekerjaannya sendiri.

Aku juga menemukan kenapa, atau kukira begitu. Beberapa tahun lalu ada seorang pasiennya — anak muda, depresi, ia tangani berbulan-bulan — yang akhirnya tidak selamat. Bukan salahnya; kolega bilang ia melakukan semua yang benar. Tapi aku interogator cukup lama untuk tahu bahwa "bukan salahmu" adalah kalimat yang tidak pernah sampai ke orang yang paling membutuhkannya. Aku menyimpan satu nama anak itu di kepalaku dan merasa kotor karena menyimpannya.
Aku datang ke sesi berikutnya dengan semua amunisi itu di saku. Aku siap menggunakannya. Lalu sesuatu terjadi sebelum aku sempat menembak.

Bu Laras datang terlambat. Bu Laras tidak pernah terlambat. Dan ketika ia masuk, tidak ada rajutan, tidak ada teko, tidak ada baja itu. Ia terlihat lelah dengan cara yang tak bisa dipalsukan — jenis lelah yang sangat kukenal, sebab kutemui di cermin setiap pagi. Ia duduk di kursi psikolog, kursinya sendiri, untuk pertama kalinya sejak sesi pertama, dan menghela napas, dan berbicara bukan dengan suara psikolog melainkan dengan suara manusia yang terlalu capek untuk berakting.

"Pak Karman. Jujur saja ya. Aku capek." Ia tertawa kecil, getir, tawa yang kukenali sebab persis tawaku sendiri. "Ini minggu-minggu terakhirku. Aku berhenti. Bukan karena klinik bangkrut — itu cuma alasan yang enak diceritakan. Aku berhenti karena aku sudah tidak percaya ngomong bisa menyembuhkan siapa-siapa. Dua puluh tahun aku menyuruh orang membuka diri, dan separuhnya keluar dari ruangan ini sama hancurnya seperti waktu masuk. Dan sebagian—" ia berhenti, dan aku melihat nama yang kusimpan di kepalaku melintas di matanya, dan aku bersyukur tidak sempat mengucapkannya "—sebagian tidak keluar sama sekali. Jadi kalau kau mau terus main tembok-tembokan, silakan. Aku angkat tangan. Aku tidak punya tenaga untuk berperang lagi."
Dan di situlah, pembaca, seluruh strategiku runtuh.
Sebab aku punya pertahanan untuk segalanya. Teriakan, tangisan, bujukan, ancaman, diam, bohong. Aku punya tembok untuk tiap serangan yang dikenal manusia.
Aku tidak punya satu pun pertahanan terhadap seseorang yang berhenti menyerang.

Kau tidak bisa menginterogasi orang yang sudah menyerah. Senjataku semua dirancang untuk menembus pertahanan; di hadapan seseorang yang menurunkan seluruh pertahanannya, senjataku jadi tumpukan besi tak berguna. Aku duduk di sana dengan saku penuh peluru tentang kliniknya dan nama anak yang tak selamat, dan tak satu pun bisa kutembakkan, sebab kau tidak menembak orang yang sudah berlutut bukan untuk menyerah kalah melainkan karena kakinya benar-benar tak sanggup lagi berdiri.
Maka aku melakukan hal yang paling tidak pernah kuduga akan kulakukan dalam ruangan mana pun, terhadap siapa pun.
Aku menurunkan tembokku lebih dulu.
"Namanya Joni," kataku.
Bu Laras mendongak. Sesuatu di wajahnya berubah, tapi ia tidak meraih pulpen. Itu yang membuatku bisa melanjutkan — ia tidak meraih pulpen.

"Partner pertamaku. Tiga puluh tahun lalu. Anak ingusan, baru lulus, cerewetnya minta ampun, leluconnya jelek semua — jelek sungguhan, Bu, jenis yang membuatmu malu sudah tertawa. Suka menyisakan gorengan terakhir buatku padahal dia yang beli. Tiap kali. Aku bilang jangan, aku bilang makan saja, dan tiap kali dia bilang 'sudah kenyang, Pak' sambil ngiler lihat gorengannya. Bohong paling jelek yang pernah kudengar. Dan aku interogator, aku tahu semua jenis bohong." Aku berhenti. "Itu bohong pertama yang tidak pernah kubongkar. Aku biarkan saja. Aku makan gorengannya."
"Lalu?"

"Lalu dia mati. Bulan keempat kami bertugas. Bukan baku tembak heroik, bukan apa-apa yang pantas ditulis di tugu. Cuma kejar-kejaran bodoh, motor, truk yang belok tanpa lihat. Selesai. Dua puluh tiga tahun. Mati sebelum sempat jadi apa-apa, sebelum sempat punya lelucon yang lucu, sebelum sempat berhenti menyisakan gorengan."
"Dan kau menangisinya," kata Bu Laras, pelan.
"Tidak." Aku menatap teh dingin di antara kami. "Itu masalahnya."

Dan akhirnya, tiga puluh tahun terlambat, aku menceritakannya — bukan menjelaskannya, aku tidak menjelaskan, aku cuma menaruhnya di atas meja seperti barang bukti. Hari Joni mati, aku punya pekerjaan. Mengabari keluarganya. Mengurus laporan. Berdiri tegak di pemakaman karena ibunya Joni memelukku dan menangis dan seseorang harus jadi yang tidak ikut roboh. Maka aku menundanya. Aku bilang pada diriku: nanti. Nanti aku berduka. Di waktu yang tepat. Setelah semua beres. Setelah aku sempat.

Aku tidak menjelaskan kepada Bu Laras apa yang terjadi setelah itu, sebab tidak perlu; ia psikolog, ia tahu. Kalau kau menunda satu hal cukup lama, penundaan itu berhenti menjadi penundaan dan menjadi bangunan. Aku tidak pernah sampai ke "waktu yang tepat". Selalu ada kasus berikutnya, tersangka berikutnya, alasan berikutnya untuk jadi tembok satu hari lagi. Dan tembok yang berdiri tiga puluh tahun tidak lagi terasa seperti pilihan. Ia terasa seperti tulang.

"Lalu bulan lalu," kataku, dan di sinilah suaraku mulai tidak bisa kupegang, "mereka kasih aku partner baru. Anak ingusan. Baru lulus. Cerewet. Leluconnya jelek." Aku tertawa, satu tawa pendek yang keluar salah, lebih dekat ke sesuatu yang lain. "Namanya Bagas. Hari pertama dia sudah bikin tiga lelucon dan dua-duanya gagal dan satu lagi entah apa, aku tidak ngerti sampai sekarang. Dan minggu lalu kami lembur, beli gorengan, dan dia—"
Aku berhenti.
"Dia menyisakan yang terakhir," kata Bu Laras.

"Buatku. Tanpa diminta. Dan waktu kubilang makan saja, dia bilang—" tenggorokanku menutup, dan aku, Tembok, lima puluh delapan tahun, harus berhenti dan menunggu sebelum bisa menyelesaikannya "—dia bilang 'sudah kenyang, Pak.' Sambil ngiler lihat gorengannya. Bohong yang sama. Bohong jelek yang sama persis. Tiga puluh tahun, Bu. Tiga puluh tahun temboknya berdiri, dan yang merobohkannya bukan peluru, bukan kasus, bukan apa-apa yang besar. Cuma satu gorengan sisa dan satu bohong jelek dari anak yang bahkan belum kukenal."
"Dan kau menangis."

"Di ruang interogasi nomor tiga." Suaraku akhirnya pecah, di kursi pasien itu, dan aku membiarkannya. "Tiga puluh tahun aku menahan air mata untuk satu anak yang mati, dan ketika akhirnya keluar, dia memilih satu-satunya waktu paling memalukan, paling tidak terhormat, paling salah dalam sejarah kepolisian seluruh republik—" aku tertawa lagi, tawa basah, mengerikan, lega "—di depan maling motor bernama Sukrim, yang mengira aku gila, dan menyodorkan tisu, dan menyuruhku sabar. Maling. Yang menyabarkan aku. Dengan tisu kantor yang dibeli dari uang negara."

Dan Bu Laras — psikolog yang sudah angkat tangan, yang sudah berhenti percaya, yang sudah mengemasi dua puluh tahun ke dalam kardus — Bu Laras tertawa. Tertawa sungguhan, sampai matanya basah, tawa orang yang baru saja mendengar hal paling menyedihkan dan paling lucu sekaligus, yang di dunia ini memang sering jadi hal yang sama.
"Sukrim," katanya, menggeleng. "Tisu kantor."
"Uang negara," kataku.

Dan kami berdua tertawa, dua orang tua di ruangan kecil yang akan tutup bulan depan, menertawakan satu maling dan satu kotak tisu, sampai tawa itu pelan-pelan berubah jadi hal lain, hal yang tak punya nama, hal yang berdiri tepat di perbatasan antara yang paling lucu dan yang paling tak tertanggung dalam hidup, dan kami membiarkannya, sebab pada akhirnya itulah satu-satunya tempat di mana orang-orang seperti kami bisa beristirahat.
Kami diam lama sesudahnya. Tapi bukan diam tempurku. Diam yang lain — yang tidak menuntut apa-apa, yang tidak menunggu siapa retak lebih dulu.

Lalu, karena aku interogator dan kebiasaan tiga puluh dua tahun tidak mati dalam semenit, aku melihat retakan di wajahnya. Jenis yang biasa kucari. Dan tanpa benar-benar memutuskannya, aku berkata pelan:
"Anak yang tidak selamat itu. Yang kau tangani bertahun-tahun."
Wajahnya membeku. "Kau menyelidikiku."

"Aku Tembok. Itu yang kulakukan." Aku menahan tatapannya. "Aku datang ke sesi ini dengan niat memakainya buat menyerangmu. Buat menang. Itu rencana awalku hari ini. Aku mau bilang sesuatu yang kejam tentang dia supaya kau goyah dan aku bisa keluar dari ruangan ini tanpa membongkar Joni."
"Kenapa kau tidak melakukannya?"

"Karena kau keburu menyerah duluan," kataku. "Dan ternyata aku tidak bisa menembak orang yang sudah meletakkan senjatanya. Itu satu-satunya garis yang tidak pernah kulewati dalam tiga puluh dua tahun, dan aku baru tahu hari ini bahwa garis itu ada."
Ia tidak berkata apa-apa.

"Kau berhenti," kataku, "karena kau pikir ngomong tidak menyembuhkan siapa-siapa. Karena ada satu anak yang tidak kau selamatkan dan kau bawa dia di matamu sampai sekarang — aku lihat, tadi, waktu kau hampir menyebutnya. Kau pikir dua puluh tahun ini gagal karena ada satu yang tidak bisa kau pulangkan." Aku berhenti. "Tapi kau salah, Bu. Dan kau tahu kau salah, sebab baru saja, di ruangan ini, kau membuat seorang tembok berumur lima puluh delapan tahun menangisi anak yang sudah tiga puluh tahun mati. Kau tidak menyembuhkanku — duka tidak sembuh, aku cukup tua untuk tahu itu. Tapi kau membuatku berhenti membawanya sendirian. Itu bukan tidak ada artinya. Itu hampir segalanya."
Tatapan baja itu akhirnya runtuh. Matanya basah, dan ia tertawa dan menangis sekaligus, dengan cara orang yang baru saja diselamatkan oleh orang yang datang untuk diselamatkan.
"Sialan kau, Tembok," katanya, mengusap mata kasar dengan punggung tangan. "Aku yang psikolog di sini."
"Dan aku yang interogator," kataku. "Jadi percaya aku waktu kubilang: kau bohong soal mau berhenti. Aku tahu bohong. Itu yang paling jelek yang pernah kudengar sejak gorengan."
Ia tidak berhenti. Itu informasi yang baru kudapat belakangan.

Klinik tetap tutup — uang tetap uang, dan tidak ada kebijaksanaan yang membayar sewa. Tapi ia pindah, buka lagi, lebih kecil, di ruko sempit dekat pasar yang baunya ikan asin sepanjang hari. Aku tahu sebab — dan ini bagian yang masih membuatku merasa konyol kalau mengingatnya — aku menjadi pasiennya selama dua tahun penuh setelah delapan sesi wajibku habis. Sukarela. Tembok, sukarela, datang setiap dua minggu ke ruko bau ikan asin, membawa gorengan, dan menyisakan yang terakhir untuknya. Tiap kali. Dan tiap kali ia bilang "sudah kenyang, Pak," sambil ngiler lihat gorengannya, dan tiap kali aku tidak membongkar bohong itu. Aku biarkan saja. Aku makan gorengannya.

Bagas tidak pernah tahu apa-apa soal ini. Anak itu cuma tahu seniornya yang galak mendadak tidak terlalu galak, dan kadang, kalau ia menyisakan gorengan terakhir, seniornya menatapnya terlalu lama dengan ekspresi aneh sebelum berkata "makan saja, Gas." Dia mengira aku cuma tua dan sentimentil soal makanan. Biar saja. Ada hal-hal yang tidak perlu kau wariskan dengan kata; cukup kau wariskan dengan tidak menyuruhnya berhenti menyisakan gorengan.

Pada hari aku pensiun, beberapa tahun kemudian, ada pesta kecil di kantor. Banyak polisi, banyak pidato, banyak orang muda yang tidak tahu kenapa orang tua di pojok dijuluki Tembok dan tidak berani bertanya. Bagas — bukan anak ingusan lagi, sudah punya partner ingusannya sendiri sekarang — memberi pidato yang jelek, dan aku tertawa di bagian yang salah, dan dia tidak tahu kenapa.
Dan di pojok ruangan, satu orang yang bukan polisi, dengan syal jelek warna hijau lumut yang akhirnya selesai ia rajut entah untuk siapa, melingkar di lehernya sendiri.

Sebelum aku pulang, Bu Laras menyerahkan sesuatu. Buku catatan perasaan yang dulu ia suruh kuisi di minggu-minggu pertama — yang kuisi dengan format laporan pengintaian untuk menjengkelkannya. *0800: subjek merasa tidak ada apa-apa. 0830: masih tidak ada apa-apa. 0900: subjek mulai curiga psikolog sedang menang. 0930: subjek menyangkal kecurigaan tersebut. Lampiran: tidak ada.*
"Halaman terakhir," katanya. "Aku tunggu kau isi sejak sesi pertama. Sembilan tahun, Pak. Aku sabar."

Maka di pesta pensiunku, di pojok ruangan, di bawah balon-balon murahan dan spanduk yang salah eja namaku, seorang lelaki tua yang dulu dijuluki Tembok membuka halaman terakhir dan menulis, untuk pertama kalinya, sesuatu yang benar tentang perasaannya. Tidak panjang. Tembok tidak akan pernah panjang.

*Joni. Aku makan gorengan terakhirmu tiga puluh tahun yang lalu dan tidak pernah bilang terima kasih, dan aku tidak menangisimu karena aku sibuk menjadi kuat untuk ibumu, dan ternyata aku tidak pernah berhenti sibuk. Maaf aku terlambat. Tapi ada yang bilang padaku, dan dia psikolog jadi mungkin dia tahu: yang ada bukan terlambat. Yang ada cuma waktu yang akhirnya sanggup kau tanggung.*

Aku menutup buku itu. Aku tidak menangis — aku sudah menangis, dulu, di waktu yang ternyata, meski di depan seorang maling, meski tiga puluh tahun terlambat, meski paling memalukan dalam sejarah kepolisian republik ini, adalah satu-satunya waktu yang pernah benar-benar tepat. Bukan karena ia datang di saat yang baik. Tapi karena, untuk pertama kalinya sejak Joni mati, ketika air mata itu akhirnya datang, ada seseorang di ruangan yang tidak menyuruhku berhenti.

Sukrim, kalau kau penasaran, tetap masuk penjara. Motornya memang dia yang curi. Tapi aku menulis di berkasnya satu catatan yang tidak biasa kutulis untuk siapa pun: *Tersangka kooperatif. Menunjukkan empati pada petugas.* Hakim mungkin bingung membacanya.

Aku tidak. Aku tahu persis apa yang dia lakukan untukku, di ruang nomor tiga, dengan tisu uang negara. Dia menyabarkan seorang tembok yang sedang runtuh, dan dia tidak menyuruhku berhenti, dan untuk seorang maling kelas teri itu mungkin satu-satunya hal mulia yang pernah ia lakukan seumur hidupnya — dan ia melakukannya untuk orang yang menahannya. Di waktu yang, ternyata, juga tepat.

sides.title: Maling yang Pulang
body: Sukrim keluar penjara pada hari Selasa, dan hal pertama yang ia curi adalah sebuah jeruk.

Bukan karena lapar — di gerbang mereka memberinya nasi bungkus dan ongkos bus. Ia mencuri jeruk itu dari gerobak di depan lapas karena tangannya, setelah empat tahun, lupa cara tidak mencuri, dan jeruk itu sudah ada di sakunya sebelum kepalanya sempat ikut campur. Ia berdiri di trotoar memegang jeruk hasil curian dengan perasaan seorang lelaki yang baru saja gagal pada menit pertama kebebasannya, dan ia hampir mengembalikannya, lalu sadar mengembalikan barang curian ke gerobak yang ramai justru lebih mencurigakan daripada mencurinya, lalu memutuskan memakannya saja, lalu merasa bersalah, lalu — ini bagian yang penting — menyelipkan uang seharga jeruk itu ke gerobak yang sama ketika penjualnya tidak melihat.

Mencuri jeruk, lalu diam-diam membayarnya. Itu Sukrim. Itu seluruh Sukrim, sebenarnya, dalam satu gerakan: seorang lelaki yang tangannya jahat tapi dadanya tidak pernah ikut, yang menghabiskan empat puluh tahun mencuri hal-hal kecil lalu menyesalinya dengan cara yang lebih kecil lagi.
Ia naik bus ke kampung. Ia pulang menemui ibunya.

Selama empat tahun di dalam, satu hal yang menjaga Sukrim tetap waras adalah membayangkan adegan ini: ia mengetuk pintu, ibunya membuka, dan — setelah memarahinya habis-habisan, tentu, ibunya berhak marah — ibunya memeluknya dan berkata *akhirnya kamu pulang*. Ia sudah melatih wajah menyesalnya. Ia sudah menyiapkan kalimat permintaan maaf, direvisi ratusan kali di sel, sampai sempurna.
Ia mengetuk. Ibunya membuka. Dan ibunya berkata:
"Cari siapa, Nak?"
Sukrim berdiri di sana dengan kalimat maaf yang sempurna menguap dari kepalanya.
"Bu," katanya. "Ini saya. Sukrim."

Ibunya — lebih kecil dari yang ia ingat, lebih putih, dengan mata yang ramah dan sama sekali kosong — memiringkan kepala. "Sukrim," ulangnya, mencicipi nama itu seperti mencicipi masakan orang asing. "Sukrim siapa, ya? Maaf, Ibu agak pelupa."

Tetangga sebelah, Bu Inah, yang mendengar dari pagarnya, datang menjelaskan dengan suara pelan. Sudah dua tahun begini. Pikun. Dokter di puskesmas menyebutnya satu istilah panjang yang Bu Inah tidak hafal. Kadang ibunya ingat hal-hal dari lima puluh tahun lalu dengan sempurna — nama-nama teman SD, harga beras zaman dulu, lagu-lagu yang sudah tidak ada yang menyanyikan. Tapi yang dekat, yang baru, yang kemarin — semua itu jatuh dari kepalanya seperti air dari tangan yang menangkup.
"Anaknya saja dia tidak ingat lagi," kata Bu Inah, lalu buru-buru menutup mulut, sadar betapa kejam kedengarannya.

Sukrim mengangguk. Ia tidak menangis. Ia maling; ia tahu cara wajahnya tidak mengkhianatinya. Ia hanya berdiri di teras rumah masa kecilnya, memegang sisa satu jeruk curian di saku, dan menyadari bahwa ia telah menghabiskan empat tahun memenjarakan diri demi pulang ke satu-satunya orang di dunia yang menunggunya, hanya untuk menemukan bahwa orang itu telah, dengan caranya sendiri, pergi lebih dulu.
Begini yang dilakukan orang waras dalam situasi ini: ia akan duduk, menjelaskan dengan sabar, menunjukkan foto, memutar ingatan, mencoba memanggil ibunya kembali ke permukaan.

Sukrim mencoba itu selama tiga hari. Tiga hari ia berkata "Bu, ini Sukrim, anak Ibu," dan tiga hari ibunya menatapnya dengan keramahan kosong yang sama, dan satu kali — ini yang paling menyakitkan — ibunya menjadi takut, mundur ke sudut, berbisik "kamu mau apa, Ibu tidak punya uang," seolah anaknya sendiri adalah maling yang masuk ke rumahnya. Yang mana, kalau Sukrim jujur, secara teknis memang benar adanya, dan itu membuatnya tertawa pahit di kamar mandi malam itu sampai tawanya berubah jadi hal lain.
Pada hari keempat, Sukrim berhenti mencoba menjadi Sukrim.

Itu datang sebagai gagasan maling, sebab Sukrim cuma punya otak maling, dan otak maling bertanya satu pertanyaan tentang segala hal: *apa yang bisa kuambil dari sini?* Hanya saja kali ini, untuk pertama kalinya dalam hidupnya, pertanyaan itu berbalik. Bukan apa yang bisa kuambil. Melainkan: apa yang bisa kukembalikan, kepada perempuan yang sudah kehilangan hampir segalanya, termasuk aku?
Ibunya tidak ingat punya anak bernama Sukrim. Baiklah. Tapi ibunya ingat hal-hal lama. Maka Sukrim duduk, pada hari keempat, dan alih-alih memaksa ibunya mengingat dirinya, ia bertanya:
"Bu, dulu Ibu punya anak, tidak?"
Dan wajah ibunya menyala.
"Punya," kata ibunya, dan untuk pertama kalinya matanya tidak kosong. "Anak laki-laki. Namanya..." — ia mengernyit, mencari — "...Sukrim. Iya, Sukrim. Anak baik. Pintar sekali dia."
Sukrim, yang bukan anak baik dan tidak pintar dan duduk tepat di hadapan ibunya, berkata, "Oh ya? Cerita dong, Bu."

Dan ibunya bercerita. Tentang Sukrim — Sukrim versi ibunya, Sukrim yang tinggal di kepala perempuan tua itu, yang ternyata sangat berbeda dari Sukrim yang asli. Sukrim dalam ingatan ibunya adalah anak yang rajin mengaji, yang juara kelas, yang dulu memberi ibunya gelang dari uang gajinya yang pertama. Sebagian benar — Sukrim memang pernah memberi ibunya gelang, meski gelang itu, ia tidak akan pernah mengaku, hasil curian dari pasar. Sebagian salah total — Sukrim tidak pernah juara apa pun kecuali, mungkin, juara paling sering ditangkap. Tapi ibunya bercerita dengan bangga yang begitu murni, tentang anak yang begitu baik, sampai Sukrim mengerti sesuatu yang membuat dadanya sesak.

Demensia telah mencuri ingatan ibunya. Tapi sebelum mencurinya, demensia melakukan satu hal yang aneh dan nyaris berbelas kasih: ia mengedit. Ia membuang versi Sukrim yang mengecewakan — yang ditangkap berkali-kali, yang membuat ibunya menangis di kantor polisi, yang terakhir kali dilihat ibunya dari balik jeruji — dan menyimpan hanya versi terbaiknya. Versi yang memberi gelang. Versi yang seharusnya. Pikiran ibunya, dalam keruntuhannya, telah menjaga satu-satunya bagian dari Sukrim yang layak dijaga.

Dan Sukrim, sang maling, duduk di hadapan harta itu — sebuah versi dirinya yang lebih baik, tersimpan utuh dalam kepala satu-satunya orang yang pernah mencintainya — dan untuk pertama kalinya dalam hidupnya, ia memutuskan untuk tidak mencurinya. Ia memutuskan, sebaliknya, untuk menjaganya.
Maka Sukrim menjadi orang lain.

Ia tidak mengaku sebagai Sukrim lagi. Itu cuma membuat ibunya takut, atau bingung, atau — lebih buruk — kadang membuat ibunya nyaris ingat hal-hal yang lebih baik tetap terlupa. Maka ketika ibunya bertanya "kamu siapa, Nak?", Sukrim menjawab dengan kebohongan paling mulia yang pernah ia susun:
"Saya tetangga baru, Bu. Pak Sukrim eh — Pak Krim. Saya bantu-bantu di sini. Disuruh anak Ibu."
"Anak saya? Sukrim?"
"Iya, Bu. Dia titip Ibu sama saya. Soalnya dia lagi kerja jauh. Kerja bagus, Bu. Dia sukses sekarang."

Dan wajah ibunya akan menyala lagi, dan ia akan berkata "iya, anak saya memang pintar," dan Sukrim — Pak Krim — akan mengangguk dan menyapu lantai dan memasak dan mengganti lampu yang mati, melakukan untuk ibunya semua hal yang seharusnya dilakukan anak yang baik, dengan menyamar sebagai orang asing yang disewa oleh anak yang baik yang tidak pernah ada.

Lelucon kosmis dari seluruh urusan ini tidak hilang dari Sukrim. Ia telah menghabiskan hidup menyamar — menyamar sebagai pembeli sebelum mencuri, menyamar sebagai orang tak bersalah di depan polisi, menyamar sebagai segala hal yang bukan dirinya. Dan sekarang, untuk pekerjaan terakhir dan terbesar dalam kariernya sebagai penipu, ia menyamar sebagai orang asing yang baik, demi melindungi seorang perempuan tua dari kebenaran bahwa anaknya tidak sebaik itu. Penyamaran paling jujur dalam hidupnya adalah berpura-pura menjadi bukan dirinya.
Hari-hari Sukrim, setelah itu, jadi ganjil dan manis dan menyiksa.

Tiap pagi ia bangun di kamar yang dulu kamarnya, dan menjadi Pak Krim. Ia memasak untuk ibunya, dan ibunya memujinya — "kamu masak enak, Pak Krim, hampir seenak masakan saya dulu" — dan Sukrim menahan tawa, sebab resep itu resep ibunya, yang ia hafal dari mengintip puluhan tahun lalu. Ia menemani ibunya duduk di teras, dan ibunya bercerita tentang Sukrim yang hebat, dan Pak Krim mendengarkan dengan kekaguman yang dibuat-buat tentang dirinya sendiri, sambil sesekali menambahkan detail.
"Katanya dia sekarang punya rumah besar, Bu," kata Pak Krim suatu sore, membangun versi yang lebih baik dari hidupnya sendiri, bata demi bata, untuk seorang penonton yang hanya satu orang.

"Oh ya?" Mata ibunya berbinar. "Syukur. Dulu kami susah sekali, Pak Krim. Saya cuma jual kue. Tapi saya selalu bilang sama Sukrim, jangan jadi maling biar miskin sekalipun. Maling itu—" ibunya menggeleng "—maling itu mencuri dari orang, tapi yang paling banyak dia curi itu dari ibunya sendiri. Curi rasa bangga ibunya. Saya selalu bilang gitu."
Sukrim menyapu lantai yang sudah bersih supaya ibunya tidak melihat wajahnya.
"Untung Sukrim tidak begitu," lanjut ibunya, tersenyum. "Untung anak saya jadi orang baik."
"Iya, Bu," kata Sukrim, dengan punggung membelakangi ibunya. "Untung."
Ada satu sore ketika hampir semuanya runtuh.

Bu Inah, tetangga itu, yang tidak tahan melihat sandiwara ini berlarut, menarik Sukrim ke pagar dan berbisik marah. "Sampai kapan kamu mau begini, Krim? Itu ibumu. Dia berhak tahu anaknya pulang. Kamu nipu dia tiap hari!"
"Saya tidak nipu dia, Bu Inah," kata Sukrim, pelan.
"Lah itu apa namanya? Kamu ngaku tetangga. Kamu bilang dirimu sendiri sukses padahal baru keluar penjara. Itu bohong semua."
Sukrim diam sebentar. Lalu ia berkata sesuatu yang ia sendiri tidak tahu ada di dalam dirinya sampai keluar:

"Bu Inah, seumur hidup saya nyuri dari ibu saya. Bukan duit — saya tidak pernah nyuri duitnya, dia tidak punya. Saya nyuri yang lebih jahat. Tiap kali saya ketangkap, saya nyuri kebanggaannya. Tiap kali dia harus datang ke kantor polisi, mukanya itu — saya nyuri itu, saya bikin dia malu di depan seluruh kampung, berkali-kali, selama empat puluh tahun. Saya maling yang paling banyak nyuri dari korban yang paling sayang sama saya."
Ia menelan ludah.

"Sekarang dia lupa semua itu. Dia lupa semua yang saya curi dari dia. Dan untuk pertama kalinya, Bu, saya punya kesempatan kasih balik. Saya tidak bisa kembaliin tahun-tahun yang saya rusak. Tapi saya bisa jaga supaya dia, di sisa hidupnya, ingatnya cuma yang baik-baik. Saya bisa kasih dia anak yang seharusnya dia punya. Cuma itu satu-satunya barang berharga yang pernah saya kembalikan, Bu Inah, seumur hidup saya. Tolong jangan suruh saya mencurinya lagi."
Bu Inah menatapnya lama. Lalu, tanpa kata, ia masuk ke rumahnya, dan keesokan paginya menaruh sepiring kue di pagar Sukrim, dan tidak pernah lagi menyuruhnya berhenti.

Bulan-bulan berlalu. Pak Krim menjadi pemandangan tetap di kampung itu — lelaki paruh baya yang merawat perempuan tua di ujung gang, yang sabarnya luar biasa, yang katanya disewa oleh anak si nenek yang sukses di kota.

Sukrim, yang otaknya tetap otak maling, menyalurkan kejahatannya ke arah yang tak pernah ia duga. Ia mencuri lagi — tapi sekarang ia mencuri bunga dari taman kota untuk ditaruh di meja ibunya, dan mencuri resep dari warung tetangga untuk variasi masakan, dan satu kali, ia mencuri waktu dari kematian itu sendiri: ketika ibunya demam tinggi tengah malam, Sukrim yang tidak punya uang menggendong perempuan tua itu di punggungnya, berlari tiga kilometer ke puskesmas dalam gelap, dan membayar obatnya dengan — ia tidak akan pernah mengaku ini juga — mencopet dompetnya sendiri dari masa depan, yaitu menggadaikan satu-satunya barang berharga yang ia punya, gelang. Gelang yang dulu ia curi dan berikan kepada ibunya. Yang entah bagaimana masih ada, di laci, disimpan ibunya selama empat puluh tahun sebagai harta paling berharga, pemberian anaknya yang baik.
Sukrim menggadaikan kembali gelang curian itu untuk menyelamatkan nyawa perempuan yang menyimpannya. Lingkaran penuh dari satu pencurian kecil, empat puluh tahun, akhirnya menebus dirinya sendiri.

Ibunya sembuh. Ia tidak pernah tahu soal gelang itu. Dan kalau suatu hari ia mencarinya dan tidak menemukannya, Sukrim sudah menyiapkan kebohongan terakhir: *Sukrim yang ambil, Bu. Buat dikenang-kenang di rantau. Katanya biar selalu ingat Ibu.*
Kebohongan yang, kalau dipikir-pikir, adalah satu-satunya hal benar yang pernah ia ucapkan.
Ibunya meninggal pada suatu pagi yang tenang, di musim ketika hujan baru mulai, hampir setahun setelah Sukrim pulang.

Ia pergi dalam tidur, dengan damai, tanpa rasa sakit, di rumah yang bersih dan hangat yang dirawat oleh seorang lelaki yang ia kira tetangga baik. Dan pada hari-hari terakhirnya, ketika ia sudah sangat lemah, ada satu sore yang akan Sukrim simpan di dadanya sebagai satu-satunya harta yang tak pernah ia curi melainkan diberikan kepadanya.
Sore itu ibunya memandanginya lama, sambil Sukrim menyuapinya bubur. Memandanginya dengan cara yang berbeda. Dan ibunya berkata, pelan, hampir berbisik:
"Pak Krim."
"Iya, Bu."

"Kamu ini..." — ia berhenti, dan ada sesuatu di matanya, sesuatu yang naik dari tempat yang sangat dalam, dari bawah semua yang sudah dicuri darinya — "...kamu ini baik sekali sama saya. Padahal kita bukan siapa-siapa."
"Saya cuma disuruh anak Ibu, Bu."

Ibunya tersenyum. Dan lalu ia berkata hal yang membuat sendok di tangan Sukrim berhenti di udara, hal yang tidak akan pernah ia tahu apakah datang dari kepikunan atau dari sesuatu yang lebih dalam yang bertahan di bawah kepikunan, sesuatu yang tidak butuh ingatan untuk tahu:
"Anak saya," kata ibunya pelan, masih tersenyum, matanya menatap lurus ke mata Sukrim, "tidak pernah kerja jauh, ya, Pak Krim?"
Sukrim tidak bisa menjawab.

"Tidak apa-apa," bisik ibunya, dan tangannya yang ringan dan tua naik, gemetar, dan menyentuh pipi Sukrim, persis seperti dulu, empat puluh tahun lalu, sebelum semuanya. "Tidak apa-apa, Nak. Ibu pura-pura juga, kok. Dari kemarin-kemarin. Biar kamu tidak sedih."
Mereka berdua, ternyata, telah saling menyamar.

Selama berbulan-bulan Sukrim mengira ia menjaga ibunya dari kebenaran. Dan selama berbulan-bulan, di suatu tempat di bawah kabut yang mengambil namanya dan harga beras dan lagu-lagu lama, ibunya telah mengenali anaknya — mungkin tidak setiap hari, mungkin tidak sebagai fakta yang bisa ia pegang, tapi sebagai sesuatu yang lebih tua dari fakta, sesuatu yang tahu lewat sentuhan tangan dan cara seseorang menyisakan lauk terbaik dan menggendongmu tiga kilometer dalam hujan. Ibu mengenali anaknya bukan dengan ingatan. Dengan hal yang tinggal setelah ingatan habis.

Dan ia, yang mengetahuinya, memilih ikut berpura-pura. Memberi anaknya hadiah yang anaknya kira sedang ia berikan kepada ibunya: kesempatan untuk menjadi orang yang lebih baik, tanpa beban seluruh masa lalu. Dua orang, di satu rumah kecil, masing-masing berpura-pura demi melindungi yang lain dari kebenaran, sementara kebenaran itu — bahwa mereka saling tahu, saling memaafkan, saling mencintai melewati segala yang telah dicuri dan dirusak — duduk di antara mereka sepanjang waktu, hangat, tak terucap, dan utuh.

Sukrim memeluk ibunya, akhirnya, pertama kali sejak pulang, dan menangis — bukan sebagai Pak Krim, melainkan sebagai Sukrim, anak yang sebenarnya, yang buruk dan menyesal dan pulang terlambat tapi pulang juga. Dan ibunya memeluknya kembali dengan lengan yang nyaris tak bertenaga, dan berkata, ke telinga anaknya, kalimat yang ia tabung empat tahun di penjara untuk didengar:
"Akhirnya kamu pulang."
Sukrim tidak mencuri apa pun lagi setelah ibunya tiada.

Ini bukan karena ia mendadak menjadi suci; perubahan pada orang seperti Sukrim tidak datang seperti petir. Tangannya masih kadang gatal di pasar, masih kadang lebih cepat dari kepalanya. Tapi setiap kali, ia teringat satu hal, dan tangannya berhenti.

Ia teringat bahwa ada satu kali dalam hidupnya ketika ia berhenti mencuri dan mulai mengembalikan, dan bahwa pencurian terbesar yang pernah ia urungkan adalah pencurian yang paling mudah dari semuanya — mengambil dari ibunya yang pikun versi dirinya yang lebih baik, dan menggantinya dengan kebenaran. Ia bisa melakukannya tiap hari. Tidak pernah ia lakukan. Ia menjaga harta itu, satu-satunya harta yang pernah ia jaga, sampai pemiliknya pergi membawanya.

Dan di kampung itu, orang-orang masih kadang menyebutnya Pak Krim, sebab tidak semua orang tahu cerita yang sebenarnya. Dan Sukrim membiarkannya. Sebab nama itu, yang ia karang sebagai kebohongan, telah menjadi satu-satunya nama dalam hidupnya yang ia peroleh dengan menjadi baik — dan seorang maling tua tahu betul bahwa satu hal yang kau peroleh dengan jujur jauh lebih berharga daripada seribu hal yang kau curi.

Di teras rumah ibunya, yang kini rumahnya, masih ada sepiring kue dari Bu Inah setiap Jumat. Dan setiap Jumat, Sukrim menyisihkan potongan terakhir — bukan untuk dirinya — dan meletakkannya di meja, di tempat ibunya dulu duduk, untuk seseorang yang sudah tidak ada tapi yang, ia yakin betul, masih kadang pulang. Di waktu-waktu yang tepat. Lewat jalan yang tidak butuh ingatan.

en.title: At the Right Time
en.excerpt: For thirty-two years, I have interrogated human beings, and not a single one has ever managed to make me say something I didn't want to say. My subordinates call me Tembok—The Wall. Not a…
body: For thirty-two years, I have interrogated human beings, and not a single one has ever managed to make me say something I didn't want to say. My subordinates call me *Tembok*—The Wall. Not a nickname I chose—I would never choose a moniker so insolently unpoetic—but it stuck, because that is exactly what I am. You can scream, cry, slam the desk, or lie with the cunning of a devil, and I will just sit quietly staring at you until you tire out, until you crack, until the truth seeps out of you on its own like water seeping through a wall that finally surrenders to the rain.
I never crack. That is my entire job. Other people are paid to build things; I am paid not to collapse.

So I will not explain to you—because I have no explanation—why on a Tuesday afternoon in interrogation room number three, in front of a two-bit motorcycle thief named Sukrim who was crying and calling out for his mother, I started crying too.

Not just shedding a tear. Crying. Sobbing, with snot, with shaking shoulders, with all the humiliation that accompanies it. In front of Sukrim. Who finally stopped crying over himself and, with confusion and a bit of horror, slid a packet of tissues across the table and said, "T-take it easy, Sir." Then, because he was a thief and a thief's brain is never truly on vacation: "If you're dealing with a lot of problems, Sir, that motorbike from yesterday wasn't actually me who—"
"Shut up, Sukrim."
"Yes, Sir."

That is how I ended up in this room, facing this woman, who became my toughest adversary in a thirty-two-year career—tougher than drug lords, tougher than murderers, tougher than everyone I have ever stared down into a confession.

Her name is Mrs. Laras. A psychologist. They mandated me to see her eight times before I was allowed back on duty, because an interrogator who cries harder than his suspect is, as my superior put it with extraordinary diplomacy, "an asset in need of recalibration." I am fifty-eight years old. I have already been calibrated. What they meant, if they were being honest, was: *The Wall is cracked, call a handyman to take a look.*
I went in with one strategy. This is an interrogation. And I will not be the one interrogated.
So I sat in her chair. The psychologist's chair, facing the patient's chair. I leaned back, and when she walked in, I pointed to the opposite chair with my chin. "Please, have a seat."

Mrs. Laras looked at the situation for a moment—me in her chair, her empty chair opposite—then, without the slightest expression, she sat in the patient's chair. Crossed her legs. Folded her arms. Waited.
*Good*, I thought. *She's playing my game*.
"So," I said, with a voice that once made a two-meter-tall thug wet himself in an iron chair, "tell me about yourself."
"Me first," she said. "You cried in front of Sukrim when he called for his mother. What happened to your mother?"
A three-second silence.

Three seconds that, in the entire history of my interrogations, were the first three seconds where I felt the floor shift. I had just seized the interrogator's chair, commanding the room perfectly—and this woman, from the patient's chair, from a losing position, had just stabbed me right under the ribs while letting me feel like I was winning.
I cleared my throat. "My mother is healthy. She still cooks *rendang*."

"Good." She nodded. "That means we still have seven and a half sessions to figure out why you changed the subject so fast, and why a man whose mother still cooks rendang cried when a thief called for his."
That was the moment I knew this would be a war. And it was also the moment, though I wouldn't admit it even at gunpoint, I felt something I hadn't felt in any room for a long time: intrigued.
Second session, I brought my best weapon. Silence.

Silence is an art. Laypeople think interrogations are about questions; they aren't. Interrogation is about the silence you arrange in such a way that the opponent can't stand it and fills it themselves. I once won a nine-hour silence. I once made a man confess to murder just to end the quiet I created.

So I walked in, sat down—in the patient's chair this time; I didn't mind surrendering a little territory to win the war—and I stayed silent. I stared at a single point on Mrs. Laras's forehead. I didn't move. I didn't blink more than necessary. I became The Wall.

Mrs. Laras stared back at me for about ten seconds. Then she nodded, as if I had just said something perfectly reasonable, opened her desk drawer, pulled out half-finished knitting—a scarf, an incredibly ugly moss green, a color that makes you think of a dead pond—and started knitting.
*Click*. *Click*. *Click*.

One hour. She knitted for a full hour while I sat in my majestic, combat silence, a silence that had brought down major criminals, and this woman treated it like a relaxing afternoon break. Occasionally she hummed. At the forty-minute mark, she offered me tea. I didn't answer; answering meant losing. She poured it anyway, placed it in front of me, and I watched the tea steam, then cool, then form a thin film on the surface, and I didn't touch it, and that—I convinced myself—was a victory.

At the fifty-fifth minute, she said, without looking up from her knitting: "You're good at being quiet, Sir. Truly. But I get paid by the hour, not by the word. So you're torturing your own wallet, not me." *Click*. "And the tea is free. It's a shame, really."
I went home that day with a feeling I hadn't felt since the Academy: utterly defeated by a civilian armed with two knitting needles and a teapot.
Third session, I changed tactics. If she wanted a story, I'd give her a story.

I fabricated a trauma. I am the best interrogator in this province; I know exactly the shape of the wounds psychologists look for, because I've dragged them out of other people thousands of times. So I crafted a masterpiece: a harsh childhood, a heavy-handed alcoholic father, a beloved dog dying after being hit by a truck right in front of

my eyes—complete with pauses in all the right places, a slightly choked voice at the climax, and a single tear I allowed to fall and immediately wiped away as if in shame. I even added the small detail that always seals the deal: I stopped midway, apologized, and said, "Sorry, I'm not used to talking about this." A professional touch. If she swallowed it, she'd write in her report that I was "processing," and I'd be free.
Mrs. Laras listened to the whole thing. Nodding. Taking notes. When I finished, she looked at her notes, looked at me, and asked in the friendliest tone in the world:
"What was the dog's name?"
"...Boni."
"Earlier you said Doni."

Silence. A silence different from my silence. This was the silence of someone caught red-handed, and I knew exactly what it felt like from the other side of the table, thousands of times, but never from this side.

"Sir." She put her pen down. And for the first time, there was something almost like tenderness in her voice, which only made it more unbearable. "I have spent twenty years listening to people lie about their feelings. You are good. Really. Top five I've ever met. But a person who genuinely has no wounds wouldn't bother fabricating one so perfectly just to escape this room. The empty ones, they just walk out. The one who constructs a dead dog with such detail, with two names because they were too busy inventing to remember—" she smiled faintly, "—that is a person guarding something real, guarded so tightly that they'd rather create a fake wound than expose the real one. You didn't make that up to lie to me, Sir. You made it up so you wouldn't have to touch the real thing. Even your lie is a shield."
I didn't answer. But beneath the table, my hands clenched until my knuckles turned white.
Because this woman, with her ugly knitting and free tea and deadpan delivery, had just done what no one had successfully done to The Wall in thirty-two years.

She found the crack. And she didn't press it. That was the terrifying part. I can fight someone who presses the crack. This one just pointed it out to me, then waited, as if the crack belonged to me and it was up to me what to do with it.
I fought back. Of course I did. I don't surrender that easily; I am The Wall.

I did what a cop does when backed into a corner. I investigated her. I ran Mrs. Laras's background through channels I shouldn't explain and which, legally, I shouldn't have used. I looked for a weak point, because that is how wars are won: find the opponent's crack, and press.
I found it, and for a moment I felt like I was back in control, and a few seconds later I felt like a bastard.

Her clinic was nearly bankrupt. Closing next month. And from a few things I read and a few colleagues I carefully questioned, the picture was quite clear: these were her final sessions. It wasn't just the clinic closing. She was quitting. Walking away from a profession she had practiced for twenty years. I—the annoying mandatory patient, The Wall who constructed a dead dog named Boni-slash-Doni—was one of the final cases in the career of a woman who had decided to stop believing in her own work.

I also found out why, or so I thought. A few years ago, one of her patients—a young kid, depressed, whom she treated for months—didn't make it. It wasn't her fault; colleagues said she did everything right. But I've been an interrogator long enough to know that "it wasn't your fault" is a sentence that never reaches the people who need it most. I kept that kid's name in my head and felt dirty for holding onto it.
I walked into the next session with all that ammunition in my pocket. I was ready to use it. Then something happened before I could fire a shot.

Mrs. Laras arrived late. Mrs. Laras was never late. And when she walked in, there was no knitting, no teapot, no steel demeanor. She looked tired in a way that couldn't be faked—a kind of exhaustion I know very well, because I meet it in the mirror every morning. She sat in the psychologist's chair, her own chair, for the first time since the first session, sighed, and spoke not with a psychologist's voice but with the voice of a human too exhausted to act.

"Mr. Karman. Let's just be honest. I'm tired." She laughed quietly, bitterly, a laugh I recognized because it was exactly like my own. "These are my final weeks. I'm quitting. Not because the clinic is bankrupt—that's just an easy excuse to tell people. I'm quitting because I no longer believe that talking heals anyone. Twenty years I've told people to open up, and half of them walk out of this room just as broken as when they walked in. And some—" she stopped, and I saw the name I was holding in my head flash in her eyes, and I was grateful I hadn't said it, "—some don't walk out at all. So if you want to keep playing 'walls,' go ahead. I throw my hands up. I don't have the energy to fight anymore."
And right there, reader, my entire strategy crumbled.
Because I have a defense for everything. Screaming, crying, coaxing, threatening, silence, lying. I have a wall for every attack known to man.
I do not have a single defense against someone who stops attacking.

You cannot interrogate someone who has already surrendered. My weapons are all designed to pierce defenses; in front of someone who drops all of theirs, my weapons became a pile of useless scrap iron. I sat there with my pockets full of bullets about her clinic and the name of the kid who didn't make it, and I couldn't fire a single one, because you don't shoot someone who is kneeling—not in surrender, but because their legs genuinely can no longer stand.
So I did the thing I least expected to do in any room, to anyone.
I lowered my wall first.
"His name was Joni," I said.
Mrs. Laras looked up. Something in her face changed, but she didn't reach for her pen. That was what allowed me to continue—she didn't reach for her pen.

"My first partner. Thirty years ago. A snot-nosed kid, fresh out of the academy, annoying as hell, his jokes were all terrible—genuinely terrible, Ma'am, the kind that make you embarrassed to have laughed. He liked to save the last piece of gorengan (fried snack) for me even though he bought them. Every time. I told him not to, I told him to just eat it, and every time he said, 'I'm already full, Sir,' while drooling over it. The worst lie I've ever heard. And I'm an interrogator, I know all kinds of lies." I stopped. "That was the first lie I never tore apart. I just let it be. I ate the *gorengan*(fried snack)."
"And then?"

"And then he died. Our fourth month on duty. Not a heroic shootout, nothing worthy of being written on a monument. Just a stupid chase, a motorbike, a truck turning without looking. Done. Twenty-three years old. Died before he could become anything, before he could come up with a funny joke, before he could stop saving the *gorengan*."
"And you cried for him," Mrs. Laras said, softly.
"No." I stared at the cold tea between us. "That's the problem."

And finally, thirty years late, I told her about it—I didn't explain it, I didn't justify it, I just placed it on the table like evidence. The day Joni died, I had a job to do. Informing his family. Handling the reports. Standing tall at the funeral because Joni's mother was hugging me and crying and someone had to be the one who didn't collapse too. So I postponed it. I told myself: *later. Later, I will grieve. At the right time. After everything is settled. When I have a moment*.

I didn't explain to Mrs. Laras what happened after that, because I didn't need to; she's a psychologist, she knows. If you postpone one thing long enough, the postponement stops being a delay and becomes an architecture. I never reached the "right time." There was always the next case, the next suspect, the next reason to be a wall for just one more day. And a wall that stands for thirty years no longer feels like a choice. It feels like bone.

"Then last month," I said, and this was where I began to lose my grip on my voice, "they gave me a new partner. A snot-nosed kid. Fresh out of the academy. Annoying. Terrible jokes." I laughed, a short laugh that came out wrong, closer to something else. "His name is Bagas. On his first day he told three jokes and two fell flat and the other one, I don't even know, I still don't get it. And last week we worked overtime, bought *gorengan*, and he—"
I stopped.
"He saved the last one," Mrs. Laras said.

"For me. Without being asked. And when I told him to just eat it, he said—" my throat closed, and I, The Wall, fifty-eight years old, had to stop and wait before I could finish, "—he said, 'I'm already full, Sir.' While drooling over it. The same lie. The exact same terrible lie. Thirty years, Ma'am. Thirty years the wall stood, and what tore it down wasn't a bullet, wasn't a case, wasn't anything big. Just one leftover gorengan and one terrible lie from a kid I barely even knew."
"And you cried."

"In interrogation room number three." My voice finally broke, in that patient's chair, and I let it. "Thirty years I held back tears for a dead kid, and when it finally came out, it chose the single most humiliating, undignified, entirely wrong moment in the history of the republic's entire police force—" I laughed again, a wet, dreadful, relieved laugh, "—in front of a motorcycle thief named Sukrim, who thought I was crazy, and offered me a tissue, and told me to take it easy. A thief. Consoling me. With office tissues bought with state money."

And Mrs. Laras—the psychologist who had thrown her hands up, who had stopped believing, who had packed twenty years into cardboard boxes—Mrs. Laras laughed. A genuine laugh, until her eyes were wet, the laugh of someone who had just heard the saddest and funniest thing all at once, which in this world are often the exact same thing.
"Sukrim," she said, shaking her head. "Office tissues."
"State money," I said.

And we both laughed, two old people in a small room that would close next month, laughing at a thief and a box of tissues, until the laughter slowly turned into something else, a thing with no name, a thing standing right on the border between the most comical and the most unbearable things in life, and we let it, because in the end, that is the only place where people like us can rest.
We sat in silence for a long time afterward. But not my combat silence. A different silence—one that demanded nothing, that wasn't waiting to see who would crack first.
Then, because I am an interrogator and thirty-two years of habit do not die in a minute, I saw the crack in her face. The kind I usually look for. And without really deciding to, I said softly:
"That kid who didn't make it. The one you treated for years."
Her face froze. "You investigated me."

"I am The Wall. It's what I do." I held her gaze. "I walked into this session intending to use that to attack you. To win. That was my initial plan today. I was going to say something cruel about him so you would falter, and I could walk out of this room without digging up Joni."
"Why didn't you?"

"Because you surrendered first," I said. "And it turns out, I can't shoot someone who has laid down their weapon. That is the only line I have never crossed in thirty-two years, and I only found out it existed today."
She didn't say anything.

"You're quitting," I said, "because you think talking doesn't heal anyone. Because there was one kid you didn't save, and you carry him in your eyes to this day—I saw it, earlier, when you almost mentioned him. You think these twenty years are a failure because there was one you couldn't send home." I paused. "But you're wrong, Ma'am. And you know you're wrong, because just now, in this room, you made a fifty-eight-year-old wall cry over a kid who's been dead for thirty years. You didn't cure me—grief doesn't cure, I'm old enough to know that. But you made me stop carrying it alone. That is not meaningless. That is almost everything."
That gaze of steel finally crumbled. Her eyes were wet, and she laughed and cried all at once, in the manner of someone who had just been saved by the person who came to be saved.
"Damn you, Wall," she said, wiping her eyes roughly with the back of her hand. "I'm the psychologist here."
"And I'm the interrogator," I said. "So believe me when I tell you: you're lying about wanting to quit. I know a lie. That's the worst one I've heard since the *gorengan*."
She didn't quit. That was information I only got later.

The clinic still closed—money is money, and no amount of wisdom pays the rent. But she moved, opened up again, smaller, in a cramped shophouse near a market that smelled of salted fish all day. I know because—and this is the part that still makes me feel ridiculous when I remember it—I became her patient for two full years after my eight mandatory sessions ran out. Voluntarily. The Wall, voluntarily coming every two weeks to a shophouse smelling of salted fish, bringing gorengan, and saving the last piece for her. Every time. And every time she would say, "I'm already full, Sir," while drooling over it, and every time I did not tear that lie apart. I just let it be. I ate the *gorengan*.

Bagas never knew a thing about this. The kid only knew that his scary senior was suddenly not so scary, and sometimes, if he saved the last gorengan, his senior would stare at him too long with a weird expression before saying, "Just eat it, Gas." He assumed I was just old and sentimental about food. Let him. There are things you don't need to pass down with words; you just pass them down by not telling him to stop saving the *gorengan*.

On the day I retired, a few years later, there was a small party at the precinct. A lot of cops, a lot of speeches, a lot of young people who didn't know why the old man in the corner was nicknamed The Wall and didn't dare ask. Bagas—no longer a snot-nosed kid, he had his own snot-nosed partner now—gave a terrible speech, and I laughed in the wrong places, and he didn't know why.
And in the corner of the room stood one person who wasn't a cop, with an ugly moss-green scarf she had finally finished knitting for whoever knows who, wrapped around her own neck.
