Before I went home, Mrs. Laras handed me something. The feelings journal she used to make me fill out in those early weeks—the one I filled out like surveillance reports just to annoy her. *0800: subject feels nothing. 0830: still feels nothing. 0900: subject suspects psychologist is winning. 0930: subject denies said suspicion. Attachments: none.*
"The last page," she said. "I've waited for you to fill it out since the first session. Nine years, Sir. I'm patient."

So at my retirement party, in the corner of the room, under cheap balloons and a banner that misspelled my name, an old man once nicknamed The Wall opened the final page and wrote, for the first time, something true about his feelings. Not long. The Wall would never be long-winded.

*Joni. I ate your last gorengan thirty years ago and never said thank you, and I didn't cry for you because I was busy being strong for your mother, and it turns out I never stopped being busy. I'm sorry I'm late. But someone told me, and she's a psychologist so she probably knows: there is no such thing as being late. There is only the time when you are finally able to bear it.*

I closed the book. I didn't cry—I had already cried, back then, at a time that turned out, despite being in front of a thief, despite being thirty years late, despite being the most humiliating moment in the history of this republic's police force, to be the only time that was ever truly right. Not because it arrived at a good moment. But because, for the first time since Joni died, when those tears finally came, there was someone in the room who didn't tell me to stop.

Sukrim, if you're curious, still went to prison. He really did steal that motorbike. But I wrote a note on his file that I don't normally write for anyone: *Suspect was cooperative. Showed empathy to the officer*. The judge was probably confused reading it.

I wasn't. I know exactly what he did for me, in room number three, with state-funded tissues. He comforted a wall that was crumbling, and he didn't tell me to stop, and for a two-bit thief, that was probably the only noble thing he ever did in his entire life—and he did it for the man who was locking him up. At a time that, as it turns out, was also right.

sides.title: The Thief Who Came Home
body: Sukrim got out of prison on a Tuesday, and the very first thing he stole was an orange.

Not because he was hungry—at the gate they had given him a wrapped portion of rice and bus fare. He stole the orange from a cart in front of the penitentiary because his hands, after four years, had forgotten how *not* to steal, and the orange was already in his pocket before his head had a chance to intervene. He stood on the sidewalk holding the stolen orange with the feeling of a man who had just failed in the first minute of his freedom, and he almost returned it, then realized that returning a stolen item to a crowded cart would look far more suspicious than stealing it, then decided to just eat it, then felt guilty, then—and this is the important part—slipped the exact price of the orange onto that same cart when the vendor wasn't looking.

Stealing an orange, then secretly paying for it. That was Sukrim. That was the entirety of Sukrim, really, in one motion: a man whose hands were wicked but whose heart never joined in, who spent twenty years stealing little things only to regret them in even littler ways.
He took the bus to his hometown. He went home to see his mother.

During his four years inside, the one thing that kept Sukrim sane was imagining this scene: he knocks on the door, his mother opens it, and—after chewing him out thoroughly, of course, she had every right to be angry—she hugs him and says, *finally you came home.* He had already practiced his remorseful face. He had prepared his apology, revising it hundreds of times in his cell, until it was perfect.
He knocked. His mother opened the door. And his mother said:
"Who are you looking for, son?"
Sukrim stood there as the perfect apology evaporated from his head.
"Mom," he said. "It's me. Sukrim."

His mother—smaller than he remembered, paler, with kind and completely empty eyes—tilted her head. "Sukrim," she repeated, tasting the name the way one tastes a stranger's cooking. "Which Sukrim? I'm sorry, I am a bit forgetful."

The next-door neighbor, Mrs. Inah, who had heard from her fence, came over to explain in a low voice. It had been like this for two years. Senility. The doctor at the clinic called it a long term that Mrs. Inah couldn't memorize. Sometimes his mother remembered things from fifty years ago perfectly—the names of elementary school friends, the price of rice back in the day, songs no one sang anymore. But the recent things, the new things, yesterday—all of it slipped from her mind like water from cupped hands.
"She doesn't even remember her own son anymore," Mrs. Inah said, then hurriedly covered her mouth, realizing how cruel it sounded.

Sukrim nodded. He didn't cry. He was a thief; he knew how to make sure his face didn't betray him. He simply stood on the porch of his childhood home, clutching the remainder of a stolen orange in his pocket, realizing that he had spent four years imprisoning himself just to come home to the only person in the world waiting for him, only to find that she had, in her own way, left first.
This is what a sane person would do in this situation: he would sit down, explain patiently, show photos, replay memories, and try to call his mother back to the surface.

Sukrim tried that for three days. For three days he said, "Mom, it's Sukrim, your son," and for three days his mother looked at him with the exact same empty kindness, and once—this was the most agonizing—his mother grew terrified, backed into a corner, and whispered, "what do you want, I don't have any money," as if her own son were a thief breaking into her house. Which, if Sukrim were honest, technically he was, and that made him laugh bitterly in the bathroom that night until his laughter turned into something else.
On the fourth day, Sukrim stopped trying to be Sukrim.

It came to him as a thief's idea, because Sukrim only had a thief's brain, and a thief's brain asks one question about everything: *what can I take from here?* Only this time, for the first time in his life, the question reversed. It wasn't *what can I take.* It was: *what can I give back to a woman who has lost almost everything, including me?*

His mother didn't remember having a son named Sukrim. Fine. But his mother remembered the old things. So Sukrim sat down, on the fourth day, and instead of forcing his mother to remember him, he asked:
"Mom, did you ever have a child?"
And his mother's face lit up.
"I did," his mother said, and for the first time, her eyes weren't empty. "A son. His name was..."—she frowned, searching—"...Sukrim. Yes, Sukrim. A good boy. Very smart, he was."
Sukrim, who was not a good boy and was not smart and was sitting right across from his mother, said, "Oh really? Tell me about him, Mom."

And his mother told the story. About Sukrim—his mother's version of Sukrim, the Sukrim who lived in the old woman's head, who turned out to be vastly different from the real Sukrim. The Sukrim in his mother's memory was a boy who diligently studied the Quran, who was top of his class, who once bought his mother a bracelet with his very first paycheck. Parts of it were true—Sukrim *did* once give his mother a bracelet, though that bracelet, he would never confess, was stolen from the market. Parts of it were entirely false—Sukrim had never been top of any class except, perhaps, the most frequently arrested. But his mother told the story with such pure pride, about a boy who was so good, that Sukrim understood something that made his chest tight.

Dementia had stolen his mother's memory. But before stealing it, dementia did something strange and almost merciful: it edited. It discarded the disappointing version of Sukrim—the one who got arrested again and again, who made his mother cry at the police station, who was last seen by his mother from behind bars—and kept only his best version. The version that gave the bracelet. The version he was supposed to be. His mother's mind, in its collapse, had guarded the only part of Sukrim worth guarding.

And Sukrim, the thief, sat across from that treasure—a better version of himself, preserved intact within the mind of the only person who had ever loved him—and for the first time in his life, he decided not to steal it. He decided, instead, to guard it.
So Sukrim became someone else.

He didn't claim to be Sukrim anymore. That only made his mother scared, or confused, or—worse—sometimes it almost made his mother remember the things better left forgotten. So when his mother asked, "who are you, son?", Sukrim answered with the noblest lie he had ever woven:
"I'm the new neighbor, Mom. Mr. Sukrim... er—Mr. Krim. I'm helping out around here. Your son asked me to."
"My son? Sukrim?"
"Yes, Mom. He entrusted you to me. Because he's working far away right now. A good job, Mom. He's successful now."

And his mother's face would light up again, and she would say, "yes, my son is indeed smart," and Sukrim—Mr. Krim—would nod and sweep the floor and cook and replace the dead lightbulbs, doing for his mother all the things a good son was supposed to do, disguised as a stranger hired by a good son who never existed.

The cosmic joke of this whole affair was not lost on Sukrim. He had spent his life in disguise—disguised as a buyer before stealing, disguised as an innocent man in front of the police, disguised as everything he wasn't. And now, for the final and greatest job of his career as a fraud, he was disguised as a kind stranger, all to protect an old woman from the truth that her son wasn't that good. The most honest disguise of his life was pretending to not be himself.
Sukrim's days, after that, became strange and sweet and agonizing.

Every morning he woke up in the room that used to be his, and became Mr. Krim. He cooked for his mother, and his mother praised him—"you cook so well, Mr. Krim, almost as good as my own cooking used to be"—and Sukrim held back a laugh, because that recipe *was* his mother's recipe, which he had memorized from peeking decades ago. He sat with his mother on the porch, and his mother would tell stories about the great Sukrim, and Mr. Krim would listen with feigned awe about himself, occasionally adding details.
"He says he owns a big house now, Mom," Mr. Krim said one afternoon, building a better version of his own life, brick by brick, for an audience of one.

"Oh really?" His mother's eyes sparkled. "Thank goodness. We used to have it so hard, Mr. Krim. I only sold cakes. But I always told Sukrim, don't be a thief even if you're poor. A thief..."—his mother shook her head—"...a thief steals from people, but what he steals the most is from his own mother. He steals his mother's pride. I always told him that."
Sukrim swept the already clean floor so his mother couldn't see his face.
"Good thing Sukrim wasn't like that," his mother continued, smiling. "Good thing my son became a good man."
"Yes, Mom," Sukrim said, with his back to his mother. "Good thing."
There was one afternoon when it almost all fell apart.

Mrs. Inah, the neighbor, who couldn't bear watching this charade drag on, pulled Sukrim to the fence and whispered angrily. "How long are you going to keep this up, Krim? That's your mother. She has the right to know her son came home. You're conning her every day!"
"I'm not conning her, Mrs. Inah," Sukrim said quietly.
"Then what do you call it? You're claiming to be a neighbor. You're saying you're successful when you just got out of prison. It's all a lie."
Sukrim was quiet for a moment. Then he said something he didn't know was inside him until it came out:

"Mrs. Inah, all my life I stole from my mother. Not money—I never stole her money, she didn't have any. I stole something far more wicked. Every time I got caught, I stole her pride. Every time she had to come to the police station, that look on her face—I stole that, I humiliated her in front of the whole village, over and over again, for forty years. I am a thief who stole the most from the victim who loved me the most."
He swallowed hard.

"Now she's forgotten all of that. She's forgotten everything I stole from her. And for the first time, Ma'am, I have a chance to give back. I can't return the years I ruined. But I can make sure that, for the rest of her life, she only remembers the good things. I can give her the son she was supposed to have. That's the only precious thing I've ever returned, Mrs. Inah, in my entire life. Please don't ask me to steal it again."
Mrs. Inah stared at him for a long time. Then, without a word, she went into her house, and the next morning she placed a plate of cakes on Sukrim's fence, and never again asked him to stop.

Months passed. Mr. Krim became a permanent fixture in the village—a middle-aged man caring for the old woman at the end of the alley, who was extraordinarily patient, who was supposedly hired by the grandmother's successful son in the city.

Sukrim, whose brain remained a thief's brain, channeled his criminality in ways he never expected. He stole again—but now he stole flowers from the city park to put on his mother's table, and stole recipes from the neighboring food stall for variety in his cooking, and once, he stole time from death itself: when his mother had a high fever in the middle of the night, a penniless Sukrim carried the old woman on his back, ran three kilometers to the clinic in the dark, and paid for the medicine by—he would never confess to this either—pickpocketing his own wallet from the future; that is, pawning the only valuable thing he owned: the bracelet. The bracelet he had stolen and given to his mother all those years ago. Which somehow was still there, in the drawer, kept by his mother for twenty years as her most prized possession, a gift from her good son.
Sukrim pawned that stolen bracelet again to save the life of the woman who kept it. The full circle of one petty theft, across forty years, finally redeeming itself.

His mother recovered. She never found out about the bracelet. And if one day she looked for it and couldn't find it, Sukrim had prepared a final lie: *Sukrim took it, Mom. As a keepsake overseas. He said it was so he'd always remember you.*
A lie which, upon reflection, was the only true thing he had ever said.
His mother passed away on a quiet morning, in the season when the rains had just begun, almost a year after Sukrim had come home.

She went in her sleep, peacefully, without pain, in a clean and warm house cared for by a man she thought was a kind neighbor. And in her final days, when she was very weak, there was one afternoon that Sukrim would keep in his chest as the only treasure he never stole but was given to him.
That afternoon his mother looked at him for a long time, while Sukrim fed her porridge. Looked at him in a different way. And his mother said, softly, almost whispering:
"Mr. Krim."
"Yes, Mom."

"You..."—she stopped, and there was something in her eyes, something rising from a very deep place, from beneath all that had been stolen from her—"...you are so very kind to me. Even though we are nobody to each other."
"I was just asked by your son, Mom."

His mother smiled. And then she said the thing that made the spoon in Sukrim's hand freeze in mid-air, the thing he would never know whether it came from senility or from something deeper that survived beneath the senility, something that didn't need memory to know:
"My son," his mother said quietly, still smiling, her eyes looking straight into Sukrim's, "is not actually working far away, is he, Mr. Krim?"
Sukrim couldn't answer.

"It's okay," his mother whispered, and her light, aged hand rose, trembling, and touched Sukrim's cheek, exactly as it had done twenty years ago, before everything. "It's okay, son. I've been pretending too, you know. For a while now. So you wouldn't be sad."
The two of them, as it turned out, had been disguised from each other.

For months Sukrim thought he was protecting his mother from the truth. And for months, somewhere beneath the fog that took his name and the price of rice and the old songs, his mother had recognized her son—maybe not every day, maybe not as a fact she could hold onto, but as something older than facts, something known through the touch of a hand and the way someone saves the best side dish and carries you three kilometers in the rain. A mother recognizes her child not by memory. But by the thing that remains after memory runs out.

And she, knowing this, chose to play along. Giving her son the gift her son thought he was giving her: the chance to be a better person, without the burden of his entire past. Two people, in one small house, each pretending in order to protect the other from the truth, while that truth—that they knew each other, forgave each other, loved each other past everything that had been stolen and ruined—sat between them the whole time, warm, unspoken, and whole.

Sukrim hugged his mother, finally, for the first time since coming home, and cried—not as Mr. Krim, but as Sukrim, the real son, who was flawed and regretful and came home late but came home anyway. And his mother hugged him back with arms that barely had any strength, and said, into her son's ear, the words he had saved up for four years in prison to hear:
"Finally you came home."
Sukrim didn't steal anything else after his mother was gone.

This wasn't because he suddenly became a saint; change in a person like Sukrim doesn't arrive like a lightning bolt. His hands still sometimes itched at the market, still were sometimes faster than his head. But every time, he remembered one thing, and his hands would stop.

He remembered that there was one time in his life when he stopped stealing and started giving back, and that the greatest theft he ever aborted was the easiest theft of all—taking the better version of himself from his senile mother, and replacing it with the truth. He could have done it every day. He never did. He guarded that treasure, the only treasure he ever guarded, until its owner took it away with her.

And in that village, people still sometimes call him Mr. Krim, because not everyone knows the real story. And Sukrim lets them. Because that name, which he fabricated as a lie, had become the only name in his life he earned by being good—and an old thief knows full well that one thing you earn honestly is far more precious than a thousand things you steal.

On the porch of his mother's house, which is now his house, there is still a plate of cakes from Mrs. Inah every Friday. And every Friday, Sukrim sets aside the last piece—not for himself—and places it on the table, where his mother used to sit, for someone who is no longer there but who, he is absolutely certain, still sometimes comes home. At the right times. Through paths that do not require memory.

title: Pabrik Mimpi
excerpt: Di pabrik itu, mimpi dibuat pada shift malam, sebab hanya pada malam hari dunia cukup sunyi untuk menuangkannya tanpa tumpah. Namanya tidak tertulis di plang mana pun. Bangunannya besar dan…
body: Di pabrik itu, mimpi dibuat pada shift malam, sebab hanya pada malam hari dunia cukup sunyi untuk menuangkannya tanpa tumpah.

Namanya tidak tertulis di plang mana pun. Bangunannya besar dan tua di pinggir kota, dengan cerobong yang tidak pernah mengeluarkan asap melainkan sesekali mengeluarkan cahaya — semburat warna yang tidak punya nama, yang naik ke langit malam dan larut di antara bintang, dan orang-orang kota yang kebetulan terjaga akan menengadah dan merasa, tanpa tahu kenapa, rindu pada sesuatu yang belum pernah mereka miliki. Itu adalah kebocoran. Mimpi yang tidak sengaja tumpah dari cerobong. Manajemen selalu menghitungnya sebagai kerugian.

Di dalam, ratusan buruh bekerja di sepanjang ban berjalan, merangkai mimpi dari bahan-bahan yang tidak akan kaupercaya kalau kusebutkan: seuntai tawa yang direkam dari anak-anak sebelum mereka belajar malu, sekilo keheningan yang dikeruk dari dasar danau, warna langit pukul lima sore yang dipanen dengan jaring halus, potongan-potongan wajah orang yang sudah tiada yang dikumpulkan dari ingatan yang membuangnya. Semua ini dicampur, ditakar, dijahit, lalu dikemas ke dalam kapsul-kapsul kecil sebening embun, dan dikirim ke seluruh dunia untuk diselipkan ke dalam tidur orang-orang yang membutuhkannya.
Dan di antara ratusan buruh itu, di stasiun paling ujung, tempat cahaya paling redup dan ban berjalan paling pelan, bekerja seorang lelaki tua bernama Pak Wangsa.

Pak Wangsa adalah perajin mimpi terbaik yang pernah dimiliki pabrik itu, dan pabrik itu memperlakukannya persis seperti dunia selalu memperlakukan yang terbaik: dengan menyerahkan kepadanya pekerjaan yang paling sulit dan paling tidak terlihat.

Ia ditugaskan di bagian mimpi-mimpi khusus. Bukan mimpi massal — bukan mimpi terbang, mimpi jatuh, mimpi ujian yang belum belajar, yang diproduksi ribuan sehari oleh mesin. Melainkan mimpi pesanan. Mimpi yang dirancang untuk satu orang, satu malam, satu kebutuhan yang tak tergantikan. Seorang ibu yang kehilangan anaknya dan cuma ingin, sekali lagi, mendengar suaranya memanggil "Bu". Seorang lelaki tua di rumah jompo yang ingin berdansa sekali lagi dengan istri yang sudah lima puluh tahun tiada. Seorang anak di rumah sakit yang ingin, untuk satu malam, berlari.

Pak Wangsa membuat mimpi-mimpi itu dengan tangannya sendiri, satu per satu, dengan ketelitian dan kelembutan yang membuat buruh-buruh muda diam-diam datang menonton ketika ia bekerja. Ia bisa merangkai wajah seseorang yang sudah tiada dari serpihan ingatan yang begitu sedikit sampai kau akan mengira mustahil, dan menyusunnya begitu sempurna sampai orang yang bermimpi akan terbangun dengan pipi basah dan hati yang, untuk pertama kalinya sejak lama, ringan.
Empat puluh tahun ia melakukannya. Empat puluh tahun ia membuat mimpi terindah di dunia, untuk orang-orang yang tak akan pernah ia temui, yang tak akan pernah tahu namanya.
Dan dalam empat puluh tahun itu, Pak Wangsa sendiri tidak pernah bermimpi.
Itu bukan kebetulan. Itu aturan.

Aturan pabrik jelas, tertulis di buku yang diberikan kepada setiap buruh di hari pertama: Perajin tidak diperkenankan mengonsumsi produk. Alasannya masuk akal, kata manajemen. Seorang perajin yang mencicipi mimpinya sendiri akan kehilangan objektivitas. Ia akan mulai membuat mimpi untuk dirinya, bukan untuk pelanggan. Ia akan, kata mereka, "terkontaminasi oleh keinginan pribadi." Maka setiap buruh, di akhir shift, melewati sebuah gerbang yang memastikan mereka tidak menyelipkan satu kapsul pun ke saku. Dan setiap buruh tidur, di rumah masing-masing, tidur yang gelap dan rata dan kosong — tidur tanpa mimpi, sebab mereka telah menghabiskan seluruh mimpi dunia untuk orang lain, dan tak ada yang tersisa untuk mereka sendiri.
Buruh-buruh muda mengeluh soal ini. Pak Wangsa tidak pernah. Ia hanya bekerja, dan pulang, dan tidur tidur kosongnya, dan kembali. Empat puluh tahun.
Tapi ada satu hal kecil yang ia lakukan, yang tidak dilarang buku mana pun sebab tak seorang pun cukup gila untuk membayangkan seseorang akan melakukannya.

Setiap tahun, di malam terakhir sebelum pabrik tutup untuk liburan tahunan, Pak Wangsa membuat satu mimpi tambahan. Di luar pesanan. Dengan bahan sisa yang dikais dari lantai — seuntai tawa yang tercecer, seujung warna senja yang tumpah, serpih wajah yang tak terpakai. Ia merangkainya diam-diam di menit-menit terakhir shift, sebuah mimpi kecil dan sederhana, mimpi yang ia buat untuk satu orang tertentu yang ia kenal betul kebutuhannya.
Mimpi itu untuk dirinya sendiri.

Dan setiap tahun, ia membawanya ke gerbang, dan berdiri di sana memegangnya, dan setiap tahun ia tidak bisa. Sebab gerbang akan mendeteksinya, dan ia akan kehilangan pekerjaannya, dan pekerjaan ini — membuat mimpi untuk orang yang berduka — adalah satu-satunya hal yang membuat hidupnya yang tanpa mimpi terasa berarti. Maka setiap tahun ia meletakkan kembali mimpi buatannya sendiri di meja, tak terpakai, dan berkata pada dirinya sendiri kalimat yang sama:
"Tahun depan, mungkin."

Dan mimpi itu akan larut di atas meja menjelang pagi, seperti embun, seperti segala hal yang tak sempat kaugunakan, dan Pak Wangsa akan pulang ke tidur kosongnya, dan kembali tahun berikutnya untuk membuat mimpi indah bagi seluruh dunia kecuali dirinya.
Pada tahun keempat puluh, sesuatu berubah, dan yang mengubahnya adalah seorang gadis kecil yang riang, dan dalam kesepakatan diam mereka mulai memanggil namanya Riang.

Tentu itu bukan nama aslinya. Namanya Lila. Ia buruh magang termuda yang pernah masuk pabrik, ditempatkan di stasiun sebelah Pak Wangsa karena — kata mandor — "biar belajar dari yang terbaik sebelum yang terbaik pensiun." Sebab itu tahun terakhir Pak Wangsa. Ia sudah tua. Tangannya mulai gemetar, dan mimpi tidak boleh dirangkai dengan tangan gemetar, dan ia tahu, dan pabrik tahu, dan tahun ini adalah tahun terakhirnya sebelum ia dilepas ke masa pensiun yang akan ia habiskan, seperti seluruh hidupnya, tanpa mimpi.
Lila banyak bertanya. Itu menjengkelkan, lalu tidak. "Pak, kenapa mimpi duka dibuat sehalus ini? Bukannya orang berduka maunya lupa?"

"Justru tidak, Nak," kata Pak Wangsa, tangannya tetap bekerja. "Orang berduka tidak mau lupa. Mereka takut lupa. Mimpi yang kita buat bukan untuk membuat mereka melupakan yang hilang. Untuk membuat mereka, satu malam, tidak kehilangannya. Beda tipis. Tapi bedanya segalanya."
Lila memikirkan itu. Lalu ia bertanya hal yang tidak seharusnya ia tanya, hal yang membuat tangan Pak Wangsa berhenti sesaat di atas ban berjalan.
"Pak Wangsa sendiri mimpinya apa?"
Pak Wangsa tidak menjawab hari itu. Tapi Lila, yang muda dan karena itu belum belajar bahwa beberapa pertanyaan sebaiknya dibiarkan, terus memperhatikan.

Dan menjelang malam terakhir tahun itu — malam sebelum liburan, malam terakhir Pak Wangsa akan pernah bekerja di pabrik — Lila melihatnya. Ia melihat lelaki tua itu, di menit-menit sepi akhir shift, mengais bahan sisa dari lantai. Seuntai tawa. Seujung senja. Serpih sebuah wajah. Ia melihatnya merangkai, dengan tangan gemetar yang untuk sekali ini ia paksa tenang, sebuah mimpi kecil. Dan ia melihat wajah Pak Wangsa saat merangkainya — wajah yang berbeda dari wajahnya saat membuat pesanan, wajah yang lebih telanjang, lebih muda, lebih penuh oleh sesuatu yang Lila tak punya nama untuknya tapi yang membuat matanya sendiri panas.
Lila mendekat, diam-diam, dan melihat mimpi apa yang sedang dibuat lelaki tua itu untuk dirinya sendiri, di malam terakhirnya.

Itu bukan mimpi kemuliaan. Bukan mimpi terbang, bukan mimpi muda kembali, bukan mimpi kekayaan atau ketenaran. Mimpi yang dibuat Pak Wangsa untuk dirinya sendiri, setelah empat puluh tahun membuat mimpi untuk seluruh dunia, adalah mimpi yang begitu kecil sampai Lila harus menahan isak:

Sebuah panggung. Kosong. Dan seseorang, di mimpi itu — sosok yang belum selesai, yang tengah dirangkai Pak Wangsa dari serpih wajah-wajah — berdiri di panggung itu. Dan di bawah, di kegelapan tempat penonton duduk, ada kursi-kursi. Ratusan kursi.

Pak Wangsa sedang membuat mimpi tentang bertepuk tangan. Atau — bukan bertepuk tangan. Mimpi tentang ditepuktangani. Mimpi seorang lelaki yang menghabiskan seluruh hidupnya membuat keindahan yang membuat orang lain menangis haru, di ruangan yang gelap, tanpa nama, tanpa penonton — dan yang, untuk satu malam sebelum akhir, hanya ingin tahu bagaimana rasanya berdiri di terang, dan didengar, dan dilihat, dan diberi tahu oleh sekumpulan orang bahwa apa yang ia lakukan seumur hidupnya itu berarti.
"Pak," bisik Lila, dan Pak Wangsa terkejut, dan tangannya menyenggol mimpi setengah jadi itu, dan hampir menjatuhkannya.
"Kamu tidak lihat apa-apa," kata Pak Wangsa, cepat, dengan malu seorang yang tertangkap sedang menginginkan sesuatu.
"Bawa pulang, Pak," kata Lila.
"Tidak bisa. Kamu tahu tidak bisa. Gerbang—"

"Bawa pulang," ulang Lila. "Ini malam terakhir Bapak. Habis ini Bapak tidak akan pernah punya kesempatan lagi. Empat puluh tahun, Pak. Empat puluh tahun Bapak bikin mimpi buat semua orang. Sekali saja. Buat Bapak sendiri. Sekali."
Pak Wangsa memandang mimpi kecil di tangannya. Panggung kosong. Kursi-kursi yang menunggu. Dan ia berkata, dengan suara yang sudah ia latih selama empat puluh tahun untuk mengatakannya tanpa patah:
"Tahun depan, mungkin."
Dan Lila, yang muda, yang belum belajar menyerah dengan sopan seperti orang tua menyerah, berkata: "Bapak tidak punya tahun depan lagi, Pak. Ini dia. Tahun depannya Bapak adalah malam ini."
Aku akan berhenti sebentar di sini, sebab yang terjadi selanjutnya adalah hal yang paling penting, dan aku tidak ingin melewatinya terlalu cepat.
Pak Wangsa tidak membawa pulang mimpinya.

Ia berdiri lama di gerbang, malam terakhir itu, memegang mimpi kecil buatannya sendiri — panggung, kursi, tepuk tangan yang belum terjadi — dan pada akhirnya ia meletakkannya kembali. Bukan karena takut. Ia sudah tua; ini malam terakhirnya; tidak ada lagi pekerjaan untuk dilindungi. Ia meletakkannya karena, pada detik terakhir, ia mengerti sesuatu tentang mimpi itu yang bahkan pembuatnya sendiri tidak sadari sampai saat itu.

Mimpi tentang ditepuktangani adalah mimpi yang, kalau ia bawa pulang dan konsumsi sendiri, hanya akan terjadi di dalam kepalanya. Di dalam tidurnya. Sendirian, dalam gelap, tanpa saksi — persis seperti seluruh hidupnya. Ia akan bermimpi ditepuktangani, dan terbangun, dan tepuk tangan itu tidak akan pernah benar-benar ada, tidak lebih nyata daripada empat puluh tahun keindahan yang ia buat di ruangan tanpa jendela. Ia akan mati sebagai lelaki yang bertepuk tangan untuk dirinya sendiri di dalam mimpi.

Maka ia meletakkannya. Dan ia berkata pada Lila, "Tahun depan, mungkin," untuk terakhir kalinya — tapi kali ini ia tersenyum saat mengatakannya, senyum yang Lila tidak mengerti, senyum seseorang yang baru saja memutuskan sesuatu.
Lalu ia pulang. Dan pabrik tutup untuk liburan. Dan Pak Wangsa pensiun, dan tidak pernah kembali.
Setahun berlalu.
Dan pada malam terakhir sebelum liburan tahun berikutnya — persis setahun kemudian — sesuatu terjadi di pabrik yang belum pernah terjadi dalam sejarahnya.

Lila, yang kini bukan magang lagi melainkan perajin penuh, ditempatkan di stasiun ujung, stasiun Pak Wangsa yang lama. Dan sepanjang tahun itu, diam-diam, di menit-menit sepi akhir tiap shift, ia telah melakukan sesuatu. Ia telah mengumpulkan. Bukan bahan sisa untuk mimpi. Ia telah mengumpulkan orang.

Sebab Lila, ternyata, telah menghabiskan setahun itu melakukan hal yang tak pernah terpikir oleh Pak Wangsa, sebab Pak Wangsa terlalu sibuk membuat mimpi untuk membayangkan seseorang membuat satu untuknya. Lila telah melacak mereka. Orang-orang yang menerima mimpi buatan Pak Wangsa selama empat puluh tahun — atau setidaknya, yang bisa ia lacak dari arsip pesanan lama. Ibu yang mendengar anaknya memanggil "Bu" sekali lagi. Lelaki tua yang berdansa dengan istrinya yang tiada. Anak sakit yang berlari, yang kini sudah dewasa dan sehat dan tidak pernah tahu bahwa larinya, malam itu, adalah pemberian seorang lelaki tua di pabrik. Ratusan orang. Lila menemukan mereka, satu per satu, dan menceritakan kepada mereka tentang perajin yang membuat mimpi yang menyelamatkan malam-malam terburuk hidup mereka, dan yang tak pernah, sekali pun, ditepuktangani.
Dan pada malam terakhir tahun itu, Lila membawa mereka semua ke pabrik.

Mereka menemukan Pak Wangsa di rumah kecilnya, tua dan sendiri, di tahun pertama pensiunnya yang tanpa mimpi. Lila mengetuk pintu dan berkata cuma satu kalimat: "Pak, ada yang mau lihat Bapak kerja. Terakhir kali."
Dan Pak Wangsa, yang bingung, yang mengira ini semacam kesalahan, dibawa kembali ke pabrik pada malam ketika pabrik seharusnya kosong — dan menemukannya tidak kosong.

Ban berjalan telah dimatikan. Lampu-lampu kerja telah digeser. Dan di lantai produksi yang luas, tempat empat puluh tahun ia berdiri di stasiun paling redup, kini ada kursi-kursi. Ratusan kursi. Dan di kursi-kursi itu, duduk ratusan orang yang tak ia kenal — dan yang mengenalnya lebih dalam daripada siapa pun di dunia, sebab mereka telah tidur di dalam mimpinya, mereka telah menangis dan tertawa dan berdansa dan berlari di dalam sesuatu yang ia buat dengan tangannya sendiri, dan mereka telah bangun menjadi lebih utuh karena itu, tanpa pernah tahu nama yang harus mereka syukuri.
Sekarang mereka tahu namanya.

Lila menuntun Pak Wangsa yang gemetar ke tengah ruangan, ke satu tempat kosong di bawah lampu yang paling terang — sebuah panggung yang bukan panggung, cuma sepetak lantai pabrik yang diterangi — dan meninggalkannya berdiri di sana, sendiri, dalam cahaya, di hadapan ratusan orang yang keindahan malamnya pernah ia buat.
Untuk sesaat tidak ada yang terjadi. Pak Wangsa berdiri di terang, bingung, tua, tangannya gemetar, tidak mengerti.
Lalu seorang perempuan di barisan depan — ibu yang anaknya memanggil "Bu" — berdiri.
Dan ia mulai bertepuk tangan.

Lalu yang di sebelahnya berdiri. Lalu yang di sebelahnya lagi. Lalu seluruh ruangan, ratusan orang, bangkit dari kursi mereka, dan pabrik mimpi yang selama empat puluh tahun hanya mengenal keheningan shift malam kini dipenuhi oleh suara yang belum pernah terdengar di dalam dindingnya: suara tepuk tangan. Bergemuruh, naik, memantul dari langit-langit tinggi, mengguncang cerobong yang tidak pernah mengeluarkan asap — sampai, kata orang yang malam itu kebetulan terjaga di kota, cerobong pabrik tua di pinggir kota itu, untuk pertama kalinya dalam ingatan siapa pun, mengeluarkan cahaya yang begitu terang dan begitu banyak warnanya sampai separuh kota terbangun dan menengadah dan merasa, tanpa tahu kenapa, bahagia.

Sebab sebuah mimpi akhirnya tumpah dari cerobong itu yang bukan kerugian. Sebuah mimpi yang tidak dibuat di ban berjalan, tidak dirangkai dari bahan sisa, tidak dikemas dalam kapsul. Sebuah mimpi yang, untuk pertama kalinya dalam sejarah pabrik itu, terjadi di dunia nyata, dengan mata terbuka, di hadapan orang yang memimpikannya — dan karena itu, tidak akan pernah larut menjelang pagi seperti embun, tidak akan pernah hilang saat ia terbangun, sebab tidak ada bangun dari sesuatu yang benar-benar terjadi.

Pak Wangsa berdiri di tengah tepuk tangan itu, lelaki tua yang menghabiskan seluruh hidupnya membuat keindahan di dalam gelap, dan untuk pertama dan satu-satunya kali, ia menangis di dalam terang, dilihat, didengar, ditepuktangani — bukan di dalam mimpi buatannya sendiri yang akan larut, melainkan di dalam sesuatu yang lebih baik daripada mimpi mana pun yang pernah ia rangkai, sebab yang ini nyata, dan yang nyata, ternyata, adalah satu-satunya bahan yang tak pernah tersedia di pabrik mana pun, dan yang harus diberikan oleh orang lain, sebab kau tidak bisa membuatnya untuk dirimu sendiri.
"Tahun depan, mungkin," pernah ia katakan, setiap tahun, selama empat puluh tahun.

Ternyata tahun depan itu datang. Ternyata seseorang datang, dan membuatnya datang. Dan Pak Wangsa berdiri di dalam tepuk tangan yang tak kunjung berhenti, di dalam terang yang tak akan larut, dan mengerti — terlambat, selalu terlambat, tapi tidak terlalu terlambat — bahwa mimpi terindah yang pernah ada hubungannya dengan dirinya bukanlah yang ia buat.
Melainkan yang dibuat orang lain untuknya, ketika ia sudah berhenti percaya ia pantas menerimanya.

en.title: The Dream Factory
en.excerpt: At that factory, dreams were manufactured on the night shift, because only at night was the world quiet enough to pour them without spilling. Its name wasn't written on any signboard. It…
body: At that factory, dreams were manufactured on the night shift, because only at night was the world quiet enough to pour them without spilling.

Its name wasn't written on any signboard. It was a massive, old building on the outskirts of the city, with a chimney that never billowed smoke, but occasionally released light—streaks of nameless colors that ascended into the night sky and dissolved among the stars. And the townsfolk who happened to be awake would look up and feel, without knowing why, a yearning for something they had never possessed. That was a leak. A dream accidentally spilled from the chimney. Management always counted it as a loss.

Inside, hundreds of laborers worked along conveyor belts, assembling dreams from materials you wouldn't believe if I named them: a strand of laughter recorded from children before they learned shame, a kilo of silence dredged from the bottom of a lake, the color of the sky at five in the afternoon harvested with a fine net, fragments of the faces of the departed gathered from the memories that had discarded them. All of these were mixed, measured, stitched, then packaged into tiny capsules as clear as dew, and shipped across the globe to be slipped into the slumber of those who needed them.
And among those hundreds of laborers, at the very last station, where the light was dimmest and the conveyor belt moved the slowest, worked an old man named Mr. Wangsa.
Mr. Wangsa was the finest dream-crafter the factory had ever had, and the factory treated him exactly as the world always treats its best: by handing him the hardest and most invisible work.

He was assigned to the special dreams section. Not mass-produced dreams—not dreams of flying, dreams of falling, or dreams of taking an exam unprepared, which the machines churned out by the thousands a day. But bespoke dreams. Dreams tailored for one person, one night, one irreplaceable need. A mother who had lost her child and just wanted, one more time, to hear their voice call out "Mom." An old man in a nursing home who wished to dance once more with the wife who had been gone for fifty years. A child in a hospital who wanted, for just one night, to run.

Mr. Wangsa crafted those dreams with his own hands, one by one, with a precision and tenderness that made the younger laborers secretly come to watch him work. He could reconstruct the face of a departed loved one from fragments of memory so sparse you would think it impossible, and arrange them so flawlessly that the dreamer would wake up with wet cheeks and a heart that was, for the first time in a long time, light.
For forty years, he did this. Forty years he crafted the most beautiful dreams in the world, for people he would never meet, who would never know his name.
And in those forty years, Mr. Wangsa himself had never dreamed.
It wasn't a coincidence. It was the rule.

The factory's rule was clear, written in the handbook given to every laborer on their first day: Crafters are not permitted to consume the product. The reasoning made sense, management said. A crafter who tasted their own dreams would lose objectivity. They would start making dreams for themselves, not for the customers. They would be, as they put it, "contaminated by personal desire." So every laborer, at the end of their shift, passed through a gate that ensured they didn't slip a single capsule into their pockets. And every laborer slept, in their respective homes, a sleep that was dark and flat and empty—a dreamless sleep, for they had exhausted all the dreams of the world for others, leaving nothing for themselves.
The younger laborers complained about this. Mr. Wangsa never did. He just worked, and went home, and slept his empty sleep, and returned. Forty years.
But there was one small thing he did, something not forbidden by any handbook because no one was crazy enough to imagine anyone doing it.

Every year, on the final night before the factory closed for its annual holiday, Mr. Wangsa crafted one extra dream. Off the books. With leftover scraps scavenged from the floor—a scattered strand of laughter, a spilled edge of twilight, an unused fragment of a face. He assembled it secretly in the final minutes of his shift, a small, simple dream, a dream he made for a specific person whose needs he knew perfectly well.
The dream was for himself.

And every year, he brought it to the gate, stood there holding it, and every year, he couldn't do it. Because the gate would detect it, and he would lose his job, and this job—crafting dreams for the grieving—was the only thing that made his dreamless life feel meaningful. So every year, he placed his own handmade dream back on the table, unused, and told himself the exact same phrase:
"Next year, perhaps."

And the dream would dissolve on the table toward morning, like dew, like all things you never got the chance to use, and Mr. Wangsa would go home to his empty sleep, returning the following year to make beautiful dreams for the whole world except himself.
On his fortieth year, something changed, and the one who changed it was a cheerful young girl, whom, in a silent agreement, they began to call Riang.

Of course, that wasn't her real name. Her name was Lila. She was the youngest apprentice ever to enter the factory, stationed at the desk next to Mr. Wangsa because—the foreman said—"so she can learn from the best before the best retires." Because it was Mr. Wangsa's final year. He was old. His hands had begun to tremble, and dreams must not be crafted with trembling hands, and he knew it, and the factory knew it, and this year was his last before he was released into a retirement he would spend, like his entire life, without dreams.
Lila asked a lot of questions. It was annoying, and then it wasn't. "Mr. Wangsa, why are grief dreams made this delicate? Don't grieving people want to forget?"

"On the contrary, child," Mr. Wangsa said, his hands still working. "Grieving people don't want to forget. They are terrified of forgetting. The dreams we make aren't to make them forget what they lost. They are to make them, for one night, not lose it. A thin difference. But the difference is everything."
Lila thought about that. Then she asked the thing she shouldn't have asked, the thing that made Mr. Wangsa's hands pause for a moment above the conveyor belt.
"What is your own dream, Mr. Wangsa?"
Mr. Wangsa didn't answer that day. But Lila, who was young and therefore hadn't yet learned that some questions are best left alone, kept watching.

And toward the final night of that year—the night before the holiday, the last night Mr. Wangsa would ever work at the factory—Lila saw it. She saw the old man, in the quiet final minutes of the shift, scavenging leftover materials from the floor. A strand of laughter. An edge of twilight. A fragment of a face. She saw him assemble, with trembling hands that for once he forced to be steady, a small dream. And she saw Mr. Wangsa's face as he crafted it—a face different from the one he wore when fulfilling orders, a face more naked, younger, more filled with something Lila had no name for, but which made her own eyes burn.
Lila approached, quietly, and looked at what kind of dream the old man was making for himself, on his final night.

It wasn't a dream of glory. Not a dream of flying, not a dream of regaining his youth, not a dream of wealth or fame. The dream Mr. Wangsa made for himself, after forty years of making dreams for the whole world, was a dream so small that Lila had to choke back a sob:

A stage. Empty. And someone, in that dream—an unfinished figure Mr. Wangsa was piecing together from fragments of faces—stood on that stage. And below, in the darkness where the audience sat, there were chairs. Hundreds of chairs.

Mr. Wangsa was making a dream about applauding. Or—not applauding. A dream about being applauded. The dream of a man who spent his entire life creating beauty that made others weep with emotion, in a dark room, nameless, without an audience—and who, for one night before the end, merely wanted to know what it felt like to stand in the light, and be heard, and be seen, and be told by a crowd of people that what he had done his whole life meant something.
"Mr. Wangsa," Lila whispered, and Mr. Wangsa startled, his hand bumping the half-finished dream, nearly dropping it.
"You didn't see anything," Mr. Wangsa said, quickly, with the shame of someone caught wanting something.
"Take it home, Mr. Wangsa," Lila said.
"I can't. You know I can't. The gate—"

"Take it home," Lila repeated. "This is your last night. After this, you'll never have the chance again. Forty years, Mr. Wangsa. Forty years you made dreams for everyone. Just once. Make one for yourself. Just once."
Mr. Wangsa looked at the small dream in his hands. The empty stage. The waiting chairs. And he said, with the voice he had trained for forty years to say it without breaking:
"Next year, perhaps."
And Lila, who was young, who hadn't yet learned to surrender politely the way the old surrender, said: "You don't have a next year anymore, Mr. Wangsa. This is it. Your next year is tonight."
I will pause for a moment here, because what happened next is the most important part, and I don't want to gloss over it too quickly.
Mr. Wangsa did not take his dream home.

He stood for a long time at the gate, that final night, holding the small dream of his own making—the stage, the chairs, the applause that hadn't yet happened—and in the end, he put it back. Not out of fear. He was old; this was his last night; there was no longer a job to protect. He put it down because, at the very last second, he understood something about that dream that even its maker hadn't realized until that moment.

A dream about being applauded was a dream that, if he took it home and consumed it himself, would only happen inside his head. Inside his sleep. Alone, in the dark, without witnesses—exactly like his entire life. He would dream of being applauded, and wake up, and that applause would never truly exist, no more real than the forty years of beauty he had crafted in a windowless room. He would die as a man applauding himself in a dream.

So he put it down. And he said to Lila, "Next year, perhaps," for the very last time—but this time he smiled as he said it, a smile Lila didn't understand, the smile of someone who had just decided something.
Then he went home. And the factory closed for the holidays. And Mr. Wangsa retired, and never returned.
A year passed.
And on the final night before the holiday the following year—exactly a year later—something happened in the factory that had never happened in its history.

Lila, who was now no longer an apprentice but a full crafter, was stationed at the end desk, Mr. Wangsa's old station. And throughout that year, secretly, in the quiet final minutes of every shift, she had been doing something. She had been collecting. Not leftover materials for a dream. She had been collecting people.

Because Lila, as it turned out, had spent that year doing the one thing Mr. Wangsa had never thought of, because Mr. Wangsa was too busy making dreams to imagine someone making one for him. Lila had tracked them down. The people who had received Mr. Wangsa's handmade dreams over the course of forty years—or at least, the ones she could trace from the old order archives. The mother who heard her child call "Mom" one more time. The old man who danced with his late wife. The sick child who ran, who was now grown and healthy and never knew that his sprint, that night, was the gift of an old man in a factory. Hundreds of people. Lila found them, one by one, and told them about the crafter who made the dreams that saved the worst nights of their lives, and who had never, not once, been applauded.
And on the final night of that year, Lila brought them all to the factory.

They found Mr. Wangsa in his small house, old and alone, in his first year of dreamless retirement. Lila knocked on the door and said only one sentence: "Mr. Wangsa, there are people who want to see you work. One last time."
And Mr. Wangsa, confused, thinking this was some sort of mistake, was brought back to the factory on the night when it was supposed to be empty—and found it wasn't.

The conveyor belts had been turned off. The work lamps had been pushed aside. And on the vast production floor, where he had stood for forty years at the dimmest station, there were now chairs. Hundreds of chairs. And in those chairs sat hundreds of people he didn't know—and who knew him more intimately than anyone else in the world, because they had slept inside his dreams, they had wept and laughed and danced and run inside something he had made with his own hands, and they had woken up more whole because of it, without ever knowing the name they should thank.
Now they knew his name.

Lila led the trembling Mr. Wangsa to the center of the room, to a single empty space beneath the brightest lamp—a stage that wasn't a stage, just a square of illuminated factory floor—and left him standing there, alone, in the light, facing hundreds of people whose beautiful nights he had once forged.
For a moment, nothing happened. Mr. Wangsa stood in the light, confused, old, his hands trembling, uncomprehending.
Then a woman in the front row—the mother whose child called "Mom"—stood up.
And she began to clap.

Then the person next to her stood. Then the one next to them. Then the entire room, hundreds of people, rose from their chairs, and the dream factory that for forty years had only known the silence of the night shift was now filled with a sound never before heard within its walls: the sound of applause. Thunderous, rising, echoing off the high ceiling, shaking the chimney that never billowed smoke—until, said the townsfolk who happened to be awake that night, the old factory's chimney on the outskirts of the city, for the first time in anyone's memory, released a light so bright and so fiercely colorful that half the city woke up and looked up and felt, without knowing why, happy.

Because a dream finally spilled from that chimney that wasn't a loss. A dream that wasn't made on a conveyor belt, wasn't assembled from scraps, wasn't packaged in a capsule. A dream that, for the first time in the factory's history, happened in the real world, with open eyes, in front of the person who dreamed it—and because of that, would never dissolve toward morning like dew, would never vanish when he woke up, because there is no waking up from something that truly happened.

Mr. Wangsa stood amidst the applause, an old man who spent his entire life crafting beauty in the dark, and for the first and only time, he wept in the light, seen, heard, applauded—not inside his own dissolving dream, but inside something far better than any dream he had ever woven, because this one was real, and the real, as it turns out, is the only material never in stock at any factory, and which must be given by others, because you cannot make it for yourself.
"Next year, perhaps," he had said, every year, for forty years.

It turned out that next year had come. It turned out someone had come, and made it arrive. And Mr. Wangsa stood within the applause that wouldn't end, within the light that wouldn't dissolve, and understood—late, always late, but not too late—that the most beautiful dream that ever had anything to do with him wasn't the one he made.
But the one someone else made for him, just when he had stopped believing he deserved it.

title: The Moon Behind My Eyes
excerpt: I kept the glass perfectly clean, believing that clarity would make it easier for the light to find me. I memorized the horizon, certain that devotion was a currency the night would…
body:
I kept the glass perfectly clean,
believing that clarity would make it easier for the light to find me.
I memorized the horizon,
certain that devotion was a currency the night would eventually accept.

The stars arrived as they always do—punctual and indifferent.
But the silver I waited for remained a rumor.
I learned then, that the sky does not negotiate with our longing.

Waiting slowly turned from a virtue into a haunting.
It became a quiet argument between my tired eyes and an empty yard.
So, I drew the curtains.
Not in anger, but in a profound surrender.

I turned my back to the glass.
I stopped asking the dark to be anything other than dark.
And in the sudden quiet of letting go, I finally closed my eyes.

There it was.
Spilling through the cracks of my own thoughts,
a pale, steady glow that didn't need a sky to exist.
Untethered to the orbit of the world.

It turns out, the universe was never keeping the moon from me.
I was just looking through the wrong window.

title: The Bird and Its Shadow
excerpt: One night, I slipped into the granary. Getting inside wasn't all that difficult, I thought at the time. The door was left slightly ajar, but I remained on guard. There is one thing that…
body: One night, I slipped into the granary. Getting inside wasn't all that difficult, I thought at the time. The door was left slightly ajar, but I remained on guard. There is one thing that separates me from the rest of the flock: I believe in my own cunning. A confidence born from how perfectly I memorize the routines, the routes, and the sheer stupidity on the face of the owner. Yes, he is my archenemy, but he also taught me one crucial thing. Stupidity is far more terrifying than death itself, and I harbor a deep, searing hatred for that stupidity.

But a brief scent of rat reached my nose from behind the granary door. The smell seemed to dance and hover right on the border of fresh and damp air. I glanced left, then right. Vigilant. This could easily be a trap. Suddenly, I remembered something and smiled. *You think that is all I am capable of? Look at these wings. No matter how clever you are, even in death, you will never taste this kind of freedom*. Proudly, I flapped my pitch-black wings. You might chase us away or kill us, but we will celebrate your demise with the greatest dance you have ever seen.

A shadow squeaked behind the door, catching my eye. Instantly, I beat my wings and glided down into the granary. With my tongue hanging out, I descended, sweeping across the floor. *Where might you be, you plump little rat?* From the corner of my eye, I spotted it—an incredibly fat, delectable rat. It looked exhausted, lugging around several long stalks of rice. Scurrying here and there, completely oblivious to the watcher of the night.

I landed right in front of it, leaning in slightly, puffing out my chest. "O, plump rat," I said softly, making it sound as menacing as possible. "Perhaps it is time you fill the belly of this grand creature."

The rat froze, blinking its tiny, sunflower-seed eyes. Its fur stood on end, its breathing ragged. Amidst the dim moonlight filtering through the gaps of the granary, a shadow formed, seemingly mimicking my every move. The silhouette mirrored me right from behind. Yet, it appeared larger, more grandiose; the flap of its wings looked infinitely more majestic, and its beak seemed far more formidable.

I approached it slowly, wearing a sharp grin, saliva pooling in my mouth. I let out the most commanding caw I could muster. The rat panicked, then fell dead silent. It dropped the rice stalks it had been carrying and lowered itself to the ground. "O, great and mighty creature. Truly, there is no goodness in this humble servant. But please, allow me to offer my praise: that shadow of yours just now... ah, how magnificent it is." It cast a brief glance behind me. "Unlike this body of yours that still must hunt. Perhaps, My Lord, you no longer need to flap your wings—simply let that shadow fly, and the world will fall to its knees."

Absorbing the rat's words, I tried to think. If my shadow is more magnificent than I am, then I am no longer needed in the lexicon of the dark; my time might have already perished within that majestic flap. I felt a pang of envy, and in that moment, I cawed fiercely. "Very well, you may go." I tilted my head upward, holding it higher than the chest that ought to be bowing. "Perhaps that is simply your path, until your body expands to such a degree," I continued with a smile.

And so, the rat backed away slowly. Silent without a word, leaving without a sound. Until it was just the two of us. Slowly, I turned and stared at the shadow. I bowed, then flapped both of my wings. I flew away, but the shadow did not follow.
Perhaps, it was already higher than me.

title: Paid in Full
excerpt: Her gaze burned, her breaths came in jagged gasps, and her face was violently flushed, as if her blood were boiling just beneath the skin. Dewi no longer felt like "Dewi" to me. The gleam…
body: Her gaze burned, her breaths came in jagged gasps, and her face was violently flushed, as if her blood were boiling just beneath the skin. Dewi no longer felt like "Dewi" to me. The gleam in her eyes that usually brought such peace had morphed into an uncontrollable flash of chaos. For a fleeting moment, I pitied her; I pitied the fragility of a soul so easily tossed by the waves—as if the mere whisper of the tide could rewrite her entire fate.

Yet, I did not falter. I stood tall and rigid, holding her gaze while my hands tightly gripped a broom. Offering a guiding hand, upholding a single promise that felt almost taboo: that I would never walk away from you, even if I had to force the pain to taste like honey.

The red in her face slowly faded, replaced by tears welling at the brims of her eyes. I was right there beside her as she opened the torn letter, a thing shredded by anger and disappointment. It surely looks strange—a corporate executive left alone with someone like me. But this is my calling; laying claim to a love I could never possibly ask for out loud. At the very least, I can fulfill my obligation as your guardian, and the simple fact that you afford me your attention is already more than enough.

And so, I offered her a respectful bow, then turned and walked out the door—leaving her space to resolve the emotions she had yet to settle. I will return to my sweeping, clearing away the dirt for her sake. But it doesn't matter. I am content with this.
As long as this feeling is paid in full, I am willing.

title: Trillions of Seconds
excerpt: I am that tiny speck, adrift within the chaos of the cosmos. Swimming through an ocean of inevitabilities, where the crashing waves whisper ceaseless curses, begging me to surrender my…
body:
I am that tiny speck,
adrift within the chaos of the cosmos.
Swimming through an ocean of inevitabilities,
where the crashing waves whisper ceaseless curses,
begging me to surrender my hope.

But no, I never pay them mind.
I harbor only a single wish:
to wash ashore on the coast of answers and longing.
You might be confused by all this rambling,
but trust me, I am just as bewildered as you are—
wondering why I seem to be the only one thinking.

I ask you to hold on just a little longer,
to wait for me,
hoping that God might steer my current toward you.
And please understand,
you are not who you think you are.

Trillions of seconds have slipped away,
spent on nothing but thought.
It seems this vessel was never designed
to truly comprehend a thing.

Once, amidst the hollow echoes of the waves,
I encountered an entity just like me.
It was merely a passing glance.
He drew a deep, heavy sigh—perhaps resigned to the tide.
I was the one who broke the silence:
*"How much do you understand yourself?"*

Briefly, from the fading distance, he called back:
*"I am you. That is enough."*
And just like that, he drifted past,
carried away by the current.

I did not quite grasp his words.
I spent who knows how long trying to forge a conclusion.
Until a sudden rush of shame washed over me.
And so, once again,
I stopped thinking.

title: The Room
excerpt: I am a room of four walls, stripped of a door. I am not particularly skilled at organizing myself, so much so that everything inside me is cluttered, perhaps entirely too full. It feels so…
body: I am a room of four walls, stripped of a door. I am not particularly skilled at organizing myself, so much so that everything inside me is cluttered, perhaps entirely too full. It feels so suffocating when I recall the belongings that almost drown me in my own space, and it is truly terrifying. I am not extraordinarily large, nor am I that small. I suppose my size is just right, even if it forces all my possessions to press tightly against one another. But I believe I am merely a compelled inevitability, or perhaps I am simply resigned to exist. Because I am certain that one day I will find something capable of arranging the things inside me—after all, I have no hands to sort them out myself.

There was a time when I was quite sure that what I stored would be of use, and I placed my faith in those belongings. So, I painted myself with the help of a wondrous brush that had suddenly slipped into my being—I don't even know since when. The paint I used was not thick; it felt light and held a sweet hue at first. It covered me gently, almost imperceptible as it sealed the pores of my concrete.

The brush continued painting the exact same color almost every day, until my shade grew richer and vividly bright. And hey, it wasn't bad. I liked it, and it was a pleasant feeling. Then, I asked a different, slightly smaller brush to trace a tiny picture over the color I already deemed beautiful, without the large brush knowing. I remember the small brush never even had the chance to draw anything, because I grew afraid. Afraid that what I did would hurt the large brush. So, I cast the smaller one away into the farthest corner.

Until one day, the large brush stopped painting me. By then, the color had become so heavy it no longer radiated beauty, so I let it rest for a while. I shifted my request; I no longer asked it to paint, but instead asked it to help me rearrange my heavy-looking furniture. It didn't matter if we took it slow, as long as the goal was clear: a neat and beautiful room.

Yes, you probably know the answer. The work did not go smoothly. Instead, the brush ruined and shattered the furniture. So I asked it to stop, with a smile and with patience, of course. Because I was fully aware that I was the one at fault this time. I still cared for that brush deeply.

Occasionally, I asked it to paint again with a different, softer color. But this time it refused, turning its face away from me in indifference. I was heartbroken and begged it to return. At that point, I didn't care if it wanted to paint again or not; I just loved it too much. Sometimes it felt close, yet other times it pulled further away than ever before. And the sinking feeling grew—this brush was deeply disappointed in me. So I let it go, letting it slip away through the cracks of my concrete walls, leaving the furniture lying in ruins.

One day, I tried forcing myself to manage the things that overwhelmed me. Because these things could not leave—I had no door to let them out. So, I forced it. I violently shook myself to one side, until all my belongings piled against a single wall. Eventually, the wall couldn't withstand the crushing weight, and it just shattered wide open. And heavens, it hurt so much. Trust me on that. Afterward, I threw almost everything out, save for two things: a small book and a desk.

If you could only imagine the piercing cold that seeped deep into my core through that gaping hole, you'd know there is no remedy that could ever cure it. I fully realized that nothing could ever make me whole again. I harbored a trace of regret—why didn't I make the brush stay in my room? But let regret remain regret; perhaps this is a penance I am bound to pay.

It is true now, my room is no longer full and suffocating. Nothing crowds me anymore, yet somehow it still feels so constricted and profoundly empty. Likewise, the paint on my walls grows dull and begins to peel. And the hole only draws in more of that unpleasant, bitter chill.

Not long after, wrapped in that sting, ache, and emptiness, a wondrous hammer and nail appeared. They arrived with kindness and a smile. Since I needed something to help me board up that empty void, I allowed them into my room.

Deftly, it brought out a plank of wood and struck it with a tiny nail. Just one nail, and the hole was completely sealed. Though it is no longer cold, this wood never quite makes me feel whole again. But I remain grateful for its presence.

This wondrous hammer is incredibly swift, moving with precision and skill. It manages to build beautiful, exquisite furniture, making me feel slightly present amidst the void. Yet, despite the hammer's brilliance, it can never paint my walls beautiful again. And the nail is forever bound to that hammer. That nail feels like a thorn embedded within my sturdy walls. And I am terrified that I will never be able to truly accept its presence.

title: Thought Log 003: The Resonance of Silence
excerpt: Is there a space in this world that truly accepts my silence? To observe the atmosphere within silence is to find a medium where the soul softly resonates amidst the monotony of the world.…
body: Is there a space in this world that truly accepts my silence?

To observe the atmosphere within silence is to find a medium where the soul softly resonates amidst the monotony of the world. The sheer madness of life’s tragedies sometimes creeps in little by little, happening in the blink of an eye before we even have the chance to dodge it. In the middle of that crossfire, silence becomes a concrete solution when you are already driven too mad by the process. I see silence as a form of remembrance—a monument to the fleeting mementos of life that pass by like the rustling wind.

We don't live merely for the sake of social formalities; making sense of it all is an absolute necessity if we are to understand our own essence as sentient human beings. We need to map out that space in the corner of our minds. Picture it as the very last document on a stacked shelf. It’s a document you find at the very end of a story, stamped with a bold, capitalized title, practically begging you to open it just once and weep alongside it. That document doesn't even need to be filled with words; an empty page is enough. You don't need to search for its meaning; just let yourself fill it with a story steeped in your own sweat and tears. And once you no longer need it, put it back at the bottom of the pile and smile. Smile because you have been strong enough to endure this ephemeral life.

You don’t have to wait for the world to hand you that narrow space, that empty document. Let yourself construct that world within your own mind. By doing so, even in the absolute center of the world's deafening noise and chaos, you can still be present. You can still hold a moment of silence with the one entity that truly needs to be spoken to: yourself.

I feel that silence is an inevitability for every human being; we are born into it. You and I are already intimately familiar with silence. Even before we were born, there was the inevitability of quiet. The silent sanctuary of the womb was exactly where you were meant to be, just as the quiet of the grave is where you will inevitably end up. I don't mean to sound like I'm preaching, but silence is the answer to all of your problems. Your brain and your soul will scream if you don't allow them to stop and rest, even for just a fraction of a second. Silence is a liberating force that empowers you to shatter the world. You don't need to seek escapism through other mediums. Just you, and only you. The world possesses a thousand and one ways to keep you busy, but you hold millions of ways to just pause, simply by talking to yourself. You have to paint that canvas on your own; don't let the world move the brush for you. You just need to speak inward.

There was a time when I felt the constant need to validate every single one of my actions to others, whether through a WhatsApp status or an Instagram note. It was as if I desperately wanted to be reassured about things that were, relatively speaking, completely unimportant. I spoke to the world, expecting a reply, even when I already knew the answers myself. Looking back, I'm baffled by that state of mind. Why did the world seem to demand that I broadcast my story? Aren't we supposed to be the observers, not the bards? The world should be guiding us, not tearing our characters apart; the world is the one that should be reciting the poetry. Yet, it feels as though the world leaves no room for us to just sit in silence without expecting something in return. A system like that is genuinely sickening. You don't need to seek validation through those external "windows." Can't you see? There is a door right inside your heart. Just knock on it, and you'll realize that this massive, intimidating world is nothing but a speck of dust compared to the universe inside you.

This anomaly is truly fascinating—a paradox of the soul, I'd call it. We aren't obligated to speak, yet you can uncover millions of answers purely through silence. I’ve found that the incessant chirping of the world gets distorted in the fog of sanity (and yes, I consider talking to oneself a true form of sanity). Your inner self is incredibly vast, and yet you let the world lull you into caring only about external achievements. What a profound irony. You talk to everyone else, to every other medium, but never to yourself. Silence is not something you need to fear; in fact, it speaks to you softly, in its own way. It weeps with you. It smiles at your triumphs.

I used to be trapped in that phase, right when I first started trying to be a "human" in my early college days. Being naturally quiet, I yearned so deeply for companionship; I just wanted to be heard, to be seen in that moment. But that desperate search only brought consecutive waves of sadness. Not a single person paid any mind. I was dominated only by the harsh reprimand of disappointment, a pursuit that led me nowhere.

But ultimately, I discovered the true essence of silence on a particular night in the middle of my first semester. It was as if my heart, shattered by loneliness, dragged me into a confrontation with myself. We talked—slowly at first, and then full of anger. I created a space for "me" and "myself" to converse, to draft scenarios together. In that exact moment, I realized just how crucial it is to talk to yourself. The echoes resonated, pulsating with a self-awareness that slowly began to take shape. As I reflected on what went wrong with my approach to making friends, a sudden rush of tears fell—tears of longing for this very feeling of internal connection. It fortified me. It forced me to introspect and truly look at my own personality. In the end, the most reliable friend we will ever have is ourselves.

Throughout this journey of life, the world actually never hid that silent space from you. You were just being too rigid with yourself. The world is perfectly capable of listening gently to your story without you ever having to raise your voice. Just find everything you need within yourself, and whisper it to the world: "*I found the answer*."

Silence and existence are inherently bound to one another; the presence of one demands the other. Silence arrives when you contemplate your existence in this world, and your existence truly begins when silence becomes a familiar comfort as your soul is breathed into your body. Your existence craves that solitary space, and allowing it to reflect will make it appreciate every single element that was ever brought into this world.
We don’t actually need to speak to be heard. That space already exists.
Just knock on the door.

title: Thought Log 002: The Dissonant Shell
excerpt: Intrinsically, our social roles are reflections of who we are. I understand that some of these roles might get distorted through various mediums—through doctrines, beliefs, and ideas…
body: Intrinsically, our social roles are reflections of who we are. I understand that some of these roles might get distorted through various mediums—through doctrines, beliefs, and ideas broadcasted from countless external sources. But ultimately, they are all still manifestations of our own choices as sentient, sensitive individuals. No matter how absurd we might become within those social constraints, it remains a representation of our unique individuality.
But what happens when those roles are completely stripped away?

Without them, all individual representations in this world cease to represent us. Everything becomes an empty, meaningless shell. Social roles are, in a way, substantive to the very fabric of life itself. If you remove them, what is left behind? Nothing but a name and bare existence. Ideas and thoughts would scatter, and principles would spill across an unsupported floor. What could you possibly hold onto in the face of such a forceful detachment? Perhaps nothing more than a dissonant, meaningless song.
This leads me to wonder: does my current life actually reflect the values I truly believe in?

I can't be entirely sure. Sometimes, I still doubt the presence and purpose of every object and being in this world. Nothing truly convinces me of an absolute truth, nor of what constitutes ultimate evil. Everything feels entirely too representative, impossible to use as a true metric for life itself. Every single event is merely a cause-and-effect born from the past, and we cannot judge something we never truly comprehended in the first place.

Which leads to how humanity eventually constructed a mechanism: separating the cause from the effect in order to judge what is 'true.' Because if they aren't separated, every related concept and truth eventually becomes a chaotic blur, leaving nothing able to be evaluated. Crimes wouldn't be judged because we wouldn't know the root cause, and virtues wouldn't be praised because we wouldn't understand the reasoning. Isn't that an inherently ironic mechanism? We slice reality into pieces just so we can make sense of it.

So, if I ask myself whether my life reflects the values I believe in... the truth is, those values no longer hold a substantive weight in my life. My principle right now is simply to walk through this fleeting flicker of time, even while doubting everything I see. Someday, I will understand the meaning of my life without having to cling to values that remain so inherently ambiguous.
And if no one is there to witness my life, would I still want to live it this way?

Yes. As I realized earlier, I will keep living my life even if there are no binding values left holding me down. The witness to my life isn't anyone else; it is myself. My footprints will eventually fade away, regardless of whether someone walks beside me or not. But there is one thing I must remember: even when those footprints are no longer visible, the process of making them remains etched deep within my soul.

title: Thought Log 001: The Cartesian Void
excerpt: The ambiguity of belief terrifies me; its presence seems to dictate my soul, forcing me to constantly question this fragile illusion of authenticity. It’s undeniable how reality and…
body: The ambiguity of belief terrifies me; its presence seems to dictate my soul, forcing me to constantly question this fragile illusion of authenticity. It’s undeniable how reality and falsehood blur together into a chaotic synergy—nothing in this world feels truly "absolute." Everything feels contaminated by the contradiction of its own original value, coming off as fake compared to the very concept of truth.

So, I don't even know how to describe myself anymore, and I find myself constantly asking: why do I feel so unlike myself? Why do I lose my composure over doubts that only exist in my own head? I think I finally understand what Descartes meant—losing our sense of self to an illusion of belief leaves us entirely unmoored. We search for a true authenticity that doesn't exist anywhere, and we humans—even I—end up questioning our own reality. That feeling of lost existence crystallizes deep within our souls.

But one thing is certain: beneath this paralyzing doubt about ourselves, something stirs deep within. Morality. It’s an abstract concept to map out, more like a feeling that organically grows. It’s a boundary that defines our true nature when we question things; when we doubt and act out of character, that barrier is there. Morality is pure and untouchable. Or, to put it bluntly, our mind is who we truly are, and morality is merely the vessel. The mind itself doesn't actually doubt; it just gets distorted—warped by ego, judgment, and all that noise. Argh, I don't know. I feel like I'm just rambling now. Sorry.
But maybe that rambling points to a bigger question. If nothing is absolute, and if there were no God, would my life still hold any meaning?

Honestly, even in the absence of a deity, I believe humanity would inevitably invent one of their own, even through the most abstract concepts imaginable. Why? Because nothing in this world exists without a purpose. No matter how confidently someone declares, "I have no purpose in life," the very words they spit out become a purpose in themselves. You make it your purpose to have no purpose. Hahaha.

What I mean is, the concept of "purpose" is born to fill a tiny void in the human heart. It assumes this emptiness doesn't exist without a reason. We have an innate need to hunt for that missing puzzle piece through whatever medium we can find, and often, God becomes that bridge. For the religious, God is the ultimate endpoint; meeting the creator is what gives life weight. So, even if you strip away religion, you'll inevitably end up deifying some other concept just to fill that space, won't you?
Knowing that—knowing we are all just desperate to fill the void and find meaning amidst the chaos—forces me to look inward again. Am I living with true integrity toward myself?

For now, I think so. I want to live for me. I want to give my integrity the breathing room it needs to grow. If I’m being honest, I lost that integrity for a while. I was deeply confused, completely losing my grip on the essence and direction of my own life. But eventually, I caught myself. Even if I haven't figured it out completely just yet, I am trying. I'm trying to live by simply doing what I actually love, holding onto the things that truly hold value to me.
